Nurse -> Juniper Ridge Hospice, this is Lena.
Caller -> Hi, Lena. This is Desmond. I'm calling about my mom. Hazel Brightwater.
Nurse -> Hi, Desmond. Her date of birth?
Caller -> February twelfth, nineteen thirty six.
Nurse -> And I have six one five, five five five, zero one six six for you.
Caller -> Yeah, that's my cell.
Nurse -> What's going on with your mom?
Caller -> Her mouth is so dry. Really dry. And her lips are cracked. It's been two days.
Caller -> And honestly, this heat is killing her. It's ninety five outside and the air conditioner in her room is barely working.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she drinking?
Caller -> Just sips. A few spoonfuls of applesauce today. That's about it.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she seem to be in pain?
Caller -> No. She's resting. She's comfortable, I think. No faces or anything.
Nurse -> Okay, good. Here's what helps. A mouth swab, the pink sponge, dipped in water, every two hours. Gently wipe the inside of her cheeks and her tongue.
Caller -> Every two hours. Okay.
Nurse -> And lip balm, a good one, without a strong scent. Ice chips, if she can swallow them. And a humidifier in the room, if you have one.
Caller -> I don't think we have any swabs left. Or lip balm.
Nurse -> I'll add both to your next delivery. That's coming Thursday.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. I'll use a washcloth until then.
Nurse -> That works. If you see white patches in her mouth, or sores, or bleeding, or she can't swallow, call us.
Caller -> White patches, sores, bleeding. Okay.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thanks, Lena.

Nurse -> Northstar Home Health, this is Priscilla.
Caller -> Hi. This is Terrence Obuya. I'm a patient.
Nurse -> Hi, Terrence. Your date of birth?
Caller -> June eighth, nineteen sixty nine.
Nurse -> And I have five one two, five five five, zero one six seven.
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> What's going on?
Caller -> My incision is itchy. On my knee, the right one. It's been two days.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there any redness, or any drainage?
Caller -> No. It looks good. No redness, no drainage.
Nurse -> Any fever?
Caller -> No. I took it this morning. Ninety eight point four.
Nurse -> That's reassuring. Itching around a healing incision is really common. It usually means the skin is healing.
Caller -> Oh good. I was worried.
Nurse -> Try not to scratch it. If it bothers you, tap it or press lightly. Keep the area clean and dry, and wear loose clothes over it.
Caller -> Okay. Tap, not scratch. Got it.
Nurse -> Your nurse is scheduled to see you Monday morning. She'll look at it then.
Caller -> Monday. Okay.
Nurse -> If you see redness, swelling, or warmth, or any drainage, or you get a fever of one hundred point four or higher, call us.
Caller -> I will.
Nurse -> How's the knee feeling otherwise? Are you doing your exercises?
Caller -> Yes. Twice a day. It's stiff in the morning but it loosens up. I can bend it almost to ninety degrees now.
Nurse -> That's great progress for two weeks. Keep it up, and keep the ice on afterwards.
Caller -> I will. My wife helps me with the ice packs.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you.

Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Ana.
Caller -> Hi, Ana. It's Paolo. I'm calling about my son, Nico. N I C O. Marchetti.
Nurse -> Hi, Paolo. Nico's date of birth?
Caller -> April third, twenty nineteen.
Nurse -> And I have three four seven, five five five, zero one eight five for you.
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on?
Caller -> It's his trach. He has a lot more secretions. For the last two days.
Caller -> I'm suctioning him about every two hours now. Before, it was every four.
Nurse -> Okay. What color are the secretions?
Caller -> Clear. Thin and clear. Not yellow, not green.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> No. I took it a few minutes ago. Ninety eight point six.
Nurse -> Okay, good. And how's his breathing? Is he working hard to breathe?
Caller -> No, no. His breathing is easy. His color is good. He's playing with his trains right now. He's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he coughing?
Caller -> A little. A mild cough. Just when the secretions build up.
Nurse -> Okay. That all sounds reassuring. Clear secretions, no fever, and breathing easily. Sometimes the secretions go up when the air is dry, or when he's coming down with a cold.
Caller -> He did have the sniffles on Sunday. Maybe that's it.
Nurse -> It could be. Is his humidifier working?
Caller -> I think so. The heated one, the one that attaches to the trach. Let me look. Yes. It's on. The water is low, though. I'll refill it.
Nurse -> Good idea. Keep it filled. And give him extra fluids, as much as he'll take.
Caller -> He loves juice. I'll give him some.
Nurse -> Perfect. Suction him as needed, whenever he sounds wet or coughs. And write down the color and amount, so we can see if it changes.
Caller -> I'll keep notes. Okay.
Nurse -> I'd like our respiratory therapist to see him tomorrow, just to check everything. Humidification, the trach tube, and his secretions.
Caller -> That would be great. What time?
Nurse -> Tomorrow afternoon. She'll call you before she comes.
Caller -> Okay. Tomorrow afternoon. I'm home all day.
Nurse -> Now, you mentioned you're running low on something?
Caller -> Oh, yes. Suction catheters. I have about six left. At this rate, that's just a couple of days.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me order those now. What size does he use?
Caller -> Ten French. Same as always.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll put in an order for ten French catheters. They should come tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, use a fresh catheter each time, as usual. If you run short before they come, call me and I'll see about getting a few from the on-call stock.
Caller -> I will. That's good to know.
Nurse -> If his secretions turn yellow or green, or have blood, or he gets a fever, or he's working harder to breathe, call us. And if he turns blue, or the tube is blocked and you can't clear it, call nine one one.
Caller -> Yellow, green, blood, fever, harder breathing. And nine one one if blue or blocked. I know the drill.
Nurse -> You do. You're a pro.
Caller -> It's been four years. I guess I'd better be.
Nurse -> And how are the nights? Is the pulse oximeter on while he sleeps?
Caller -> Yes. Every night. It reads ninety seven, ninety eight. No alarms in the last few days, thankfully.
Nurse -> That's great. Keep it on. And who's covering overnight?
Caller -> My wife and I take turns. We alternate nights. It's tiring, but we manage.
Nurse -> You're both amazing. Tell your wife I said so.
Caller -> I will. She'll appreciate that. She always says you're her favorite.
Nurse -> Ha. Mutual. How's Nico doing at school? Is he going in person?
Caller -> He's going three days a week. His teacher is amazing. She learned to suction him, and she has a nurse in the classroom too.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Is he enjoying it?
Caller -> He loves it. He has a best friend, Marcus. They sit together and build things. The two of them are always making trains out of blocks.
Nurse -> Ha. That's so sweet. Does he have a favorite?
Caller -> The big blue one, Thomas. He sleeps with him at night. Thomas goes everywhere.
Nurse -> Perfect. Well, tell him I said hello.
Caller -> I will. He'll want to say hi himself, he always asks for you.
Nurse -> Ha. Put him on.
Caller -> Hang on. Nico, say hi to Ana. He's shaking his head. He's shy today.
Nurse -> That's okay. Hello, Nico. I'll see you soon.
Caller -> He waved. Okay. Thank you, Ana.
Caller -> Oh, before I go. His sister has a recital Saturday and he wants to go. Is that okay with the secretions?
Nurse -> It should be fine if he's well and you bring the suction machine and supplies. Sit near the back so you can step out.
Caller -> That's the plan. We'll bring the whole kit.
Nurse -> Perfect. Take care, Paolo.

Nurse -> Maple Lane Home Care, this is Beth.
Caller -> Hi, this is Kyle from the call center. I have a daughter on the line for a patient. The patient is Lorena Quintero. Q U I N T E R O.
Nurse -> Okay, Kyle. Go ahead and transfer.
Caller -> Okay. Here she comes.
Caller -> Hello? Hi. This is Camila. I'm her daughter.
Nurse -> Hi, Camila. What's your mother's date of birth?
Caller -> September thirtieth, nineteen fifty one.
Nurse -> And your number, in case we get cut off?
Caller -> Seven eight six, five five five, zero one six eight.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on?
Caller -> So my mom is up two pounds. Since yesterday. She weighs herself every morning, like the nurse told her.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she short of breath?
Caller -> No. No, she's breathing fine. She's sitting up in her chair, eating a banana.
Nurse -> Okay. Any swelling?
Caller -> A little in her ankles. A little more than usual.
Nurse -> Okay. What did she eat yesterday?
Caller -> We had a family dinner. She had soup, and ham. The ham was salty. I told her.
Nurse -> That might be part of it. Okay. For today, low salt meals. No canned soup or deli meat. And she can have her fluids as her doctor allows.
Caller -> Okay. No soup, no ham. I'll make her oatmeal and an egg.
Nurse -> And keep weighing every morning, after she uses the bathroom and before she eats. Write it down.
Caller -> She does that already. I'll check the paper.
Nurse -> If she gains three pounds in a day, or five in a week, or the swelling gets worse, or she's short of breath, call us. And if she can't catch her breath, nine one one.
Caller -> Three in a day, five in a week. Okay.
Nurse -> I'll call tomorrow morning to see her weight.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you, Beth.

transcript:
Nurse -> Juniper Ridge Hospice, this is Lena.
Caller -> Hi, Lena. This is Helen Ostrowski. I'm calling about my husband, Walter.
Nurse -> Hi, Helen. Walter's date of birth?
Caller -> June fifteenth, nineteen forty.
Nurse -> And I have five one three, five five five, zero one nine oh for you.
Caller -> Yes, that's the house phone. Everybody uses it.
Nurse -> How is Walter doing?
Caller -> He's sleeping a lot. A whole lot. About twenty hours a day, I'd say, now. For about five days.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he wake up at all?
Caller -> A little. For a few minutes. He'll open his eyes, say a word or two. Mostly he sleeps.
Nurse -> Okay. And is he eating or drinking?
Caller -> Hardly anything. A few sips of water. And two spoonfuls of ice cream today. That's all.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he in pain?
Caller -> I don't think so. He's not grimacing, he's not moaning. He looks peaceful.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good.
Caller -> Oh, hold on. Danny! Danny, can you take the kids outside? Grandpa is sleeping. Thank you, honey. Sorry, Lena. That's my grandson. They're all here.
Nurse -> Oh, that's lovely. How many are there?
Caller -> Our three children, and five grandchildren, and a couple of spouses. It's a full house. I've been cooking for an army.
Nurse -> Ha. It sounds wonderful. And exhausting.
Caller -> Both. Yes. I'm tired, I'll admit it. But it means so much that they're here.
Nurse -> Helen, has there been any change in his breathing? Long pauses, or noisy breathing?
Caller -> Sometimes there are pauses. He'll stop for a few seconds, and then take a big breath. It scares the kids.
Nurse -> That's called Cheyne Stokes breathing. It's a common pattern near the end of life. It usually isn't uncomfortable for him, though it can be hard for the family to watch.
Caller -> That's what the other nurse said. It still scares me every time.
Nurse -> Of course it does. If it helps, you can tell the kids it's his body's way of settling down.
Caller -> I'll tell them. My youngest, Katie, is only seven. She keeps asking if Grandpa is cold.
Nurse -> A soft blanket is fine, if his hands feel cool. Hands and feet often feel cool near the end. It's circulation, not discomfort.
Caller -> I'll get the quilt his mother made. The blue one. He's had it since he was a boy.
Nurse -> That sounds perfect.
Nurse -> Is he passing urine?
Caller -> Less. The brief is only wet once or twice a day now. It's dark yellow.
Nurse -> That's expected, since he's drinking so little.
Caller -> Okay. I wondered about that.
Nurse -> Who is staying near him at night?
Caller -> Our oldest, Mark, sleeps on the couch next to the bed. And I check on him every hour or so.
Nurse -> Make sure you rest too. Let Mark and the others take turns.
Caller -> I'll try. It's hard to leave his side.
Nurse -> I understand. Even short naps help.
Nurse -> Of course. Let me pull up Walter's chart, so I can go over what he's on.
Caller -> Please.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm seeing metoprolol, atorvastatin, and tamsulosin on his list.
Caller -> We stopped those last week. The doctor said we could, since he couldn't swallow them anymore.
Nurse -> Okay, that makes sense. And for comfort I see lorazepam, point five milligram, as needed for restlessness. Has he needed it?
Caller -> Once. Two nights ago. He was restless, and he was picking at his sheet. I gave him one. He settled right down and slept.
Nurse -> Okay. That's exactly what it's for. If he gets restless like that again, go ahead and give it.
Caller -> Okay. Even if it's the middle of the night?
Nurse -> Yes. Even in the middle of the night. You don't need to call first.
Caller -> That's a relief.
Nurse -> Helen, I want to tell you what to expect, because it can be frightening if no one tells you. When someone is near the end of life, they sleep more, they eat and drink less, and sometimes their breathing patterns change. It's part of the body slowing down.
Caller -> I know. The nurse told me some of this. But it helps to hear it again.
Nurse -> Of course. So please don't force food or fluids. If he wants a sip, great. If not, that's okay. It's not starving him. It's not hurting him.
Caller -> That's hard. I want to feed him. It's what I do.
Nurse -> I know. It's love. But what he needs now is comfort. Keep his mouth moist with a swab dipped in water, and use lip balm.
Caller -> I do that already. His mouth gets so dry.
Nurse -> Good. And turn him gently every two hours, so he's comfortable. And play his favorite music, and keep talking to him. Hearing is the last sense to go.
Caller -> We have the polka station on all day. He loves a good polka.
Nurse -> Ha. A man of taste. Does he have a favorite?
Caller -> The Beer Barrel Polka. Naturally. The kids play it at full volume. They think he can feel the beat in his feet.
Nurse -> I'm sure he can. That's wonderful, Helen.
Caller -> He met me at a polka dance. In nineteen sixty four. He stepped on my foot and I told him to watch it.
Nurse -> Ha. What a story. And you've been together ever since?
Caller -> Sixty two years in October. He still steps on my feet.
Nurse -> That's beautiful.
Caller -> It is. Thank you for letting me ramble.
Nurse -> Ramble all you want. I love it. Now, would you like a nurse to come see him tomorrow?
Caller -> Yes, please. Just so someone can look him over, and I can ask my questions.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll arrange a visit tomorrow morning.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Thank you.
Nurse -> Is there anything else the family would like? A visit from the chaplain, or the social worker?
Caller -> The chaplain, actually. Our priest is out of town. If someone could come and say a prayer with us, it would mean a lot.
Nurse -> Absolutely. I'll message our chaplain tonight, and ask her to call you.
Caller -> Thank you, Lena. That's very kind.
Nurse -> And Helen, you can call us any time, day or night. Even if you just want to talk.
Caller -> I will. I really will. Thank you so much.
Caller -> Can I ask you something, Lena? When it happens. Should we call the funeral home first, or you?
Nurse -> Call us first. Please don't call 911 or the funeral home before you call us. Our nurse will come, and she'll help with everything, including calling the funeral home when you're ready.
Caller -> That's a relief. I didn't want to get it wrong.
Nurse -> You won't get it wrong. There's no rush at that moment. You can sit with him as long as you like.
Caller -> Thank you. We've already picked out the funeral home. Walter planned it all. He even chose the music.
Nurse -> That sounds like a thoughtful man.
Caller -> He is. He wrote down every song. Beer Barrel Polka is first, he says, and nobody's allowed to cry during it.
Nurse -> Ha. That's wonderful.
Caller -> I'll try. No promises.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself, too. Eat something. Sit down for a minute.
Caller -> I'll make a plate. The kids brought pierogi. Potato and cheese, and the sauerkraut ones, from the Polish church on Elm.
Nurse -> Ha. Now I'm really hungry.
Caller -> The ladies at the church bring food every Friday. They've been so good to us. Mrs. Kowal even brought a babka.
Nurse -> That's a lot of love around you.
Caller -> It is. I'm grateful for every bit of it. Walter would be too, if he were awake. He'd be telling them all to sit down and eat.
Nurse -> He sounds like a generous man.
Caller -> He is. Always was. Okay, enough from me.
Nurse -> Ha. Now I'm hungry.
Caller -> I'll save you one. Good night, Lena. Thank you for everything, truly.
Nurse -> Good night, Helen. Hug the kids for me, and call if you need anything at all.

Nurse -> Northstar Home Health, this is Priscilla.
Caller -> Hi. This is Wendy. I'm calling about my mother, Dolly Fairweather.
Nurse -> Hi, Wendy. Dolly's date of birth?
Caller -> November fifth, nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> And I have four oh four, five five five, zero one six nine on file.
Caller -> Yes, that's me.
Nurse -> What's going on?
Caller -> Okay. So, my brother stopped by Mom's this morning. And he said, he thinks she might have been on the floor last night. But he's not sure.
Nurse -> Okay. What made him think that?

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom. This is Tamika, I'm a nurse at Cedar Crest Care Center. I'm calling about one of your residents. Lucille Armitage.
Nurse -> Hi, Tamika. Lucille's date of birth?
Caller -> December eighth, nineteen thirty three.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> The nurses' station. Seven oh four, five five five, zero one eight six.
Nurse -> Got it. What's going on with Lucille?
Caller -> I just took over from the day shift, and the report I got is confusing. I wanted to check with you. Her pain seems worse, and she's not eating well.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what you know.
Caller -> So the day nurse said her pain was a three. A three out of ten. In her left hip. But when I went in to see her just now, she was grimacing, and she told me it's a six.
Nurse -> Okay. So three earlier, and six now.
Caller -> Right. Or I think the three was this morning, and the six was this evening. I'm not sure. The day nurse is gone, I can't ask her.
Nurse -> Okay. So the pain may have gone up during the day.
Caller -> Maybe. Or maybe she just reported it differently. I really don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. What about her eating?
Caller -> The aide said she ate about a quarter of her lunch. But the dietary sheet says she ate half. So I don't know which is right.
Nurse -> Okay. So between a quarter and half.
Caller -> Yes. I'm sorry that I can't be more precise.
Nurse -> No, that's fine, you're doing your best with what you have. Let me ask a few other things. Does she have a fever?
Caller -> No. I checked. Ninety eight point two.
Nurse -> Any falls?
Caller -> No falls.
Nurse -> Okay. What does she have for pain?
Caller -> She has oxycodone, five milligrams, every four hours as needed. The day nurse wrote that she gave one at two this afternoon.
Nurse -> Okay. So the last dose was at two. It's after eight now, so it's been more than four hours.
Caller -> Right. So she could have another.
Nurse -> Yes. Since she's grimacing, and the pain is at least moderate, I'd give the oxycodone now. As long as the pain is above a four, and it's been at least four hours, she can have it.
Caller -> Okay. It's above a four, for sure. I'll give it.
Nurse -> Good. And please start recording a pain score every four hours, along with her expression. Also, write down a percentage after each meal. That will help us see what's really going on.
Caller -> I can do that. I'll put a note on the chart, for all the shifts.
Nurse -> Perfect. Reposition her every two hours, with a pillow between the knees. And offer her favorite foods.
Caller -> She likes the pudding. And ice cream. I'll bring some.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll send a nurse to see her tomorrow morning, to look at both the pain and the intake.
Caller -> Oh good. That would help.
Nurse -> And I'll call you after the visit, to go over what she found.
Caller -> Okay. Tomorrow. I'm on again at seven.
Nurse -> Great. Then I'll call you around nine.
Caller -> Perfect.
Nurse -> If her pain goes over a seven, or she gets very sleepy, or runs a fever, or falls, call us right away.
Caller -> Okay. Over seven, sleepy, fever, fall. Got it.
Nurse -> Tamika, is she awake and alert, apart from the pain? Does she know who you are?
Caller -> She's alert. She knows me. She called me by name when I came in. She's a little tired, but she's oriented.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring. And her bowels? When was the last movement?
Caller -> Yesterday, I think. I'd have to check the flow sheet. I can look when we hang up.
Nurse -> Please do, and let me know if it's more than three days.
Caller -> I will. We're short staffed tonight, so I'm covering two halls. I'm sorry if I sound rushed.
Nurse -> You sound great. We appreciate your calling when something seems off.
Caller -> Thank you. That means a lot, after a long shift.
Nurse -> Is she comfortable now?
Caller -> She's resting. She seems okay. I'll give the medicine and sit with her a minute.
Nurse -> That's nice of you. Does she have family who visit?
Caller -> Her granddaughter comes on Sundays. She brings her little dog. Lucille lights up when she sees that dog.
Nurse -> Aw. That sounds like good medicine too.
Caller -> It is. The whole floor loves when the dog comes.
Nurse -> Ha. Is it okay for the dog to visit, with the other residents?
Caller -> Oh yes. The facility has a pet policy. Therapy dogs and family pets are welcome.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Okay, Tamika. Thank you for calling, and for taking good care of her.
Caller -> Thank you, Tom. I'll write everything down. Goodnight.

Nurse -> Sorry, Bernice. And a number for you?

Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Is he comfortable otherwise? Any dizziness, or did he fall when he bumped it?

Nurse -> Good. His skin is fragile, so it's worth padding sharp corners if you can.
Caller -> I'll put some foam on the door frame. Good idea.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Rhonda.
Caller -> Hi, Rhonda. This is Monica. I'm calling about my dad. Stefan Kowalski.
Nurse -> Hi, Monica. Stefan Kowalsky. And his date of birth?
Caller -> October twelfth, nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your phone number?
Caller -> Two four eight, five five five, zero one eight seven.
Nurse -> Okay, got it. And what's going on with your father, Mr. Kovalski?
Caller -> He hasn't had a bowel movement in three days.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he having any pain in his belly?
Caller -> Some bloating. His belly feels full, and it's a little puffy. But not terrible pain.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he throwing up?
Caller -> No. No vomiting.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me look at his orders. Okay. He recently had the hip repair, right?
Caller -> Yes. Two weeks ago. He's been on the pain pills, and he's not moving much. I think that's why.
Nurse -> That's very likely. Pain medicine and less movement both slow the bowels. I see MiraLAX on his list as needed. Do you have it?
Caller -> We do. At home. I haven't used it. I wasn't sure if I should.
Nurse -> What is he taking for pain right now?
Caller -> The oxycodone. Five milligrams, twice a day. He says it helps.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he using it every day?
Caller -> Every day, morning and night. He hates to miss it.
Nurse -> That may be contributing to the constipation.
Caller -> I figured. Should he stop it?
Nurse -> No, not on your own. Keep giving it as prescribed, and let's treat the constipation. The surgeon can adjust the pain plan if needed.
Caller -> Okay. I won't stop it.
Nurse -> And how's his appetite?
Caller -> He's eating less, because he feels full. A few bites at a time.
Nurse -> Okay. That fits with the constipation too. I'd go ahead and give him one capful of the MiraLAX today, in eight ounces of water or juice.
Caller -> One capful. Okay. In juice is fine?
Nurse -> Juice is fine.
Nurse -> It's the bottle on the bathroom shelf, I think.
Caller -> Okay. The bathroom shelf. I'll find it. Thank you.
Nurse -> And a lot of fluids, like water, and prune juice, and fiber, like fruit and oatmeal. And short walks with the walker, every couple of hours.
Caller -> He walks to the kitchen and back. I'll get him to do more.
Nurse -> That's great. I'm also going to send a nurse out tomorrow, to check on his bowels, and look at how he's doing.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you.

Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom. Hi. It's Tamar. I'm calling about my grandmother. Bernadette Oyelowo.
Nurse -> Hi, Tamar. Can you spell the last name for me?
Caller -> O Y E L O W O.
Nurse -> Thank you. And Bernadette's date of birth?
Caller -> August twenty second, nineteen thirty two.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Seven oh six, five five five, zero one nine one.
Nurse -> Okay. Seven oh six, five five five, zero one nine one.
Caller -> Yes. That's me.
Nurse -> What's happening with Bernadette tonight?
Caller -> She's agitated. She started around nine. She's pulling at her covers and she keeps talking to my grandfather. He's been gone twelve years.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she saying anything?
Caller -> She keeps saying, Joseph, come here, Joseph. She thinks he's in the room. She's not upset about it, exactly. She's just restless. And it's been hours.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she in pain, do you think?
Caller -> I think so. When we turn her, she grimaces. And she says ow. Her hips, I think.
Nurse -> How bad would you say it is?
Caller -> Maybe a five? I don't know. It's hard to tell with her.
Nurse -> Okay. What's she been given tonight?
Caller -> My mom gave her something around eleven last night. The hello peridol. For the agitation.
Nurse -> The what?
Caller -> The, um, hello peridol. I can't say it. It starts with an H.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me look at her chart, and I'll read what I see. I see haloperidol, point five milligram, by mouth, every six hours as needed for agitation. Is that the one?
Caller -> Yes. Yes, that's it. Haloperidol. That's what's on the box.
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I'm terrible with these names.
Nurse -> Don't be sorry. They're hard. Did she get any today?
Caller -> No. Just last night at eleven. Nothing since. Because she was calm until tonight.
Nurse -> Okay. So it's been more than six hours. She can have another dose now.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I'll get it.
Nurse -> Go ahead and give her the haloperidol, point five milligram.
Caller -> Okay. Mom! Mom, can you wake up? Mom, I need to get Grandma's medicine. It's in the kitchen. Okay. She's asleep, I don't want to wake her.
Nurse -> That's fine. Let her sleep. Is it nearby?
Caller -> In the cabinet over the stove. Hold on.
Caller -> I have it. Okay. I'm going to give it to her now. It goes under the tongue?
Nurse -> Yes. A tablet that dissolves, under the tongue.
Caller -> Okay. Grandma, open up. Under your tongue. There. Good. She took it.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, I see her other comfort medicine on the list too, for anxiety and restlessness. Has she had any of that?
Caller -> The lorezapam? Yes. This morning. My mom gave her one around eight. And she had one yesterday too. The lorezapam.
Caller -> I think that's how you say it. Lorazepam? Lorezapam? Something like that.
Nurse -> Okay. That was this morning, so you can check on that later with the nurse. For now, we'll focus on the other one.
Caller -> Okay. Is it okay that she had that in the morning too?
Nurse -> That's fine. Each one has its own schedule.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> I'm also looking at her other medications on the chart. Metoprolol and levothyroxine.
Caller -> We stopped those last week. The doctor said she didn't need them anymore, since she can barely swallow.
Nurse -> Okay. That makes sense. Tamar, how has she been eating and drinking?
Caller -> Barely. Just sips of water for the last two days. She won't open her mouth for food.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have a fever?
Caller -> No. I put the thermometer on her forehead, and it said ninety eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. I'm going to send our on-call nurse to see her tonight, to check on the pain and the agitation.
Caller -> Tonight? Oh, thank you. Thank God.
Nurse -> She should be there within two hours. I'll also message the hospice doctor about her pain.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. That would be so good.
Nurse -> Has she had a bowel movement, or passed urine, tonight?
Caller -> She's in a brief. It was wet when we changed her at nine. No bowel movement today, I don't think. My mom keeps a log, I can ask her later.
Nurse -> That's fine. The nurse will check that when she comes. Is her mouth dry?
Caller -> A little. We've been using the swabs. And I put some of that lip balm on her.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's exactly right.
Caller -> My mom is the one who knows everything. I'm just helping. She does the nights, usually, but she's been up for two days straight, so I told her to rest.
Nurse -> That was kind of you. You're a good granddaughter.
Caller -> Grandma raised me, actually, for part of my childhood. When my mom was working two jobs. So this is the least I can do.
Nurse -> That's a special bond.
Caller -> It is. She used to sing in the church choir. She'd practice her solos in the kitchen while she cooked. I'd sit on the counter and listen.
Nurse -> What a lovely memory. Maybe the gospel music will remind her.
Caller -> That's what I'm hoping. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll call you in thirty minutes, to see how Bernadette is doing after the haloperidol.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay.
Nurse -> In the meantime, dim the lights, talk softly, and play her favorite music, if you have it. And put a pillow between her knees, and turn her gently.
Caller -> She loves gospel. I have it on my phone. I'll play it softly.
Nurse -> Perfect. And don't argue with her about what she sees. If she wants to talk to Joseph, let her. Just stay calm.
Caller -> I won't argue. I just say, he's here, Grandma. I sit with her.
Nurse -> That's exactly right. Keep the bed low, and stay close.
Caller -> I'm right next to her.
Nurse -> And if she becomes combative, or hard to wake up, or has trouble breathing, call me right away.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> How are you holding up, Tamar? It's late.
Caller -> I'm okay. I work from home, so it's easier for me to stay. I'm a graphic designer. I've been designing a logo for a bakery. At least when I'm sitting here I can sketch.
Nurse -> That sounds like a nice way to pass the hours.
Caller -> It is. Grandma used to bake the best sweet potato pie. The bakery owner asked if I could make her pie the logo.
Nurse -> Ha. What a tribute.
Caller -> I know. She'd love that. She's the one who taught me to draw, actually. She used to sketch flowers in the margins of her church bulletin.
Nurse -> That's such a lovely thing. Maybe you can show her the logo.
Caller -> I will. I'll show her tomorrow. Maybe she'll be more awake.
Nurse -> I hope so.
Caller -> Hang on, someone's at the door. It's my aunt. Oh, she heard the phone. Hi, Auntie. Yes, it's the nurse. They're sending someone. Okay. She's going to sit with Grandma while I finish the call.
Nurse -> That's good. Is your mother up now?
Caller -> Yes. She woke up when Auntie came in. She's checking on Grandma. She says thank you.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Tell her I'll call in thirty minutes.
Caller -> I will. Thank you again, Tom.
Caller -> One more question, if that's okay. Should we call the rest of the family? My uncles are in Atlanta and Houston.
Nurse -> It's up to you and your mother. If you feel the family would want to be here, it's a good time to let them know, so they can decide. I'm not saying it's tonight, but she is declining.
Caller -> I understand. I'll talk to my mom when she wakes up. I think she'll want to call them tomorrow.
Nurse -> That sounds right. And the nurse who comes tonight can talk with her about what to expect, too.
Caller -> Okay. That helps. Thank you for being honest.
Nurse -> Always. Take care. Talk soon.

Caller -> Yes. I have it open on the kitchen table. There are four bottles, and a few syringes, and a sheet of instructions.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's take them one at a time. Pick up the first bottle, and read me the label.
Caller -> Okay. The first one says morphine sulfate. Oral solution. Twenty milligrams per milliliter.
Nurse -> Good. And below that, do you see the directions?
Caller -> It says, point two five milliliters under the tongue every two hours as needed for pain or shortness of breath.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's the morphine. You'll use it if your mother seems to be in pain, like grimacing or moaning, or if her breathing looks hard. A quarter of a milliliter, which is a very small amount, and it goes between her cheek and her gum, or under her tongue.
Caller -> A quarter of a mil. That's tiny.
Nurse -> It is. It's a concentrated medicine. Use the syringe that came with it, not a kitchen spoon.
Caller -> Okay. The syringe with the little markings.
Nurse -> Right. And always write down the time of every dose.
Caller -> I have a notebook on the table. I'll start tonight.
Nurse -> Perfect. Next bottle.
Caller -> The second one says lorazepam. Point five milligram. Tablets. Under the tongue, every four hours as needed for anxiety or restlessness.
Nurse -> Right. That's the lorazepam. If she seems anxious, restless, or can't settle, that's what you'd use. It dissolves under the tongue.
Caller -> What's the difference between that and the morphine? How do I know which one?
Nurse -> Good question. Morphine is for pain and for the feeling of breathlessness. The lorazepam is for anxiety and restlessness. If she seems to be hurting, morphine. If she seems unsettled or worried, lorazepam. Sometimes you can use both.
Caller -> Okay. Pain, breathing, morphine. Restless, anxious, lorazepam.
Nurse -> Exactly right.
Caller -> What if I can't tell?
Nurse -> Then call us. That's what we're here for. We'll help you decide.
Caller -> Okay. That makes me feel better.
Nurse -> Next bottle.
Caller -> Third one. Haloperidol. Point five milligram. Every six hours as needed for agitation, nausea, or confusion.
Nurse -> Right. The haloperidol. That's for agitation or confusion, when she's restless in a way that's different from anxiety, like picking at the sheets, or seeing things that aren't there. It's also used for nausea.
Caller -> Okay. So that's the one if she gets confused.
Nurse -> Yes. Or if she's nauseous.
Caller -> Got it.
Nurse -> Last bottle.
Caller -> It's a little dropper bottle. Atropine. One percent. Two drops under the tongue, every four hours as needed for secretions.
Nurse -> Okay. That's the atropine. Near the end of life, sometimes a person gets noisy, gurgling breathing, because they can't clear their saliva. This dries the secretions. It's for the family's comfort as much as hers.
Caller -> Gurgling. Oh. Okay. I've heard that. Is it painful for her?
Nurse -> Usually it's not painful for the patient. It sounds worse than it feels. But the drops can help.
Caller -> Two drops, under the tongue. Okay.
Nurse -> Right. Calvin, you're doing great.
Caller -> I'm trying. Honestly, I'm afraid of giving the wrong one, or too much.
Nurse -> I understand. That's very common. That's why I'd like our nurse to come tomorrow, and show you in person how to give each one.
Caller -> That would be great. What time?
Nurse -> Tomorrow at eleven. She'll bring a practice syringe, and you can try it with water.
Caller -> Perfect. I'll be here. My sister is coming too, she wants to learn.
Nurse -> Wonderful. The more family members who know, the better. And keep the kit in one place, away from children and pets. Put our phone number on top of the box.
Caller -> I'll write it on a piece of tape. Right on the lid.
Nurse -> Perfect. And remember, you can call us any time, day or night, before you give anything, if you're not sure.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Caller -> Can I ask a couple more questions? What if she can't swallow anything at all?
Nurse -> Good question. These are all made to absorb in the mouth, between the cheek and gum or under the tongue, so she doesn't need to swallow. That's why we use them at this stage.
Caller -> Oh, that's reassuring. I was worried about that.
Caller -> And what if I give one and it doesn't seem to work?
Nurse -> Give it time. Most of them take fifteen to thirty minutes to work. If she's still uncomfortable after thirty minutes, call us, and we'll tell you what to do next.
Caller -> Fifteen to thirty minutes. Okay. I'll watch the clock.
Caller -> And what do I do with them when we're done? After.
Nurse -> The nurse will help you with that. We'll take care of the disposal. You don't need to worry about it now.
Caller -> Okay. I'm just trying to think of everything.
Nurse -> You're doing great. This is a lot to take in.
Nurse -> Any other questions about the kit?
Caller -> Just one. How do I know if she's comfortable? She can't tell me.
Nurse -> Good question. Look for a relaxed face, relaxed hands, and slow, easy breathing. If you see frowning, groaning, or restlessness, those are signs she may need something.
Caller -> Okay. A relaxed face is good. Frowning is not.
Nurse -> Right.
Caller -> My sister says our mother used to hum when she was content. Like, in the kitchen. We haven't heard it in a while.
Nurse -> That's a lovely sign to listen for. Maybe you'll hear it again.
Caller -> I hope so. She hummed hymns. Old ones. Her favorite was Amazing Grace.
Nurse -> It's a beautiful one. Maybe play it softly for her.
Caller -> I will. I'll put it on tonight.
Nurse -> And Calvin, how are you doing? This is a lot.
Caller -> It is. I took leave from work, and I'm staying here. I'm tired, but I'm okay. I'm glad I can be here.
Nurse -> That's a gift, for her and for you.
Caller -> Thank you. I needed to hear that. Alright. I'll let you go.
Nurse -> One more thing. Does anyone else live in the home, or visit? Any children, any pets?
Caller -> My sister is here. Her kids visit on weekends. They're six and nine. And my mother has a cat, Pepper. She sleeps on the bed with her.
Nurse -> Then please keep the box up high, on a shelf or in a cabinet, away from the kids and Pepper.
Caller -> I'll put it on top of the refrigerator. They can't reach that.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Take care, Calvin. See you tomorrow, well, the nurse will.
Caller -> Ha. Thanks, Lena. One more silly thing, can I tell my mom that you said hello? She won't hear, but I'd like to.
Nurse -> Please do. Tell her Lena says hello, and that we're thinking of her.
Caller -> I will. I'll tell her tonight when I put the hymn on.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely. Good night, Calvin.
Caller -> Good night.

Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Ana.
Caller -> Hi, Ana. It's Hannah. I'm calling about my son, Aiden. A I D E N, Rosenthal.

Nurse -> What's going on?
Caller -> I think my mom took two days of pills at once. Her pillbox. The Tuesday and the Wednesday compartments are both empty, and it's only Tuesday.
Nurse -> Okay. Take a breath. Tell me what you know.
Caller -> I came by at noon, and I looked at her pillbox because I always check it. And Tuesday is empty. Which is right, because it's Tuesday. But Wednesday is empty too.
Nurse -> Okay. And did you see her take them?
Caller -> No. No, I wasn't here. I think she took them around eight this morning. She says she took her morning pills. But she doesn't remember taking two days. I'm not sure.
Nurse -> Okay. So you're not certain. But it's possible.
Caller -> Yes. And she's acting funny. She's confused. She keeps asking me the same questions, and she keeps drifting off. It started about ten this morning, according to her neighbor.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she awake now?
Caller -> She's awake. She's sitting at the table. But she's slow. She's not herself.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she fainted or almost fainted?
Caller -> No. No fainting. No chest pain. She says she feels woozy.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a blood pressure cuff?
Caller -> I do. Hang on. I'm putting it on her. Mom, hold still. Okay. It says ninety eight over fifty eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Ninety eight over fifty eight. And the pulse?
Caller -> Fifty four.
Nurse -> Okay. Those are both on the low side. Celeste, what is usually in the pillbox? Do you have the medication list?
Caller -> Yes. I have the pharmacy printout right here. There are three that are in there for the morning. Metoprolol, twenty five milligrams. Furosemide, twenty milligrams. And amlodipine, five milligrams. Each once a day.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me check my chart. I'm seeing metoprolol, furosemide, amlodipine. Also atorvastatin and famotidine at night.
Caller -> Yes. The night ones are in a different box. Those weren't touched.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a relief. Celeste, the three morning ones all lower blood pressure or pulse, and doubling them could make her too low. That's what I'm worried about.
Caller -> I figured. That's why I called.
Nurse -> You did exactly the right thing. I'm going to page our on-call doctor right now. Hold on. Okay, I've sent it.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'm going to call poison control, to get their guidance on the combination.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. Is it that serious?
Nurse -> I want to be careful. It's a precaution. Poison control gives very specific guidance for this, and I'd like to make sure we do exactly what they recommend.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense.
Nurse -> Celeste, is this the first time something like this has happened with her pills?
Caller -> No, actually. Last month I found her pillbox on the wrong day. She'd been skipping around. I thought it was a one time thing. I should have said something.
Nurse -> It's helpful to know. I'll note it for the nurse who's coming.
Caller -> And she's been more forgetful lately. Her neighbor, Mr. Delacroix, mentioned it. He sees her every morning, they have coffee on the porch.
Nurse -> Is Mr. Delacroix there now?
Caller -> No, but he's the one who called me this morning. He said she was acting odd, and he thought I should come. That's why I came at noon.
Nurse -> He sounds like a good neighbor. Please thank him for me.
Caller -> I will. He's eighty five himself, and sharp as a tack. He's worried about her.
Nurse -> I'm glad she has people watching out for her.
Caller -> She does. Oh, she's looking at me. Mom, I'm fine. I'm talking to the nurse. Yes. She's asking who I'm talking to.
Nurse -> That's okay. Tell her it's the nurse from the home health agency, and that she's doing fine.
Caller -> I told her. She said, thank you, dear. She's polite even when she's confused.
Nurse -> Ha. That's lovely.
Nurse -> I'm also sending a nurse to your mother's house, within two hours.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in ten minutes, with what the doctor and poison control say.
Caller -> Ten minutes. Okay.
Nurse -> Until then, please don't give her any more pills today. Not the night ones either. No metoprolol, no furosemide, no amlodipine, nothing, until we call you back.
Caller -> Okay. No more pills. Got it.
Nurse -> Have her lie down, or at least sit in a good chair. If she needs to stand, she should go slowly, and not walk alone. And please stay with her.
Caller -> I'm not leaving. I'll stay right here.
Nurse -> Check her pulse and blood pressure every fifteen minutes, and write the numbers and the time.
Caller -> I'll write them on the back of the printout.
Nurse -> If she faints, or has chest pain, or any trouble breathing, or her pulse goes under fifty, or you can't wake her, call nine one one right away. Don't wait for me.
Caller -> Nine one one. Okay. Under fifty. Okay.
Nurse -> Celeste, how are you doing?
Caller -> I'm shaking. This is my fault. I should have put her pills out myself. She insisted on doing it.
Nurse -> This isn't your fault. Many people want to keep their independence, and that's understandable. But we can make it safer going forward.
Caller -> How?
Nurse -> A pillbox that has all the pills for one day in one compartment, and a log she checks off. And maybe you or the nurse can fill it with her once a week.
Caller -> That makes sense. I'll do that. I'll fill it every Sunday.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's a good plan.
Caller -> She's going to be so embarrassed. She's very proud.
Nurse -> It can happen to anyone. We'll make sure she knows that.
Caller -> Thank you. She worked as a bookkeeper for forty years. She was always the one catching other people's mistakes.
Nurse -> Ha. I bet she was. Well, this time she gets a pass.
Caller -> She'd never forgive herself, if she remembered. Oh, Mom, don't try to stand up. Stay there. I'm on the phone with the nurse. Okay.
Nurse -> Is she trying to get up?
Caller -> She wanted the bathroom. I'm helping her. We'll go slowly. Hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time. Be careful. Hold her arm.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. She's okay. She's lying down on the couch now. She said she feels a little better.
Nurse -> Good. Keep her lying down. Keep checking her numbers. I'll call you in ten minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Priscilla. You've been a lifesaver.
Caller -> Priscilla, before you go. When the nurse comes, should I have anything ready? Like the bottles?
Nurse -> Yes. Please gather all of her medicine bottles, the pillbox, and the pharmacy printout, and put them on the table. The nurse will go through everything.
Caller -> I'll do that now. I'll put the pillbox right next to the printout, with the empty compartments facing up.
Nurse -> Perfect. Don't throw anything away, not even empty bottles.
Caller -> Okay. I'll leave it all exactly as it is.
Nurse -> Thank you. That's very helpful.
Caller -> Is there anything else I should be doing?
Nurse -> Just what we talked about. Keep her lying down, keep her warm, give her sips of water if she's thirsty, and keep checking those numbers.
Caller -> Sips of water. Okay. She's asking for tea. Is that okay?
Nurse -> A small cup of warm decaf tea is fine, if she's awake enough to swallow safely. Sit her up a little first.
Caller -> Okay. I'll make it in a minute, after I finish with you.
Nurse -> Go ahead and do that now. I'll call you in ten minutes.
Caller -> Thank you. Talk soon.
Nurse -> Talk soon, Celeste.

transcript:
Nurse -> Northstar Home Health, this is Priscilla.
Caller -> Hi, Priscilla. This is Josephine Arbuckle. I'm a patient. I'm sorry it's so late.
Nurse -> Hi, Josephine. Don't apologize. We're here all night. Can I get your date of birth?
Caller -> November second, nineteen eighty.
Nurse -> And a number for you? I have four oh four, five five five, zero one nine four.
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> What's going on tonight?
Caller -> I can't sleep. I haven't been able to sleep for weeks. I lie there, and my mind just races.
Nurse -> How much are you sleeping, would you say?
Caller -> Maybe three hours. If I'm lucky.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds exhausting.
Caller -> It is. And I'm just, I'm so tired of everything. The treatments, the appointments. The fear.
Nurse -> Of course you are. You've been through so much. How long since the diagnosis?
Caller -> Four months. It feels like four years.
Nurse -> Okay. How have you been feeling emotionally?
Caller -> Honestly? Not good. I don't enjoy anything anymore. Not my garden, not my books. I used to love my garden. Now I just look out the window and feel nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. That's an important thing to say out loud.
Caller -> I haven't told anyone. Not even my husband.
Nurse -> I'm glad you told me. Josephine, I'd like to ask you something. Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself, or of not wanting to be here?
Caller -> Sometimes I wish I wouldn't wake up. In the morning.
Caller -> I'm not saying I'd do anything. It's not like that. I just, some nights I think, it would be easier if I didn't wake up.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for being so honest. That took courage. I'm really glad you called.
Caller -> I didn't plan to say that. It just came out.
Nurse -> I'm glad it did. I want to ask a few more questions, so I can understand and help. Is that okay?
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Do you have a plan? Have you thought about how you might do it?
Caller -> No. No plan. I haven't thought about that. I wouldn't know how.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have any guns in the house?
Caller -> No. We don't have any guns. My husband hates them.
Nurse -> Okay. And are you thinking of doing anything tonight?
Caller -> No. No, I'm not going to do anything. I just needed to talk. I couldn't talk to Dennis because he's at work.
Nurse -> Okay. Dennis is your husband?
Caller -> Yes. He works nights at the hospital. He's a respiratory therapist. He gets home around seven in the morning.
Nurse -> Okay. So you're alone right now.
Caller -> Yes. The house is so quiet at night.
Nurse -> Is there anyone else who could come and be with you? A friend, or family?
Caller -> My sister, Hannah. She lives about thirty minutes away.
Nurse -> Would you be okay if I called Hannah, with your permission?
Caller -> I don't want to wake her. She has two little kids.
Nurse -> I understand. But I think it would help to have someone with you tonight. And she'd want to know. Would you let me call her?
Caller -> I guess so. Okay. But can you call Dennis instead? He's at work, but he'd want to know. I'd feel better if he knew.
Nurse -> Of course. I can call Dennis. Is it okay if I tell him what you told me tonight?
Caller -> Yes. I want him to know. I just couldn't say it myself.
Nurse -> Thank you. I'll call him as soon as we finish. Is that okay?
Caller -> Yes. Thank you.
Nurse -> Josephine, what are you taking right now? Any medicines for mood?
Caller -> The sertraline. Fifty milligrams, once a day. They started it three weeks ago.
Nurse -> Okay. Has it helped?
Caller -> I don't notice a difference yet. Maybe I'm not giving it enough time.
Nurse -> It can take a few weeks. But I want your provider to know how you're doing, so they can adjust things if needed. I'm going to let them know tonight.
Caller -> I'd like that. I really would.
Nurse -> And I'm going to have our counselor call you today. She'll call within two hours. She's wonderful, she works with people going through cancer treatment, and she knows how heavy it can be.
Caller -> Okay. That sounds good. I'd like to talk to someone.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in thirty minutes, to check on you.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> I want to give you a number, Josephine. Nine eight eight. It's a crisis line. You can call or text it any time, day or night. And if you ever form a plan, or you feel like you might act on the thoughts, call nine one one.
Caller -> Nine eight eight. Okay. I know that one. I never thought I'd need it.
Nurse -> You don't have to be in an emergency to call. Even if you're not sure.
Caller -> Okay. I understand.
Nurse -> And for tonight, please keep your medicines to just the daily amount, nothing extra. And if Dennis or Hannah can stay with you, that would be best.
Caller -> I only have what I take. I'll make sure it stays that way.
Nurse -> And if the thoughts get stronger tonight, you call us right away. Any time.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Caller -> Can I tell you what scares me the most? I feel like I'm a burden. Dennis has taken so much time off work. He drives me to every appointment. He cooks, he cleans. I feel like I'm ruining his life.
Nurse -> That's a heavy thing to carry, Josephine. And a very common feeling for people in treatment. Have you told him that?
Caller -> No. I don't want to make him feel worse. He's trying so hard.
Nurse -> Sometimes the person who loves us most wants to know exactly what we're feeling, even the hard parts. And I think he'd tell you that you are not a burden.
Caller -> He would. He says it all the time. But I don't believe him.
Nurse -> That makes sense when you're this tired. Depression and exhaustion tell us things that aren't true.
Caller -> That's what the oncology social worker said once. I didn't want to hear it then.
Nurse -> Maybe you'll be ready to hear it now. And our counselor can pick up where she left off.
Caller -> Maybe. I think I would like that.
Nurse -> What helps you when you can't sleep, Josephine? Is there anything that calms you?
Caller -> Tea, sometimes. Chamomile. And music. I used to play the cello. I haven't touched it since the chemo made my hands numb.
Nurse -> The cello. That must have been a big part of your life.
Caller -> It was. I played in a community orchestra for twelve years. I miss it so much.
Nurse -> That's a real loss. Maybe the counselor can talk with you about it, and about ways to ease back in.
Caller -> Maybe. I'd like that. It feels good to say it out loud.
Caller -> I still have the cello. It's in the living room, in the corner. Sometimes I look at it and think, I should just try.
Nurse -> Maybe tomorrow, even for a few minutes. Even just holding it.
Caller -> Maybe. My hands tingle, but they're not numb all the time. Some days are better.
Nurse -> Then it might be worth trying on a good day. Without any pressure to play well.
Caller -> Ha. That's what Dennis says. He says he'll listen to anything, even scales.
Nurse -> He sounds like a keeper.
Caller -> He is. Okay. I'm going to cry, I think. But I think it's a good cry.
Nurse -> That's okay. Let it out. I'm here.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Why don't you make some of that chamomile tea while I call Dennis? I'll check on you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. I'll do that. I'll put the kettle on right now. Thank you, Priscilla. Really.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Josephine. You did something brave tonight. Dennis will be glad you reached out, and so will the counselor.
Caller -> Thank you. I'll keep the phone next to me. Bye.

Caller -> Hi, Beth. It's Joan. Joan Pellegrino. I'm calling about my husband, Anthony.

Nurse -> Okay. And your number is two oh one, five five five, zero one five seven?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> What's going on with Anthony?
Caller -> He's got a cough. And a runny nose. It started Monday. So, two days.
Caller -> It's not terrible. It's kind of a dry cough.
Nurse -> Okay. Any fever?

transcript:
Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice, this is Carla.
Caller -> Hi, Carla. This is Liv. I'm calling about my mother, Agnes. Agnes Thorvaldsen.
Nurse -> Hi, Liv. Can you spell the last name for me?
Caller -> T H O R V A L D S E N. It's Norwegian. Nobody ever gets it right.
Nurse -> Ha. Thank you. And Agnes's date of birth?
Caller -> September seventeenth, nineteen thirty four.
Nurse -> Okay. And your number, Liv?
Caller -> Six one two, five five five, zero one six five.
Nurse -> Got it. Six one two, five five five, zero one six five.
Caller -> Yes. That's right.
Nurse -> So what's on your mind today?
Caller -> Nothing urgent. I just wanted to check in. I wasn't sure if I should call or wait until Thursday.
Nurse -> No, I'm glad you called. Tell me how Agnes is doing.
Caller -> Well. She's sleeping more. A lot more. She sleeps most of the day now. I get her up for meals, and then she's right back down.
Nurse -> Okay. How long has that been going on?
Caller -> About two weeks, I'd say. It's been gradual.
Nurse -> Okay. And how's she eating?
Caller -> She eats about half. Half of what she used to. She likes her oatmeal, and her tea with sugar. Other than that, she picks.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she drinking?
Caller -> Yes, she drinks her tea. That's the main thing. And some juice.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. Any pain? Is she grimacing, or moaning?
Caller -> No. No, she seems comfortable. She doesn't moan or make faces. She just sleeps.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to hear.
Caller -> Mama? Mama, it's the nurse. No, don't wake up. She's fine. She just opened her eyes. She's looking right at me. Okay. She's going back to sleep.
Nurse -> Ha. Hello, Agnes.
Caller -> She likes hearing voices. Even when she's sleeping.
Nurse -> I'm sure she does. Okay, Liv. Is there anything else you've noticed?
Caller -> Her skin. Her legs. The skin on her shins is really dry. And itchy. She's been scratching.
Nurse -> Okay. How long?
Caller -> About a week. She scratches in her sleep. I found a little scratch mark on her left leg yesterday.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the skin broken?
Caller -> Just a scratch. Not open. Just red. It's not bleeding.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me pull up her chart, so I can see what she has. Hold on.
Caller -> Sure. Take your time.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm looking at her medication list. Levothyroxine, for her thyroid. Famotidine, for her stomach. Atorvastatin, her cholesterol.
Caller -> Yes. She still takes those. In the morning. With her oatmeal. We crush them and mix them in. She doesn't even notice.
Nurse -> Okay. That's smart. Those are fine for now. And I see a tube of hydrocortisone cream, one percent.
Caller -> Oh, yes. I have that. In the bathroom cabinet. I haven't used it. I didn't know if it was for the itching.
Nurse -> Yes, it can be. Here's what I'd suggest. First, an unscented lotion, twice a day, all over her legs. Right after a bath, when her skin is still a little damp.
Caller -> Twice a day. We have the Eucerin. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's perfect. And if she's still itchy after a couple of days, you can put a thin layer of the hydrocortisone cream on the itchy spots, once a day. Don't use it for more than three days in a row.
Caller -> A thin layer, once a day, no more than three days. Okay.
Nurse -> And not on any broken skin. Just the itchy, dry areas.
Caller -> Okay. Not on the scratch. Got it.
Nurse -> Also, short, lukewarm baths, not hot. Cotton clothes. And keep her nails short, so the scratching doesn't hurt her skin.
Caller -> I'll trim her nails today. I have the little clippers.
Nurse -> Good. How are you doing, Liv? You're taking care of her all day, right?
Caller -> Yes. I live with her. I'm doing okay. I'm tired. Honestly, I'm more tired than I thought I'd be.
Nurse -> That's very common. Do you have help?
Caller -> The hospice aide comes Tuesdays and Fridays. She's lovely. And my daughter, she's twenty three, she comes on the weekends.
Nurse -> That's good. Is there anyone who can give you a break, an afternoon off, now and then?
Caller -> Not really. I mean, my daughter, on Sundays. But I feel guilty leaving.
Nurse -> I understand. A lot of caregivers feel that way. I'd like to have our social worker call you. She can talk about respite options, and just check in on how you're doing.
Caller -> Oh. That would be nice. Yes. I'd like that. I think I need that.
Nurse -> Good. I'll send her a message today.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> And the nurse is coming Thursday at ten, right? She'll check the skin, and weigh Agnes, and go over everything.
Caller -> Yes. Thursday at ten. I'll have her ready.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, about the eating. Don't force food. If she wants a bite of oatmeal or a sip of tea, great. Offer her favorite things in small amounts.
Caller -> Her favorite is lefse. With butter and sugar. I make it myself.
Nurse -> Oh, that sounds wonderful. What is lefse?
Caller -> It's a Norwegian flatbread. Made with potatoes. You roll it really thin. My mother taught me. And I taught my daughter.
Nurse -> That's a beautiful tradition. And I bet the smell alone makes her happy.
Caller -> It does. She'll take a little bite, and she smiles. Even sleeping, I swear she smiles.
Nurse -> That's what matters. Little bites of what she loves.
Caller -> Yes. We make it every Christmas. Dozens and dozens. The whole house smells like it.
Nurse -> Ha. I can imagine. Is she having regular bowel movements and passing urine okay?
Caller -> Yes, I think so. Every couple of days. And she's wet every few hours, the brief is wet when I change it. I keep track on the little chart.
Nurse -> That's great that you keep track. That's really helpful for us to see on Thursday.
Caller -> I write down everything. What she eats, when she sleeps, when she's awake. I have a whole notebook.
Nurse -> Bring the notebook out when the nurse comes. She'll love it.
Caller -> I will. My husband used to tease me for being so organized. Before he passed.
Nurse -> I'm sorry for your loss.
Caller -> Thank you. It's been six years. But I still think of him whenever I make the lefse. He always stole the first piece.
Nurse -> Ha. That's such a sweet memory.
Caller -> It is. Okay. Sorry, I'm rambling.
Nurse -> Not at all. I enjoy it. Liv, the sleeping more and eating less are very common at this stage. It's part of her body slowing down. It doesn't mean you're doing anything wrong.
Caller -> I know. But it helps to hear it from you.
Nurse -> Just keep an eye on her breathing and her comfort. If you notice anything different, any change, call us. Day or night.
Caller -> Okay. I will. I didn't want to bother anyone.
Nurse -> You're never bothering us. Call anytime.
Caller -> Thank you, Carla. You're so kind. Oh, one more thing. The neighbors keep bringing food, and I don't know what to do with it all. I feel bad throwing it out.
Nurse -> Don't feel bad. Freeze what you can, and share the rest. People bring food because they want to help.
Caller -> That's true. Mrs. Halvorsen next door brought a whole hotdish yesterday. Tater tot, with the cream of mushroom soup.
Nurse -> Ha. A Minnesota classic.
Caller -> Is there any other kind? Okay. I'll freeze half. Thank you.
Nurse -> Anytime, Liv. Truly.
Caller -> My daughter says I should write a cookbook. Our family recipes. Lefse, and krumkake, and the hotdish.
Nurse -> You absolutely should. I'd buy it.
Caller -> Ha. Maybe someday. First I have to find time.
Nurse -> One step at a time.
Caller -> I'll let you go. Thanks again.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself, Liv. And give Agnes a squeeze from me.
Caller -> I will. Bye now.

Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom. This is Gideon. I'm calling about my dad, Roland Vickers.
Nurse -> Hi, Gordon. Roland Vickers. And his date of birth?
Caller -> It's Gideon. G I D E O N. May twenty second, nineteen forty.
Nurse -> Sorry about that, Gideon. And I have four oh four, five five five, zero one six four for you?
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> What's going on with your dad?
Caller -> His pain is worse. It's his hips, and his lower back. It's been getting worse the last three days.
Nurse -> Okay. How bad is it, zero to ten?
Caller -> He says a five. Maybe a five. It was a three last week.
Nurse -> Okay. What is he taking for pain?
Caller -> The meth a dome. Ten milligrams, three times a day.
Nurse -> And how's that going?
Caller -> It was working. But now it's not enough. So I wanted to ask if I could give him more. Like double the meth a dome.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he sleeping a lot?
Caller -> He sleeps most of the day. More than before.
Nurse -> Okay. And is he throwing up?
Caller -> No. No vomiting.
Nurse -> Okay. Gideon, I can't change the dose over the phone. His pain medicine is one that needs to be adjusted carefully, because it builds up in the body.
Caller -> Okay. But he's hurting.
Nurse -> I understand. I'm going to message our hospice doctor tonight, and ask him to review the pain plan.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll call you tomorrow morning with the doctor's answer.
Nurse -> When was his last bowel movement?
Caller -> Yesterday morning. It was normal.
Nurse -> Good. And how's his appetite?
Caller -> He's eating a little. A few bites at each meal. Mostly he likes the vanilla pudding.
Nurse -> That's fine. Whatever he enjoys.
Caller -> Yeah. He used to be a big eater. A truck driver, thirty years. He could eat a whole pie.
Nurse -> Ha. Which pie?
Caller -> Pecan. Always pecan.
Nurse -> A man with good taste.
Caller -> My mother used to bake it every Thanksgiving. He still talks about it.
Nurse -> That's a lovely memory. Maybe your sister can make one for him.
Caller -> That's a great idea. I'll ask her. She's the baker.
Nurse -> Even a bite of it might make his day.
Caller -> It would. Thank you for that.
Caller -> One more thing, can I ask? He keeps asking for his old truck keys. He's confused sometimes in the evening. Is that normal?
Nurse -> It can be. Some confusion in the evening is common, especially when someone is sleeping more and not eating much. It's not a surprise, but I'll note it for the doctor.
Caller -> Okay. I just go along with it. I tell him they're in the kitchen drawer.
Nurse -> That's a kind way to handle it. Gentle, no arguing.
Caller -> He gets upset if I correct him. So I don't.
Nurse -> Exactly right. Reassure him, keep the lights on in the evening, and keep things calm.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. That helps, knowing I'm not doing it wrong.
Nurse -> You're doing it right, Gideon.
Nurse -> Does he have a hospice aide coming to help with bathing?

transcript:
Nurse -> Maple Lane Home Care, this is Beth.
Caller -> Beth, hi. I think I need some help. It's Vikram Rao. It's about my wife, Sunita.
Nurse -> Hi, Vikram. What's Sunita's date of birth?
Caller -> April eighteenth, nineteen fifty two.
Nurse -> And a number to reach you, in case we get cut off?
Caller -> I'm calling from the house phone. You have it on the chart. I can't remember it right now, I'm sorry. My mind is blank.
Nurse -> That's okay. I'll use the one on file.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> What's going on?
Caller -> I think my wife took one of my pills. By mistake. My metoprolol.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> So we keep our pills in the same cabinet. On the same shelf. Her bottles, my bottles. And mine is fifty milligrams. Hers are different.
Caller -> I counted tonight, because I was going to take mine. And there's one missing. I had exactly the right number. And now I'm one short.
Nurse -> Okay. So you think she took one.
Caller -> I think so. She was in the kitchen about forty minutes ago, she took her evening pills with her tea. And now, she says she feels a little dizzy.
Nurse -> Okay. Did she say she took one of yours?
Caller -> No. She doesn't know. She says she took her pills like always. I don't know. Maybe I miscounted. I'm not sure. But I think she took mine.
Nurse -> Okay. So you're not certain.
Caller -> No. I'm not certain. It's possible I dropped one, or took one this morning and forgot. But the timing, with her being dizzy, I'm worried.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a good instinct, to call. Is Sunita there with you?
Caller -> Yes. She's sitting on the couch. She's okay. She's talking.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she fainted, or almost fainted?
Caller -> No. No fainting. And no chest pain, no trouble breathing. Just a little lightheaded.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a blood pressure cuff?
Caller -> Yes. We have one. Hang on. Sunita, give me your arm. Okay.
Caller -> It says one ten over seventy. And the pulse is sixty two.
Nurse -> Okay. One ten over seventy, pulse sixty two. Those are on the lower side, but they're not alarming. Is her pulse usually around that?
Caller -> I think she's usually around seventy something. Maybe seventy five.
Nurse -> Okay. So it's a bit lower than normal. That could fit with a beta blocker like metoprolol. Let me look at her chart so I know what she takes.
Caller -> Sure. Take your time.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm seeing lisinopril, ten milligrams once a day. Atorvastatin. Famotidine.
Caller -> Yes. She takes the lisinopril in the morning. This morning at eight. The atorvastatin and the famotidine at night.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. The lisinopril can lower blood pressure too, so I want to be extra careful.
Caller -> I see. Yes.
Nurse -> Vikram, a couple of quick questions, because they matter with this kind of medicine. Does Sunita have asthma, or diabetes, or any heart rhythm problems?
Caller -> No asthma. No diabetes. No heart rhythm thing that I know of. She just has the blood pressure, and the cholesterol. And the stomach acid.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Thank you.
Caller -> Is that good? That she doesn't have those?
Nurse -> It's reassuring. It means fewer things to worry about with the extra pill.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I'm trying to breathe.
Nurse -> Take a slow breath. You're doing fine.
Caller -> Sunita is asking what the nurse said. I told her. She says, don't fuss. She says she's fine.
Nurse -> Ha. That sounds like a wife. But we're going to fuss a little anyway.
Caller -> I told her that. She rolled her eyes.
Nurse -> Vikram, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to page our on-call doctor right now. Hold on. Okay. I've sent the page. She'll call us back shortly.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> Meanwhile, I want Sunita to lie down, or at least sit in a good chair. And if she needs to stand up, she should go slowly, and not walk alone.
Caller -> Okay. Sunita, lie down on the couch. Put your feet up. There. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. And no more of your metoprolol, none, not even a half. If she has any more of your pills, I'd like you to take that bottle out of the cabinet now.
Caller -> I took it out. It's in my pocket. I'll put it in my bedroom.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll call you back in fifteen minutes, either way.
Caller -> Fifteen minutes. Okay.
Nurse -> Check her pulse and blood pressure every fifteen minutes, and write down the numbers and the time.
Caller -> Okay. I have a pad. I'll write.
Nurse -> If she faints, or has chest pain, or any trouble breathing, or her pulse drops under fifty, call nine one one right away. Don't wait for us.
Caller -> Nine one one. Under fifty. Okay.
Nurse -> Vikram, how are you holding up?
Caller -> Not great. I'm shaking, honestly. I just feel so terrible. I should have kept our pills apart.
Nurse -> It happens to a lot of couples. It's an easy mistake. But let's fix it going forward. Use a separate pill organizer for each of you, labeled with your names. And keep them in different places.
Caller -> I have two organizers. I just never used hers. I'll do that tomorrow. I'll label them.
Nurse -> Good. And if you can, write the name of each person on the bottles with a marker.
Caller -> I'll do that tonight. I can do that now, while I wait.
Nurse -> Perfect. That'll keep your mind busy, too.
Caller -> Yes. It will. I might ask Sunita to read the labels back to me, so we double check each bottle.
Nurse -> That's a great idea. Two sets of eyes.
Caller -> She's better at reading small print than I am. She has her glasses on. I always lose mine.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the story of every household. Where are yours?
Caller -> On my head. As usual. Sunita just pointed to them.
Nurse -> Ha. There you go.
Caller -> Thank you for the laugh. I needed that. You know, our son keeps telling us to move closer to him. In Chicago. He says it's not safe, two old people alone.
Nurse -> It's a lot to think about. How do you feel about it?
Caller -> I don't want to leave our home. Forty years in this house. Sunita planted every tree in that yard.
Nurse -> That's a big attachment. It sounds like something to talk through with your son, and maybe with our social worker too.
Caller -> Maybe. Tonight made me realize we do need more help, though. More eyes.
Nurse -> That's a wise thing to realize. We can talk about options when things are calmer.
Caller -> I'd like that. Okay.
Caller -> Oh, hold on. The other line. It's my daughter. She's calling. I'll let it go to voicemail. She's calling from Chicago.
Nurse -> No worries. Does she know what's going on?
Caller -> Not yet. I don't want to worry her. But I will call her back as soon as we're done.
Nurse -> That's a good plan. Let's get through this first.
Caller -> Sunita is saying she feels a bit better. She says it's passing.
Nurse -> Good. Keep resting. Keep checking the numbers.
Caller -> Okay. I will. We've been married forty eight years. I can't imagine, if anything.
Nurse -> Vikram, she's talking, her pulse and pressure are okay, and help is on the way. You did the right thing by calling.
Caller -> Thank you. You're very calm. It helps.
Nurse -> I'm here. And Vikram, forty eight years. Do you have any special plans for the anniversary?
Caller -> We usually go to the same Indian restaurant. Little place on Fifth. The owner knows us. He always brings out the gulab jamun for free.
Nurse -> Oh, I love that. Ha. That sounds like a great tradition.
Caller -> It is. We have a table by the window. Same one every year.
Nurse -> I hope you'll still be able to go this year.
Caller -> We will. She'll be fine. I just have to be careful with these pills. I'll be more careful.
Nurse -> You will. Okay. Talk to you in fifteen.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

Nurse -> Ashford Home Care, this is Delia.
Caller -> Hi, uh, yes. Is this the nurse line? For the home health?
Nurse -> It is. How can I help you?
Caller -> I'm Gus Tarkington. I live next door to Ottoline Pembry. I'm not family, I'm just the neighbor.
Nurse -> Okay, Gus. Thanks for calling. Is Ottoline all right?
Caller -> She's okay. I think. Her daughter's out of town till Sunday and asked me to keep an eye on her. And I'm, um, I'm worried about her leg.
Nurse -> Which leg?
Caller -> The right one. The shin. She's got a bandage on it, a big square one, and it came loose. It's flapping.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there any drainage?
Caller -> A little. There's some yellow stuff coming through the gauze. Not a lot. About, uh, about the size of a quarter on the bandage.
Nurse -> Any blood?
Caller -> No blood that I can see. It's more yellowy. Watery.
Nurse -> Okay. And you've seen the wound itself?
Caller -> I looked at the edge. I didn't take it off. I didn't want to hurt her. I'm not a medical person. I fix cars.
Nurse -> That was the right call, Gus. Don't peel anything off.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I just didn't know.
Nurse -> I need to pull up her chart. Do you know her date of birth?
Caller -> Oh, no. No idea. I know she's in her eighties. She tells everyone she's twenty-nine, so.
Nurse -> Ha. That's fine. I can find her by name and address. What's the best number to reach you?
Caller -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one four one.
Nurse -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one four one. Got it.
Caller -> That's my cell. I'm home all day.
Nurse -> Perfect. How is she doing otherwise? Is she warm to the touch, or does she seem feverish?
Caller -> I, I don't think so. I didn't take her temperature. She doesn't have a thermometer, I don't think. She felt normal when I held her hand. Not hot. But I'm not, you know, I'm not a nurse.
Nurse -> That's okay. Is she eating and talking normally?
Caller -> Yeah. She had oatmeal this morning. She told me three different stories about her cat. She's talking my ear off.
Nurse -> Ha. That sounds like a good sign.
Caller -> Yeah. She's sharp. She just sits too long in that chair.
Nurse -> Is she having any pain in the leg, that you know of?
Caller -> She says it's fine. She always says it's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll take that with a grain of salt.
Caller -> Ha. Yeah.
Nurse -> Is the bandage still covering the wound, or is the wound open to the air?
Caller -> It's mostly covering it. The bottom corner is up. Like, peeled up. And the tape is, uh, the tape is curled.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have clean gauze at the house? Dry gauze pads and tape?
Caller -> She's got a box in the bathroom. The daughter keeps it there. There's the square ones and a roll of white tape.
Nurse -> Good. Here's what I'd like you to do. Wash your hands with soap, and then lay a clean dry gauze pad over the whole thing, over the old dressing. Tape it down on all four sides. Don't take off any other dressing.
Caller -> Over the top. Don't take the old one off. Okay.
Nurse -> Right. And have her keep that leg propped up on a pillow while she sits.
Caller -> She's got a footstool. I'll make her use it.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Is it, is it bad? The yellow stuff?
Nurse -> It's hard to say without seeing it. A little clear yellow fluid can be normal. I'd still like a nurse to look at it. I'm going to send someone out tomorrow morning.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. She'll be home. She's always home.
Nurse -> And I'll call her daughter today, so she knows. Do you happen to have her number?
Caller -> I don't. Ottoline would. It's on the fridge, I think. Hang on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> It's on a magnet. A, it's a pizza place magnet. No, wait. That's the pizza number. Hang on.
Nurse -> No rush.
Caller -> Okay. Sorry. It's right here by the phone. But I'll tell you what, it's easier if you look in your records. It's the daughter, Charlotte.
Nurse -> We should have it in the chart. I'll call her myself this afternoon.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I'll tell Ottoline you're calling.
Nurse -> Perfect. Gus, I'd like you to watch for a few things between now and tomorrow. If she gets a fever, or seems confused, or you see red streaks going up the leg, or the bleeding gets heavy, call us right back. If it's an emergency, call nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. Fever. Confused. Red streaks. Heavy bleeding. Nine one one. I'm writing it on my hand.
Nurse -> Ha. Whatever works.
Caller -> I've got a pen right here.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Can I ask something? Is it okay that I'm doing this? I'm not family. I don't want to get in trouble.
Nurse -> You're fine, Gus. You're doing the right thing by calling. We can't share her full chart with you, but we can listen and tell you what to do.
Caller -> That's fine. I just want her okay.
Nurse -> That's what we all want.
Caller -> She makes me banana bread when I help. So I have an interest.
Nurse -> Ha. Then you've got a good reason.
Caller -> I do. Her bread's the best.
Nurse -> Then keep her happy. Anything else I can help with?
Caller -> I don't think so. Oh. Her pills. Does she need her pills?
Nurse -> I can't go over her medicines with you, but she should be taking them as usual. Her daughter set up a pill organizer, right?
Caller -> Yes. The big one with the days. She's, uh, she's been using it.
Nurse -> Then she's fine. Just keep an eye on her.
Caller -> Will do. Thanks, Delia.
Nurse -> Thank you, Gus. Take care.
Caller -> You too. Bye.
