Nurse -> Northstar Home Health, this is Colleen.
Caller -> Hi, Colleen. It's Rosalind Achterberg. I'm an aide. I'm with Winston Abernathy today, and, um, I think he took his heart pill twice.
Nurse -> Okay, Rosalind. Let's slow down. Is he awake and talking to you?
Caller -> Yes. He's talking. He's in his recliner. He says he's a little dizzy.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll want details on that in a second. First, which pill?
Caller -> The metoprolol. The twenty five milligram. It's the one in the blue organizer.
Nurse -> And what happened?
Caller -> So I come in at eight. He's already taken it. He told me. Then at ten I'm doing the dishes and he says, did I take my pill? And I said you did. And he said no I didn't. And I looked in the organizer and the morning slot was empty and the, uh, the noon slot was empty too.
Nurse -> The noon slot?
Caller -> No, sorry. I got that wrong. The morning slot is empty. He took it at eight. Then he must have taken another one around ten. Out of the wrong day. Because Thursday's got one missing too.
Nurse -> So two metoprolol this morning. One at about eight, one at about ten.
Caller -> Yes. I think so. Yes. I'm pretty sure. Two.
Nurse -> Is metoprolol twice a day for him?
Caller -> Twice a day, yes. Morning and evening. Twenty five each time.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Now tell me about the dizzy. How bad?
Caller -> He says the room is, like, tilting a little. When he stands. When he's sitting it's better.
Nurse -> Did he stand up already?
Caller -> Once. To go to the bathroom. I held his arm. He wobbled.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a blood pressure cuff?
Caller -> I do. The wrist one. The agency left it. Let me, hang on.
Nurse -> Take your time. Have him sit still.
Caller -> Okay. It's, uh, it's thinking. Okay. It says ninety six over fifty eight.
Nurse -> Ninety six over fifty eight. What does he usually run?
Caller -> Oh, a hundred thirty something. Over, I don't know. Seventies, I think. That's what's in the book.
Nurse -> Okay. That's lower than usual. What's his heart rate?
Caller -> It says fifty four.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Has he fainted or passed out? Any chest pain?
Caller -> No. No fainting. He didn't hit anything. No chest pain. He'd tell me. He tells me everything.
Nurse -> Good. Is he short of breath?
Caller -> No. He's breathing fine. He's just, he says he feels like a wet noodle.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Is he sweaty or clammy?
Caller -> No. His skin is, um, just normal.
Nurse -> Can I get his date of birth?
Caller -> June twelfth, nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> And a number I can reach you on?
Caller -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one two three.
Nurse -> Got it. Rosalind, here's what I need you to do. I want him to stay seated or lying down. If he has to get up, you stand right next to him and help him up slowly. Do not leave him alone.
Caller -> Sit or lie down. Help him up slow. Don't leave him. Okay.
Nurse -> And do not give the evening metoprolol tonight. Hold it until the clinician calls you back.
Caller -> Hold the evening one. Okay. I won't. I'm here until six. His son comes at six.
Nurse -> Good. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now about the extra dose and the low pressure.
Caller -> Okay. Please. I feel awful. I should have checked the organizer.
Nurse -> It's not your fault, Rosalind. It's easy for a mix up to happen. You did the right thing by calling.
Caller -> I just, I was doing the dishes. I'm usually so careful.
Nurse -> I know. It's okay. Is he drinking fluids?
Caller -> He had juice at breakfast. I can get him water.
Nurse -> Yes, offer small sips. And I'm also sending a nurse out this afternoon to check him.
Caller -> This afternoon. Okay. Good. What time?
Nurse -> I'll have the scheduler call you with the window. It'll be after one.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be here.
Nurse -> If he faints, has chest pain, or gets hard to wake up, call nine one one right away. Don't wait for us.
Caller -> Faints, chest pain, hard to wake. Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> And keep the organizer away from him, so he doesn't take another by mistake.
Caller -> I took it. It's in my bag.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Should I write this down? For the book?
Nurse -> Yes. Write the time and what you saw, and the blood pressure numbers.
Caller -> Ninety six over fifty eight, and heart rate fifty four. Okay.
Nurse -> The clinician will call within about fifteen minutes. Keep your phone near you.
Caller -> I will. I'll keep it in my hand.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> He's asking if he can have his coffee.
Nurse -> Decaf is fine, or just water for now.
Caller -> I'll make him water. He won't like it.
Nurse -> Ha. That's fine.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Colleen. Sorry again.
Nurse -> No need to be sorry. Talk soon.

Nurse -> Juniper Ridge Hospice, this is Pilar.
Caller -> Hi, Pilar. This is Marisol Duquette. I'm a med tech at Cedar Court Assisted Living. I'm calling about one of our residents, Alphonse Greaves. He's one of yours. He's in a lot of pain.
Nurse -> Okay, Marisol. Thank you for calling. Tell me what's going on.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little rattled. I've only been here since seven.
Nurse -> You're doing fine. Take your time.
Caller -> So he's been, um, he started hurting this morning. In his hip. And his lower back. It's the left side. He was fine at breakfast, then around nine he started moaning.
Nurse -> How bad is it? Zero to ten, ten being the worst.
Caller -> I asked him. He said eight. He said eight out of ten. And he's a tough guy. He never complains.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he had anything for it?
Caller -> Yes. I gave him morphine. The five milligram. It was about eleven. So two hours ago, I guess. It's on the PRN sheet. Every four hours as needed.
Nurse -> And did it help at all?
Caller -> Not really. Maybe a little at first. I'm not sure. He's still, he's still grimacing. He keeps shifting around and he can't get comfortable.
Nurse -> Is he eating?
Caller -> He won't. He refused lunch. The aide brought it and he pushed the tray away.
Nurse -> That isn't like him?
Caller -> No. He loves the pot roast on Wednesdays. He loves it.
Nurse -> Ha. Then it's definitely not normal.
Caller -> Exactly.
Nurse -> Okay. Did he fall? Hit anything? Any new injury?
Caller -> No. We checked the incident log. No falls. Nobody saw anything. He's been in bed mostly.
Nurse -> Is he having trouble breathing? Any shortness of breath?
Caller -> No, he's breathing normally. It's just the pain.
Nurse -> Okay. And is he awake and talking?
Caller -> Yes. He's talking. He's, he told me to quit hovering, so.
Nurse -> Ha. That sounds like him.
Caller -> Yeah. But I can tell he's hurting.
Nurse -> I need his date of birth to pull up his chart.
Caller -> February nineteenth, nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> Got it. And what's the best number to reach you at the facility?
Caller -> Three one two, five five five, zero one six two. That's the med room. I'll stay by it.
Nurse -> Perfect. I see his orders here. Marisol, I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now. His pain isn't controlled and he'll need new orders.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Should I give him another dose? It's only been two hours.
Nurse -> No. Please do not give any more morphine until the clinician calls you with orders. I don't want you to double up. Write down the time you gave the last one.
Caller -> No more until they call. And chart the time. Eleven. Okay.
Nurse -> And while you wait, there are a few things you can do to make him more comfortable. Put a pillow between his knees and ease him onto his right side. Do you have a heating pad?
Caller -> We have the warm packs. The ones you heat in the microwave. They're in the supply closet.
Nurse -> Those are good. Wrap it in a towel and put it on his lower back for about twenty minutes. Check his skin so it's not too hot.
Caller -> Pillow between the knees. Warm pack in a towel, twenty minutes. Okay. I'll get one.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send one of our nurses over. She should be there within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. Do I need to tell his daughter?
Nurse -> It's up to the facility, but yes, I'd call her. I'll let the clinician know the daughter's number is in the chart.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let the director know. She'll call the daughter.
Nurse -> Good. Is there a nurse at the facility today?
Caller -> There's one down the hall, but she covers the whole second floor. I'm the one with him.
Nurse -> Okay. Stay with him if you can.
Caller -> I will. I'll go sit with him now.
Nurse -> Good. Keep your voice low and calm.
Caller -> I will. He likes the radio. I'll put on his station.
Nurse -> When the clinician calls, they'll ask about his pain score again and what he's had. Have the sheet in front of you.
Caller -> Yes. Last dose, time, amount. I know the drill.
Nurse -> You do. Thank you.
Caller -> Yes. I've got it. I'll grab the clipboard.
Nurse -> Marisol, is anyone else with him? Family there?
Caller -> No. His daughter comes Sunday. He doesn't have anyone else.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell him we're on our way. It helps to hear it.
Nurse -> One more thing. Is the door to his room easy for the nurse to get to?
Caller -> Yes. I'll leave it propped. She can come straight in.
Caller -> I will. I'll tell him help is coming.
Nurse -> Thank you. He's lucky to have you.
Caller -> I just want him to stop hurting. It's hard to watch.
Nurse -> I know. We'll get it under control.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Pilar.

Caller -> Hard to wake. Breathing. Okay. I'll watch.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cobalt Bay Home Health, this is Teodoro.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Teodoro. It's Philippa Okonkwo. I'm calling about my brother, Cordell. Cordell Hathaway.
Nurse -> Hi, Philippa. Can you spell his last name for me?
Caller -> H A T H A W A Y. Hathaway. It always gets turned into Hathaway with an E. People just assume.
Nurse -> Ha. Happens to everyone.
Caller -> Cordell just laughs it off. He says it's a family tradition.
Nurse -> Got it. H A T H A W A Y. Cordell Hathaway. What's going on?
Caller -> It's his mask. The BiPAP mask. The cushion part, the part that sits on his face, it's cracked and it's leaking air all night. And I need a new one.
Nurse -> Okay. How long has it been cracking?
Caller -> A few days. It was a little crack. Now it's, you can see through it. Along the side, by the nose.
Nurse -> Does he have a spare?
Caller -> We have one. But it's the wrong size. It's a medium and he wears a small. I don't know why they sent us a medium. It's been in the drawer since the spring.
Nurse -> Okay. So one cracked small, and one spare medium.
Caller -> Yes. That's all we have.
Nurse -> What's his date of birth, Philippa?
Caller -> September fourth, nineteen seventy three. He's fifty two. He's too young for this.
Nurse -> I'm so sorry. How is he sleeping?
Caller -> Not great. The leak makes a whistling sound, and it blows air in his eyes, and he keeps waking up. He's tired in the day.
Nurse -> Is he able to breathe comfortably when he's awake, off the machine?
Caller -> Yes. He's fine awake. He's sitting up right now doing his crossword. He doesn't seem short of breath.
Nurse -> Good to hear.
Nurse -> And is he with you?
Caller -> I'm at his house. I come over in the morning, I do his meds and breakfast. His wife works nights, so I cover. She's a nurse, actually.
Nurse -> Oh, that's a hard schedule.
Caller -> It is. They manage. He doesn't like asking for help. So I just show up.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sister.
Caller -> I try. He says I hover.
Nurse -> What number can I reach you at?
Caller -> Four one four, five five five, zero one four three.
Nurse -> Four one four, five five five, zero one four three. Got it. And what brand is the mask? Is there a name on the box?
Caller -> Let me go look. Hang on, I have the box in the closet.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. It's a, uh, nasal mask. It says size small on the little tag. The cushion has a number, I can read it.
Nurse -> I don't need the number. I'll get it from the chart. I'll order a small cushion.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. A small. Not a medium.
Nurse -> Right. I'll order the small cushion for him.
Caller -> Okay. Good. How long will it take? Because tonight he's going to need to sleep.
Nurse -> I can get it to you tomorrow afternoon.
Caller -> Tomorrow afternoon. So tonight we're stuck with the leaky one.
Nurse -> Yes. For tonight use the cracked one. Make sure the chin strap is snug, and keep the head of the bed raised so it seals better. Don't use the medium. A wrong size will leak even worse.
Caller -> Cracked one. Snug strap. Head up. Don't use the medium. Okay.
Nurse -> And if the air leaks into his eyes, you can put a little tape on the crack from the outside. Only if you have to. A small piece of medical tape.
Caller -> I have the paper tape. I'll try that.
Nurse -> Good. Philippa, I also want to go over when to call nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. Go ahead.
Nurse -> If he cannot get air, if his lips or face turn blue, or if he's hard to wake up, call nine one one right away.
Caller -> Can't get air. Blue. Hard to wake. Nine one one. Yes. His wife told me the same thing.
Nurse -> Good. She'd know.
Caller -> She knows all of it. She keeps a list on the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is there anything else you need? Tubing? Filters?
Caller -> I think the filters are okay. I changed one last week. Tubing's fine. It's just the cushion.
Nurse -> Alright. Do you want me to have the delivery person call before they come?
Caller -> Yes. Call my cell. I'll let them in. Cordell sleeps late.
Nurse -> I'll note that.
Caller -> Thank you. I really appreciate it.
Nurse -> Anytime. We'll get him a good seal.
Caller -> I hope so. He needs his sleep. They said at the clinic that sleep helps. For the, you know. For the muscles.
Nurse -> It does. Rest is important.
Caller -> Yeah. I just don't want him to give up on the mask.
Nurse -> He won't. A good fit makes all the difference.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell him it's coming.
Nurse -> Tell him I said hello.
Caller -> I will. He likes you guys. He says the nurse with the bow tie is his favorite.
Nurse -> Ha. That would be Rafael. I'll tell him.
Caller -> Okay. Bye now.
Nurse -> Bye, Philippa.

transcript:
Nurse -> Maple Lane Home Care, this is Ingrid.
Caller -> Hi, Ingrid. It's Linus Ballantyne. I'm calling about my mom, Eugenia Ballantyne. She's on your service.
Nurse -> Hi, Linus. How can I help?
Caller -> I have a pill question. About her leg pain meds. I think I'm confused about which is which.
Nurse -> Sure. Let's sort it out together.
Caller -> Thanks. I've been staring at these bottles for twenty minutes.
Nurse -> That's what I'm here for. Which medicines are you looking at?
Caller -> There's two. One is the gabapentin. And one is the oxycodone. I've got the bottles on the counter.
Nurse -> Okay. Read me the gabapentin label.
Caller -> Gabapentin. One hundred milligrams. Three times a day. No wait. Hang on. Let me look at it again. I'm reading the wrong line. It's three hundred milligrams. Three hundred. Three times a day.
Nurse -> Three hundred milligrams, three times a day. Okay. When was her last dose?
Caller -> At noon. I gave it with her lunch.
Nurse -> Good. And the oxycodone?
Caller -> Oxycodone, five milligrams. Every four hours as needed for pain. It says one tablet.
Nurse -> When did she last have it?
Caller -> Two o'clock. Right after her nap. She said her leg was killing her. So I gave her one.
Nurse -> Okay. Did it help?
Caller -> Yes, some. She said it went from a seven to a five. But it's still there. It's a dull, throbby ache in the calf.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she sleepy? More sleepy than usual?
Caller -> No. She's awake. She's watching her game shows. She's, you know, she's herself. She's yelling at the contestants.
Nurse -> Does she get the answers right?
Caller -> Mostly. She's insufferable about it.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign.
Caller -> Yeah. She's got opinions.
Nurse -> What's her date of birth, Linus?
Caller -> November thirtieth, nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> And your number in case I need to call back?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one five eight.
Nurse -> Got it. So what's your question exactly?
Caller -> I don't know which one she's supposed to take when. Like, the gabapentin, is that for the pain? Or is that a different thing? And can I give the oxycodone right now, because she's hurting again? It's almost five.
Nurse -> Good question. They work differently. The gabapentin is for nerve pain. She takes it three times a day, every day, on a schedule, whether or not she's hurting. It builds up and works over time.
Caller -> Okay. So that's not a, an as needed one.
Nurse -> Right. It's scheduled. The oxycodone is the as-needed. You give it only when she has pain, and there has to be at least four hours between doses.
Caller -> Four hours. Two o'clock, so, six o'clock.
Nurse -> Correct. It's almost five now, so she'd have to wait until after six.
Caller -> Okay. But she's hurting now. What do I do for the next hour?
Nurse -> Try a warm compress on the calf, keep the leg propped up, and see if she'd like a distraction. Is her next gabapentin due at dinner?
Caller -> Yes. At dinner. Around six.
Nurse -> That's fine. Give the gabapentin at dinner. You can give the oxycodone at six too, if she still needs it. It's safe to give them close together as long as she isn't very sleepy.
Caller -> At six. Both. If she needs it. Okay. And if she's sleepy?
Nurse -> Then skip the oxycodone and call us. Some people get drowsy when both are in their system.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense. I'll watch her.
Nurse -> Did you give any other medicine for the leg? Tylenol? Ibuprofen?
Caller -> No. Just those two.
Nurse -> Good. Please don't add any other pain pills without asking us.
Caller -> Okay. I won't.
Nurse -> I'm going to call you tomorrow morning to see how she did overnight.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. That's great. What time?
Nurse -> Between nine and ten.
Caller -> I'll be here. I work from home.
Nurse -> That helps. Is she alone when you're on calls?
Caller -> No, I set up in the living room next to her. She talks through my meetings.
Nurse -> Perfect. And Linus, call us if she gets very sleepy, confused, or if the pain stays high even after the oxycodone.
Caller -> Sleepy. Confused. Pain doesn't budge. Okay.
Nurse -> Is the leg swollen or red or warm?
Caller -> No. It looks the same as last week. The nurse looked at it on Monday.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring.
Caller -> Do you want me to write down the times? Like a log?
Nurse -> Yes, that's a great idea. Write the drug, the dose, and the time every time you give it.
Caller -> I have a notepad on the fridge. I'll put it there.
Nurse -> Good. Also keep both bottles on a high shelf, away from the TV tray.
Caller -> They are. I put them in the cabinet after each dose.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I'm sorry I got the gabapentin mixed up. I'm still learning all this.
Nurse -> You caught it yourself, Linus. That's exactly what we want. Always read the label twice.
Caller -> Twice. I'll make it a rule.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Ingrid.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Talk tomorrow.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Sandpiper Home Health, this is Bettina.
Caller -> Hello. Yes. Hello. Um, my name is Hester Quill. I'm calling about my friend. Ludmila Voss. She's one of yours. I'm from her church.
Nurse -> Hi, Hester. Thanks for calling. What's going on?
Caller -> I hope it's okay that I'm calling. I'm not family.
Nurse -> Of course. We're glad you did.
Caller -> It's her water pill. I think the, there's a mix up with the dose and I don't know who to ask. She's, well, she's a little foggy on the details.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's go through it. Which water pill?
Caller -> Furosemide. The bottle says furosemide.
Nurse -> And what does the label say for the dose?
Caller -> Twenty milligrams. Once a day. In the morning. It says take one tablet.
Nurse -> Okay. And what's the problem?
Caller -> Well, the paper from the hospital. The discharge paper. It says forty. Forty milligrams, once a day. And I said, Ludmila, which is it? And she said she thinks it's, oh, I don't know, she said the little white one. Both of them are white.
Nurse -> Ha. That doesn't help us much.
Caller -> No. They're twins.
Nurse -> So the bottle says twenty and the hospital paper says forty.
Caller -> Yes. That's the whole thing. I don't know which to follow.
Nurse -> Okay. Did she take it today?
Caller -> This morning. One tablet. From the bottle. I watched her.
Nurse -> One tablet of the twenty.
Caller -> I think so. I think. It's the bottle in the kitchen. It says twenty. I haven't checked if there's another bottle somewhere.
Nurse -> Is there a pillbox, or just the bottles?
Caller -> Just the bottles. She doesn't like the weekly boxes.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. How are her ankles?
Caller -> Puffy. Both of them. She's got those, what do you call, sock marks. The marks where the socks dig in. And her shoes don't fit.
Nurse -> Is the swelling worse than it was at discharge?
Caller -> I can't say. I wasn't here last week. But it's not going down, that I can tell. Not yet.
Nurse -> Does she have any trouble breathing? Lying flat, or walking across the room?
Caller -> No. No, she's breathing fine. She walked to the kitchen and back. She was a little tired. But no huffing.
Nurse -> Good. Any chest pain?
Nurse -> Dizzy or lightheaded when she stands?
Caller -> A little at the church picnic, she said. Not today.
Caller -> No.
Nurse -> Okay. I need her date of birth to find her in our system.
Caller -> Oh, goodness. Let me think. Hang on. It's on the, here, I have the paper. August fourteenth, nineteen thirty six.
Nurse -> August fourteenth, nineteen thirty six. Thank you. And your number?
Caller -> Nine oh one, five five five, zero one five one.
Nurse -> Is that a cell?
Caller -> My home line. I have an answering machine, so leave a message if I'm out.
Nurse -> Got it, Hester. So here's the situation. I can't tell you over the phone which dose is right. I don't want to guess. Sometimes the hospital changes a dose at discharge and the pharmacy is still using the old bottle. Sometimes the paper is wrong.
Caller -> Oh. So it could be either one.
Nurse -> It could. I need to check the actual order with her doctor's office. I'll call the discharging physician's office today to find out.
Caller -> Oh, thank goodness. Thank you.
Nurse -> Until we know, please give only what's on the bottle label. That's the pharmacy's most recent fill. One tablet of the twenty in the morning. Don't double up, and don't skip it.
Caller -> Just the bottle. The twenty. Okay. And not the forty.
Nurse -> Right. And keep the bottle and the discharge paper together so the clinician can look at both.
Caller -> I'll put them in a bag. A plastic bag. On the table.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll call you back by the end of the day once I know.
Caller -> By the end of the day. Okay. What if I don't hear?
Nurse -> Then call us again. Ask for me, Bettina.
Caller -> Bettina. Okay. I'm writing it.
Nurse -> Good. And Hester, your name again for the chart?
Caller -> Hester. H E S T E R. Quill.
Nurse -> Another thing. Does she weigh herself?
Caller -> I don't think so. There's a scale in the bathroom. Under the sink. It's covered in dust.
Nurse -> Ha. Wipe it off first.
Caller -> I will. I'll bring a rag.
Nurse -> Could you have her step on it tomorrow morning, after she uses the bathroom, and write it down? Same time every day.
Caller -> I can do that. I'll come by at nine.
Nurse -> Great. Call us right away if she has trouble breathing, any chest pain, or she gains more than a couple of pounds overnight. If she can't breathe or has chest pain, call nine one one.
Caller -> Breathing. Chest pain. Weight gain. Nine one one for the first two. Okay.
Nurse -> Does she have family nearby?
Caller -> A niece in Ohio. She calls on Sundays. Mostly it's the church ladies. We take turns. I have Tuesday and Thursday.
Nurse -> That's a lovely group.
Caller -> We try. She's done so much for the church. She ran the bake sale for thirty years.
Nurse -> Ha. A legend.
Caller -> She makes a lemon bar you would not believe.
Nurse -> I'd like to have the recipe.
Caller -> Oh, she'll never give it up. She'll take it to the grave.
Nurse -> Ha. Well, Hester, thank you for calling and for looking out for her.
Caller -> Of course. I'll wait for your call.
Nurse -> Talk soon.
Caller -> Thank you. Bye bye.

Caller -> He's in the bed. He's awake. He's, he's calm. He was crying before. Now he's calm.
Nurse -> Is he talking to you?
Caller -> A little. He said he's sorry. I told him there's nothing to be sorry for.
Nurse -> Are you with him?
Caller -> I'm in the bedroom door. I'm looking right at him.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he taken any extra pills? Anything tonight beyond his usual?
Caller -> No. No. I don't think so. I gave him his nine o'clock ones. I was here. I took the bottles out. They're in the kitchen now. On the counter. I counted.
Nurse -> You did the right thing taking them out. Did you count them against the log?
Caller -> I counted. I think it's right. I'm shaking. I can't tell. I think it's right.
Nurse -> That's okay. We'll go over it together in a minute. Has he said anything like this before?
Caller -> Not like this. He said once he's tired of fighting. But never about the pills.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he in pain tonight?
Caller -> Yes. It's his belly. He keeps holding it. He says it's a six. A bad six. Maybe seven.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll make sure the clinician knows about the pain too.
Caller -> Yes. I think the pain is part of it. He hasn't slept in two days.
Nurse -> Okay. When did he last have something for it?
Caller -> At nine. And before that, six.
Nurse -> Alright. Calista, I want to stay on the phone with you. Can you tell me his date of birth?
Caller -> March twenty first, nineteen seventy eight. He's forty eight.
Nurse -> And a number in case we get cut off?
Caller -> Six one zero, five five five, zero one zero seven.
Nurse -> Got it. Here's what I want you to do. Stay with him. Don't leave him alone in the room, even for a minute. Is there anyone else in the house who can sit with him?
Caller -> My sister's on her way. She lives ten minutes away. I called her first.
Nurse -> Does she know what's going on?
Caller -> Yes. I told her on the phone. She's bringing her husband to stay overnight.
Nurse -> Good. Keep all of his medicines locked up or in a place he can't reach. You give every dose yourself, and write it down. Do you have a lockbox?
Caller -> We have a, there's a small safe in the closet. For the passports. I can put them in there.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Do that now, while I'm on the line.
Caller -> Okay. Hang on. I'm going to the kitchen. Don't hang up.
Nurse -> I'm right here.
Caller -> Okay. I have the bottles. I'm going to the closet. Okay. It's in. The safe is closed.
Nurse -> Where's the key or the code?
Caller -> It's a code. Only I know it. I'll change it anyway.
Nurse -> Great. Thank you. Is his bedroom door open? Can you hear him?
Caller -> Yes. I can hear him. He's breathing. He's just lying there.
Nurse -> Is he looking at you, answering when you speak?
Caller -> Yes. He just nodded at me. He's tired.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now. And I'll reach our social worker, too. Someone will call you back very soon.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Yes. Please.
Nurse -> And I'm sending a nurse out to you. She should be there within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. I'll unlock the door. Or no, I'll wait by the door.
Nurse -> Good. The social worker will reach out to you both in the morning.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Calista, I want you to have a number. If at any time you or he feels like he might hurt himself, call or text nine eight eight, the crisis line. It's free and it's all day and night. And if he tries to take pills or hurt himself, call nine one one.
Caller -> Nine eight eight. Nine one one. Okay. I'll write it on my hand. I need a pen. Hang on.
Nurse -> No rush.
Caller -> Okay. I have it.
Nurse -> It might help to talk with him gently. Ask him how he's feeling. You don't have to fix it. Just listen.
Caller -> I don't know what to say. I'm afraid I'll say the wrong thing.
Nurse -> You won't. You know him better than anyone.
Nurse -> There's no wrong thing. Tell him you love him and that you're here. Ask him if he's afraid.
Caller -> Okay. I can do that.
Nurse -> And you're not alone in this. We'll all help.
Caller -> Thank you. I'm sorry for crying.
Nurse -> Never apologize. You're doing everything right.
Caller -> I just feel like I should have seen it.
Nurse -> This is not your fault. It is a lot to carry, and you're carrying it.
Caller -> My sister's here. I can hear the car.
Nurse -> Good. Let her in. Is the nurse's number in your phone?
Caller -> Yes. I have the hospice card on the fridge.
Nurse -> Great. The clinician will call within about ten minutes. Please keep this line free.
Caller -> I will. I'll hang up now and wait. Okay. Thank you, Octavia.
Nurse -> I'm here if you need me. Take care.

transcript:
Nurse -> Larkspur Home Health, this is Wendell.
Caller -> Hi, Wendell. This is Briony Castellanos. I'm calling about my grandfather. Anselm Castellanos.
Nurse -> Hi, Briony. How can I help?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm on my lunch break, so I'm eating a salad and calling.
Nurse -> No problem. Chew first.
Caller -> Ha. Okay.
Caller -> He forgot to take his pill this morning. The predisone. And it's two in the afternoon. I don't know if he should take it now.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me make sure I have the right one. Predisone, is that what it says on the bottle?
Caller -> That's how I say it. It's the steroid one. It's a little white pill. I'll read you the label. Hang on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> It says, um, predisone. Ten milligrams. Take one tablet by mouth every morning with food.
Nurse -> Got it. That sounds like his prednisone.
Nurse -> Is there a pharmacy name on the label?
Caller -> Yes. The one on Fifth. They're always so nice.
Caller -> Yes. That one.
Nurse -> When was his last dose?
Caller -> Yesterday morning. He took it with his oatmeal. Today he got up late, and he went straight to the garden. And I was at work. I'm here now on my break.
Nurse -> Okay. So he missed this morning.
Caller -> Yes. I came over at lunch, and I saw the pill still in the organizer.
Nurse -> Did you see him at lunch?
Caller -> I did. He's fine. He had a sandwich. He's been out in the yard moving rocks. At eighty five.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a lot of rocks.
Caller -> He's a lot of man.
Nurse -> Does he wear his hat out there, and drink water?
Caller -> The big straw hat. And I make him carry a bottle.
Nurse -> What's his date of birth, Briony?
Caller -> February second, nineteen thirty nine.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Two one two, five five five, zero one five six.
Nurse -> Perfect. How has he been feeling otherwise?
Caller -> Honestly? Kind of wired. He's been up at three in the morning the past few nights. Wandering the kitchen. Making toast. He's not tired but he's, like, buzzing.
Nurse -> That can be from the steroid. Is his appetite okay?
Caller -> Oh my gosh. He's eating everything. He ate a whole pie on Sunday. Not a slice. A pie.
Nurse -> Ha. Also a steroid effect.
Caller -> I figured. Is that normal?
Caller -> The pie, I thought we'd have to call you.
Nurse -> Ha. No emergency for a pie.
Nurse -> It's common. Any stomach pain, or heartburn? Black or dark stools?
Caller -> No. No stomach complaints. He'd tell me. And no, nothing dark. I help him in the bathroom sometimes.
Nurse -> Good. Okay, here's what to do. Give him the ten milligram tablet now, with some food. A sandwich or yogurt, something in his stomach. Then tomorrow morning give his regular dose as usual. Don't double up. And don't ever stop it suddenly.
Caller -> Give it now with food. Tomorrow regular. Don't double. Okay. He'll be annoyed. He thinks he doesn't need it.
Caller -> I'm writing it on a napkin. Napkin from the salad.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Ha. A lot of people feel that way. But the body gets used to it, so stopping fast can make him sick.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell him. I'll say the nurse said.
Nurse -> Say the nurse said. It works every time.
Caller -> Ha. Yes.
Nurse -> Give the pill in the morning, always. It's best early in the day, because later doses can keep him awake. The restlessness and the big appetite should ease when his dose goes down. Keep an eye on his stomach, and let us know if you see any pain or black stools.
Caller -> Morning. Watch his stomach. Black stools. Okay.
Nurse -> Could you set an alarm or put a sticky note on the organizer?
Caller -> I'll put a note on the coffee pot. He never misses the coffee.
Nurse -> That's a smart place.
Caller -> I'm full of ideas.
Nurse -> Does he live alone?
Caller -> With my grandmother. She's the one who takes his blood pressure every night. She's strict.
Nurse -> I'll call you tomorrow morning to see how the night went and how he's feeling.
Caller -> That's great. I'll be at my desk. Call my cell. I'll pick up.
Caller -> Is nine okay? I have a meeting at ten.
Nurse -> Nine is fine. I'll call at nine.
Nurse -> Will do. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Oh, can he have coffee in the afternoon? He wants a cup.
Nurse -> Maybe decaf. Too much caffeine on top of the steroid won't help his sleep.
Caller -> Decaf. He'll complain. Okay.
Nurse -> Ha. Let him complain.
Caller -> I should go, my break's almost over.
Nurse -> Go ahead. One last thing, did he take anything else today?
Caller -> Just his water pill and the vitamin. I checked the organizer.
Caller -> Thank you, Wendell. I feel better.
Nurse -> Anytime. Bye, Briony.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Redwood Home Health, this is Matilda.
Caller -> Hi, Matilda. It's Odalys Fenwick. I'm one of the aides. I'm with Bartholomew Yeager today. Just a regular update.
Nurse -> Perfect timing. I was about to start the afternoon calls.
Caller -> Ha. I'll be quick.
Nurse -> Hi, Odalys. Good to hear from you. How's he doing?
Caller -> Pretty good. He's two weeks out from the hip.
Nurse -> Right. Tell me about his pain.
Caller -> He says a three. Sometimes a four after the walk. He takes his Tylenol in the morning and that's about it.
Nurse -> Okay. And getting around?
Caller -> He's using the walker. He gets to the bathroom on his own. I walk behind him. He doesn't love me walking behind him.
Caller -> I told him, I'm not judging, I'm just your shadow.
Nurse -> Ha. He'll get used to it.
Caller -> He says he's not an invalid.
Nurse -> How's his eating?
Caller -> Great. Three meals. Eggs this morning. A turkey sandwich at noon. He eats like a teenager.
Nurse -> Good protein is important for healing.
Caller -> I'm sneaking in extra eggs.
Nurse -> Good. Let's talk about the incision. Anything unusual? Redness, swelling, drainage?
Caller -> No. I looked this morning when I helped with the dressing. It's dry. It's closed. There's a little pink at the ends, but that's all. No fluid, no smell.
Nurse -> That's expected at this stage.
Nurse -> That's what I like to hear. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> I took it at ten. Ninety eight point four.
Nurse -> Wonderful. Can I have his date of birth?
Caller -> December ninth, nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Five oh five, five five five, zero one seven eight.
Nurse -> Got it. Was there something you needed today besides the update?
Caller -> Yes. A question. He wants to take a shower. He says he's tired of the sponge bath. Can he?
Nurse -> Not yet. Until the surgeon clears him, he should sponge bathe. Keep the incision dry and covered. Water on it too soon can bring in infection.
Caller -> No shower. Sponge bath. Okay. He's going to be grumpy.
Nurse -> I'm sure. Maybe a nice warm washcloth and a clean shirt will help.
Caller -> I'll put a towel in the dryer so it's warm. He likes that.
Nurse -> Great idea.
Caller -> Also, he asked about his therapy. He thought the therapist was coming Thursday but the paper says Friday.
Nurse -> I'll check the schedule. I'm going to message the therapist to confirm which day.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. He'd hate to miss it. He actually likes her.
Nurse -> Ha. A fan of the therapist.
Caller -> He says she's the only one who doesn't talk down to him.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. Is he doing his exercises?
Caller -> Mostly. He does the ankle pumps. The leg lifts he skips when he thinks I'm not looking.
Nurse -> Ha. Encourage him. The therapist will want to see progress.
Caller -> I will. I'll tell him she's going to check.
Nurse -> Tell him that. Now, safety. Is the walker always within reach?
Caller -> Next to the chair. Next to the bed. I made him a little parking spot.
Caller -> With tape on the floor. He thinks it's hilarious.
Nurse -> A parking spot, I love it. Is the path to the bathroom clear?
Caller -> I moved the rug. And the cat's food dish.
Nurse -> Good. What does he wear on his feet?
Caller -> Slippers. The soft ones with the rubber on the bottom.
Nurse -> Perfect. Non-slip. Keep that up.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And Odalys, if he gets a fever, or the incision gets red, or starts draining, or if his calf is swollen or painful, call us right away.
Caller -> Fever. Red or draining. Calf swelling. Okay. I'll watch the calf. He sits so much.
Nurse -> Good. Also if he gets short of breath or chest pain, call nine one one.
Caller -> Nine one one. Understood.
Nurse -> Walking every hour or two helps. Short walks.
Caller -> We do a lap of the living room every hour. I set a timer on my phone.
Nurse -> That's a lovely routine.
Caller -> I try. He tells me stories while we walk. Last time it was about his Navy days.
Nurse -> Oh, that must be something.
Caller -> He was a cook on a destroyer. He makes the best chili.
Nurse -> Ha. I'd like a bowl.
Caller -> He'll give you the recipe if you ask. It's classified.
Caller -> He says his mother took the recipe to her grave and he's following her lead.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Anything else?
Nurse -> Is his daughter still coming Sunday?
Caller -> She is. She's bringing groceries and a casserole.
Caller -> No. That's it. Thanks, Matilda.
Nurse -> Thank you for the update.
Caller -> Okay. I'll call back if the sponge bath turns into a fight.
Nurse -> Ha. We're here.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Meridian Home Health, this is Roxanne.
Caller -> Hi. Um. I saw something online. A job. For a, a nursing assistant. Is that still open?
Nurse -> I'm on the clinical line. I don't handle hiring. Which posting did you see?
Caller -> It was on one of those job sites. It said home health aide, nursing assistant, part time or full time. Evenings.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like one of ours. You'll want to apply through the careers page on our website.
Caller -> Okay. Can I just ask a couple of things first? Because I don't have the certificate yet.
Nurse -> Which certificate?
Caller -> The CNA. I'm in the class. I finish in March. But I have a lot of experience. I took care of my grandmother for three years.
Nurse -> That's great experience. I can't speak to the requirements. Human resources can tell you if you can start before you're certified.
Caller -> Do you know, like, what it pays?
Nurse -> I don't. It's not something I'm able to quote on this line.
Caller -> Okay. That's fair. Is there a number for human resources?
Nurse -> The number is on the website, under careers. They're open weekdays, eight to five.
Caller -> Weekdays eight to five. Okay. I'll look.
Nurse -> You can also leave your information with them and they'll call you back.
Caller -> Do they, like, drug test? Because I'm not worried, I just wanted to know.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, I don't have those details. HR will walk you through the whole process.
Caller -> Okay. Thanks. I'm sorry for bothering you. I didn't know who else to call.
Nurse -> It's no bother. Good luck with your class.
Caller -> Thanks. It's a lot of studying. Vital signs. Infection control. My brain hurts.
Nurse -> Ha. It gets easier. You'll do great.
Caller -> Thank you. Have a good day.
Nurse -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Meridian Home Health, this is Roxanne.
Caller -> Roxanne, hi, it's Priya Venkataraman, I'm an aide at Briarwood Assisted Living. I need help. Rosendo Alcantar is choking, kind of. He's coughing and gurgling.
Nurse -> Okay, Priya. Is he awake? Can he breathe?
Caller -> Yes, yes, he's breathing, I think. I'm sorry, I'm shaking.
Nurse -> It's okay. Answer what you can.
Caller -> He's awake. He's breathing but it's wet. It's gurgly. He started during lunch, a few minutes ago. He was eating the, the pureed chicken.
Nurse -> Is he able to speak?
Caller -> He's trying. It's just a whisper. He can't get a whole sentence out.
Nurse -> Does he seem to be pointing at his throat or his chest?
Caller -> His throat. He keeps touching his neck.
Nurse -> Okay. Look at his lips. What color are they?
Caller -> They're, I think a little blue. Like a purple. Around the mouth.
Nurse -> Do you have a finger oxygen monitor?
Caller -> I do. It's on him. It says, hold on, eighty six. Eighty six percent.
Caller -> Is that bad? That's bad, right?
Nurse -> It's lower than we want. That's why we're calling for help.
Nurse -> Priya, I want you to call nine one one right now. Hang up with me and call. Or have someone else call while you stay with him.
Caller -> Okay, okay, I'll yell for Marcus. Marcus! Call nine one one! Rosendo's choking! Sorry. He's going.
Nurse -> Priya, are you there?
Caller -> Yes. Sorry. I yelled. He's calling.
Nurse -> Good. Is Marcus calling?
Caller -> Yes. He's on the desk phone. Okay.
Nurse -> Sit Rosendo straight up. Lean him a little forward. Don't lay him back.
Caller -> He's upright. I'm holding him. He's still coughing. He's coughing hard.
Caller -> Is it okay to rub his back?
Nurse -> Not yet. Just hold him steady.
Nurse -> That's good. Coughing means air is moving. Let him cough. Don't pat his back unless he stops coughing and can't breathe.
Caller -> Okay. He's coughing. It's getting a little clearer. A little.
Nurse -> Do not give him anything by mouth. No water, no food. Nothing.
Caller -> Not even a sip? His mouth is dry.
Nurse -> Not even a sip. The paramedics will decide.
Caller -> Nothing. Right. No water.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now and let them know.
Caller -> Okay. Please.
Nurse -> What's his date of birth, Priya? For the paramedics.
Caller -> Um. April seventeenth, nineteen thirty two.
Nurse -> April seventeenth, nineteen thirty two. Does he have any allergies, any DNR?
Caller -> Not that I know. Penicillin maybe. I'll check.
Caller -> I don't, hold on. He has a full code. I think. It's in the front of the chart. Marcus will have it. Marcus, grab Rosendo's chart!
Nurse -> Good. Keep him upright. Stay with him.
Caller -> I'm here. I'm right here. His color's a little better. It's pink. It was blue.
Nurse -> Check the monitor again.
Caller -> Hold on, it's jumping around because he's moving. It's, ninety one. Ninety one.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep the finger still if you can.
Caller -> Ninety one. It's coming up. Ninety one.
Nurse -> Okay. That's improving. But he still needs to go to the hospital. The paramedics will check him.
Caller -> Yes. They're coming. Marcus says five minutes.
Nurse -> Perfect. What number are you calling from?
Caller -> It's the nurses' station. Five oh five, five five five, zero one five three.
Nurse -> Got it. Is there a family member to call?
Caller -> His son lives across town. He visits Sundays. Rosendo has a whole picture wall of grandchildren.
Caller -> His son. Marcus has the number. We'll call him once the ambulance is here.
Nurse -> Good. Priya, you're doing great.
Caller -> I'm so scared. He's like my grandpa. He tells me jokes every morning.
Nurse -> Stay calm. Talk to him. Tell him help is on the way.
Caller -> He likes when I sing. I'll hum something. Sorry, this is silly.
Nurse -> It's not silly. Anything that keeps him calm.
Caller -> Rosendo, help's coming. You're okay. He's nodding. He squeezed my hand.
Nurse -> That's good. Keep him calm and upright.
Caller -> They're asking me questions. What do I say?
Nurse -> Tell them what you told me. Coughing at lunch, pureed chicken, blue lips, eighty six percent, now ninety one.
Caller -> Okay. Coughing, chicken, blue, eighty six, ninety one.
Caller -> I hear the siren. They're here! They're here. Marcus is letting them in.
Caller -> Marcus is getting his medication list too. The one with the heart pills.
Nurse -> Good. Tell the paramedics what happened, and give them his chart. They'll take it from here.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I have to go. Thank you!
Nurse -> Go ahead. I'll update the clinician.
Caller -> Bye!

Nurse -> Juniper Ridge Hospice, this is Genevieve.
Caller -> Hi, Genevieve. It's Ruthanne Gallagher. I'm calling about my father, Cornelius Mabry.
Nurse -> Hi, Ruthanne. It's the middle of the night. Is he all right?
Caller -> He's, he's okay. I think. He's hurting. And I can't figure out the morphine. The measuring.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's take it one thing at a time. I'm here.
Caller -> Thank you. I've been staring at this bottle for twenty minutes. I'm sorry to call so late.
Nurse -> Never apologize. That's what the line is for.
Caller -> I keep thinking I'll wake him. The house is so quiet.
Nurse -> Speak softly. He'll hear your voice and feel safer.
Caller -> My brother usually does the medicines. He's on a flight. He's flying in tonight, he lands at seven. So tonight it's me. Alone with Dad.
Nurse -> Okay. You've got me. Let's go through it. Can you read me the label on the morphine bottle?
Caller -> Hang on. I'm turning the light on. Okay. It says morphine sulfate oral solution. Twenty milligrams per milliliter. And then it says, concentrate. In bold. And then the directions say, give point two five milliliters every two hours as needed for pain.
Nurse -> Okay. And do you remember what the dose is in milligrams?
Caller -> The paper from the nurse says five milligrams. Five milligrams every two hours as needed.
Nurse -> That matches. Point two five milliliters is five milligrams, because the bottle has twenty milligrams in every full milliliter.
Caller -> Okay. But I don't understand. Five milligrams or point two five? Which one do I give?
Nurse -> Both mean the same thing. Five milligrams is the dose. Point two five milliliters, or a quarter of a milliliter, is how much liquid that is.
Caller -> Oh. So the milliliters is the amount of liquid. And the milligrams is the amount of medicine.
Nurse -> Exactly right.
Caller -> Okay. That helps. I was thinking milligrams meant I had to measure five of something.
Nurse -> It's a common mix up. Do you have the little oral syringe?
Caller -> I have two. The ones with the purple tops. They have lines on the side. There's a one, and a point five, and a lot of little lines.
Nurse -> Those are the ones. Look at the syringe. Which line is a quarter of a milliliter?
Caller -> There's, hold on, there's a line between the zero and the point five. A little one in the middle. Is that it?
Nurse -> That's it. Halfway to the point five line. That's a quarter.
Caller -> Okay. Halfway. I see it.
Nurse -> Draw the liquid up until the top of the black plunger tip lines up with that line. Not the end of the plunger, the top edge of the black part.
Caller -> The black part. Okay. Okay. Hold on. I drew some up. It's a little past. It's past the line.
Nurse -> Push a tiny bit back into the bottle until it lines up.
Caller -> Okay. Pushing. Okay. It's on the line. I think. Can you see it? Sorry. That's a silly question.
Nurse -> Ha. I can't, but it sounds like you've got it. Check at eye level.
Caller -> Eye level. Yes. It's on the line.
Nurse -> Now, when did he last have a dose?
Caller -> Ten o'clock tonight. It was a long time ago. It's almost four. No, it's three forty. I looked at the clock.
Nurse -> Okay. That's well over two hours. So he can have the dose now.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Where do I put it? Do I put it in his mouth?
Nurse -> Yes. Squirt it slowly in the pocket between his cheek and his gum. Not straight to the back of the throat. A little at a time.
Caller -> Cheek and gum. Slowly. Okay. He's awake, so he can swallow.
Nurse -> Good. Tell me how he's doing. How bad is his pain right now?
Caller -> He says a six. I asked him. He mumbled six. He's grimacing when I move him.
Nurse -> Where is the pain?
Caller -> I wish I could take it for him.
Nurse -> I know. That's what love does.
Caller -> He taught me to ride a bike on this street. Now I'm learning how to do this.
Nurse -> You're learning fast. And you don't have to do it perfectly.
Caller -> His back. Down low. And his hip. It's the same place it always is.
Nurse -> Okay. Go ahead and give the dose, and I'll stay on the line.
Caller -> Okay. I'm giving it. Slowly. Okay. He swallowed. He's making a face.
Nurse -> It tastes bitter. That's normal.
Caller -> Should I give him a sip of water after?
Nurse -> A tiny sip is fine, to rinse his mouth.
Caller -> Yes. He said yuck. That's a good sign. He's got some spunk.
Nurse -> Ha. Absolutely. Write down the time and the amount. A quarter of a milliliter. Five milligrams.
Caller -> I have the log. It's three forty five. Quarter milliliter. Five milligrams. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. The pain should ease in about twenty to thirty minutes. How many syringes do you have left? You said two.
Caller -> Two. I think. Let me look. Yes. Two. The one I just used and a clean one.
Nurse -> Okay. Rinse the used one with warm water, let it air dry, and reuse it. And I'll order more. I'll send a pack of syringes with the nurse in the morning.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. I was worried about that.
Nurse -> No need to worry. I'll make sure.
Caller -> I'm so glad I called. I almost didn't. I thought I'd figure it out.
Caller -> I kept saying, it's just a measuring thing, I'm a grown woman.
Nurse -> And a tired one. It's three forty in the morning.
Caller -> Ha. True.
Nurse -> You did figure it out. You just needed someone to say yes.
Caller -> Ha. Yes.
Nurse -> Can I get his date of birth, Ruthanne? I want to make sure I'm in the right chart.
Caller -> October twenty sixth, nineteen forty.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number to reach you, in case I need to call back?
Caller -> Two one two, five five five, zero one eight five. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Got it. Now, I'd like to ask a few more things while I have you. Has he had a bowel movement?
Caller -> No. Not for three days. Three. I'm counting. He strains and nothing comes.
Nurse -> Is he on anything for that?
Caller -> The senna. The eight point six milligram. Twice a day. He had it tonight with dinner. Or with his applesauce, I guess. He didn't eat dinner.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep giving the senna twice a day. Don't skip it. And tell the nurse about the constipation when she comes in the morning, so she can add something if it's needed.
Caller -> Senna twice a day. Tell the nurse. Okay.
Nurse -> Is he on any other medicine tonight? Anything we haven't talked about?
Caller -> Just the usual. The anti-nausea one at bedtime. He took it.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> You said he didn't eat dinner. What did he have today?
Caller -> Just sips. Water. A few spoons of applesauce, and he threw away the rest. A sip of ginger ale. That's all.
Nurse -> Okay. That's common with the constipation and the pain. Don't force him. Offer small sips if he wants. Are his lips and mouth dry?
Caller -> Yes. They're cracked. He keeps licking them.
Nurse -> Do you have the little pink mouth swabs?
Caller -> I do. In the comfort box. And the lip balm, the one that's not petroleum.
Nurse -> Perfect. Wet the swab with water and wipe the inside of his mouth and his lips. Then put a bit of balm on. Do it every hour or two. It feels good to him.
Caller -> Swab. Water. Lips. Balm. Every hour or two. Okay.
Nurse -> And turn him gently from side to side every couple of hours. A pillow behind his back.
Caller -> I'll do that. He likes the pillow shaped like a banana.
Nurse -> Is the bed rail up on the side he's turning toward?
Caller -> Yes. I keep both up. My brother showed me.
Nurse -> Ha. A banana pillow. That's perfect.
Caller -> My mother bought it. It's the only thing he'll sleep on.
Nurse -> Then use it. Is his breathing okay? Any gurgling or noisy breathing? Hard work to breathe?
Caller -> No. It's quiet. He's snoring a little, but that's him. It's the normal snoring.
Nurse -> Does he wake easily?
Caller -> When I say his name, yes. He opens his eyes and goes back.
Nurse -> Good. That's what I like to hear.
Caller -> He's lucky to have you all. Honestly. I don't know what we'd do.
Nurse -> Thank you. That's kind.
Caller -> Can I tell you something? My dad was a pharmacist. For forty years. And he can't tell me how to measure his own morphine.
Nurse -> Oh, that's an irony. Did he try to help?
Caller -> He said, in his sleep, something about milliliters. That's all I got.
Nurse -> Ha. Some habits are strong.
Caller -> I laughed. Then I cried.
Nurse -> That's allowed.
Caller -> Dad would hate me crying. He'd say, go count something.
Nurse -> Ha. Count the syringes, then.
Caller -> Two. Still two.
Caller -> I know. Okay. I'm better now.
Nurse -> Good. I'm sending a nurse to see him in the morning. She should be there around nine.
Caller -> Around nine. Okay. My brother will be there by then, I hope. He lands at seven. The airport's an hour away.
Nurse -> He'll make it. Tell him to take a car, not the train, if he's tired.
Caller -> I texted him. He said he'll sleep on the plane.
Nurse -> That works. She'll check the pain and the bowels, and bring the syringes.
Caller -> Good. Perfect. Thank you.
Nurse -> Ruthanne, one more thing. If his pain isn't better in an hour, or you're unsure about a dose at any point tonight, call us right back. Any hour. Don't wait.
Caller -> Any hour. Okay. I will.
Nurse -> The next dose can be given at five forty five if he needs it. Not before.
Caller -> Five forty five. I'll set my phone alarm.
Nurse -> Perfect. And write it all down. It helps the morning nurse.
Caller -> I'm writing. Quarter ml. Five mg. Three forty five.
Nurse -> Read me the whole line from your log, so I know it's right.
Caller -> Three forty five. Morphine. Quarter milliliter. Five milligrams. By mouth.
Nurse -> That's perfect.
Nurse -> Beautiful. How is he now?
Caller -> He's calmer. He's lying back. His face looks softer. I think it's starting to work.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Stay close to him. Hold his hand if he wants.
Caller -> I'm going to sit on the bed. Is that okay? I won't bump him.
Nurse -> Sit by his good side. Slowly. That's fine.
Caller -> I am. He's holding mine. He squeezed it.
Caller -> You know, he hasn't done that in two days.
Nurse -> Then the pain is easing. Stay with him.
Nurse -> That's a good sign. Anything else I can help with tonight?
Caller -> Should I wake him for his bedtime pills?
Nurse -> No. He's had them. Let him rest unless he wakes on his own.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let him sleep.
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Thank you so much, Genevieve. I really mean it.
Nurse -> You're doing a beautiful job. Call if you need anything.
Caller -> I will. Goodnight.
Nurse -> Goodnight, Ruthanne.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willowbrook Home Health, this is Fabian.
Caller -> Hi, Fabian. This is Cordelia Pettibone. I'm calling about my mother. Marguerite Tillotson. She's confused today and I'm worried.
Nurse -> Hi, Cordelia. I'm sorry to hear that. Margarita, is she with you?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little frazzled. I haven't had coffee yet and it's two in the afternoon.
Nurse -> Take a breath. I'm listening.
Caller -> She's at her house. I'm there now. I came over at lunch because she didn't answer her phone.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the confusion.
Caller -> She woke up this way. She thinks it's Tuesday. She keeps asking where my father is. He passed twelve years ago.
Nurse -> Does she know who you are?
Caller -> Yes, she knows me. She just thinks I'm there to help with the garden.
Nurse -> That's new for Margarita?
Caller -> Brand new. She's sharp. She does the crossword in pen. This morning she called me the wrong name and didn't know she'd done it.
Nurse -> Has anything changed lately? New medicine, a new place, anything stressful?
Caller -> Nothing new. Same pills. Same routine. The only thing was the cold snap last week and she wouldn't turn up the heat.
Nurse -> Ha. Confident.
Caller -> She's never been wrong about a word in her life. Until today. She wrote a seven letter word in a four letter box.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she had any fever?
Caller -> I took it. It was a hundred point two. I used the ear one.
Nurse -> Was it in both ears or one?
Caller -> I did both. Hundred point two and a hundred point one. So about the same.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> A hundred point two. Okay. Any other symptoms? Pain when she urinates? Changes in the urine?
Caller -> She hasn't said anything about pain. But I went in the bathroom and the smell. It was strong. Really strong. And dark.
Nurse -> Any blood that you could see?
Caller -> No. Just dark, like tea.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she had urinary infections before?
Caller -> Twice. Last year and the year before. Both times it started with the confusion. Before the burning, before anything. The doctor said that's how it goes with her age.
Nurse -> That's right. It's very common in older adults.
Caller -> I wish someone had told me the first time.
Nurse -> That's helpful. Is she drinking?
Caller -> Hardly. I put out a glass of water and a cup of tea this morning and neither one was touched. She had maybe a few sips of juice.
Nurse -> Has she been to the bathroom today, as far as you know?
Caller -> I don't think so. I didn't see her go. I came at noon and the toilet hadn't been flushed since the morning.
Caller -> I tried a straw. She waved it away.
Nurse -> Sometimes a straw is easier. Or a spoon.
Nurse -> Did she fall? Hit her head? Any bruises?
Caller -> No. No falls. I looked her over. No bruises. She's been in her chair. I checked her walker and it's right where it should be.
Caller -> And the stairs are fine. She hasn't gone near them.
Nurse -> Good. And can I have her date of birth?
Caller -> May thirtieth, nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number for you?
Caller -> Four one four, five five five, zero one two nine.
Nurse -> Got it. Cordelia, how is her breathing?
Caller -> Normal. She's not short of breath. Her color is okay.
Nurse -> Any chest pain, cough?
Caller -> No cough. She'd tell me if her chest hurt. She complains about everything else.
Nurse -> Ha. Good.
Nurse -> Is she able to swallow and take her pills?
Caller -> I haven't tried the pills. I didn't want to give her anything without asking.
Nurse -> That's wise. Let's hold her morning pills until the clinician calls. She hasn't had any Tylenol?
Caller -> No. Nothing. I wasn't sure about the Tylenol.
Nurse -> Wait for the clinician on that, too.
Caller -> Okay. I'll wait.
Nurse -> I'll tell the clinician you're holding them.
Caller -> Thank you. I wasn't sure what was safe.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call clinician now, and I'll tell them what you told me. Confusion, a hundred point two, strong urine, and hardly drinking.
Caller -> Please. Thank you. I'm so scared it's the same as last time. She ended up in the hospital for a week.
Nurse -> I understand. We'll try to catch it early. I'm also scheduling a nurse to visit this afternoon.
Caller -> This afternoon. What time?
Caller -> I need to move my mother's cat off the chair so the nurse can sit.
Nurse -> Ha. Good luck with that.
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a window. It'll probably be between two and four.
Caller -> I'll be here. I took the day off.
Caller -> I work at the post office. They were fine. They said family first.
Nurse -> Good for them.
Nurse -> Good. In the meantime, let's get some fluids into her. Offer small sips of water or juice every fifteen minutes. Don't force it, but keep offering. And keep track of what she drinks, and when she last went to the bathroom.
Caller -> Small sips every fifteen minutes. Write down what she drinks. Write down the bathroom. Okay. I have a pen.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Should I take her to the emergency room?
Nurse -> Not right now. Let the clinician decide. They'll call you back shortly. If anything changes, we'll reconsider.
Caller -> Okay. What would change it?
Nurse -> If she can't be woken up, if she has a seizure, or if she has trouble breathing, call nine one one right away.
Caller -> Can't wake her. Seizure. Trouble breathing. Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> Anything else you notice, call us.
Caller -> I will. She's resting now. She's dozing in the chair.
Nurse -> Let her rest. But if she's sleeping a lot, try to wake her for sips.
Caller -> She sleeps most of the afternoon anyway. How do I tell the difference?
Nurse -> If she wakes easily to her name and can sip, that's okay. If she's hard to wake or won't respond, call us right away.
Caller -> Okay. Easy to wake is okay. Hard to wake is not.
Caller -> I will. Her cat's on her lap. It's the only thing keeping her calm.
Nurse -> Ha. A good nurse.
Caller -> He doesn't leave her side. He sleeps on her feet at night.
Caller -> The best. Winston. He's a big orange thing.
Nurse -> Does she have her glasses nearby?
Caller -> She's wearing them on top of her head like a headband.
Caller -> Yes. On her head. Where she always loses them.
Nurse -> Ha. Of course.
Caller -> Do you want me to keep the phone line open for the clinician?
Nurse -> Yes. Keep your cell near you. They'll call within fifteen minutes.
Caller -> Should I call my brother too? He's in Denver.
Nurse -> Yes, let him know. Family should be aware, especially if she goes to the hospital.
Caller -> I'll call him after we hang up. He'll want to fly out.
Caller -> Okay. I'll keep it in my hand.
Nurse -> Thank you, Cordelia. We'll take good care of Margarita.
Caller -> Fabian, do you think it's a urinary infection again?
Nurse -> It could be. The clinician and the nurse will check. I don't want to guess over the phone.
Caller -> That's fair. I just want to be ready.
Caller -> It's Marguerite, but that's okay. She'd laugh.
Nurse -> Oh, I'm sorry. Marguerite.
Caller -> No worries. Everyone gets it wrong.
Caller -> It's spelled M A R G U E R I T E. French. Her mother was from Quebec.
Nurse -> Beautiful name. I'll make sure the chart has it spelled that way.
Nurse -> I'll fix it in the chart.
Caller -> One more thing, can I use the bathroom while she's dozing, or should I stay right here?
Nurse -> Go ahead, but keep the door open and listen for her.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you for putting up with me.
Nurse -> You're doing a great job.
Caller -> Thank you. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cypress Home Health, this is Lorenzo.
Caller -> Hi, Lorenzo. It's Lorraine Dufresne. I'm a patient of yours. I have the colostomy. I'm running low on stuff and I've got a skin problem too.
Nurse -> Hi, Lorraine. Okay. Let's start with the supplies. What are you running low on?
Caller -> The wafers. The skin barriers. I have three left. And I'm out of the paste. The little tube. I used the last of it Wednesday.
Nurse -> Three wafers. And no paste.
Caller -> Right. And I'm going through them faster because the bag keeps leaking. I'm changing it every day, and it's supposed to be every three or four.
Nurse -> Okay. That's the skin issue you mentioned?
Caller -> Yes. The skin around the stoma is red. It's kind of irritated. It's like a ring. It burns when I change the bag. It's about this big, around the whole thing.
Nurse -> Is it open? Any weeping, or blisters, or pus?
Caller -> I appreciate you being patient with me.
Nurse -> Not a problem at all.
Caller -> No. It's just red. No pus. No yellow. It's not open. It's like a sunburn.
Nurse -> And any fever?
Caller -> Can I ask you to hold for a moment? The kettle is going.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> No. I feel fine. I take my temperature every morning because I'm paranoid. It's been normal.
Nurse -> Ha. A little paranoia is good. What's your output like?
Caller -> Normal. Regular. Soft. Twice a day. No change.
Nurse -> Good. Date of birth, Lorraine?
Caller -> One sec. My phone is making that beeping sound.
Nurse -> No worries, I'll wait.
Caller -> January thirteenth, nineteen sixty eight.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> Three oh three, five five five, zero one one zero.
Nurse -> Perfect. So here's what I'm going to do. I'll order the wafers, a couple of tubes of paste, and a barrier powder to help the skin.
Caller -> Oh, the powder. Yes. My last nurse used it. I don't have any.
Nurse -> That's what the redness needs. I'll also send a nurse to see how the pouch is fitting and look at the skin. She'll come Tuesday.
Caller -> Tuesday. Okay. Is there anything I can do until then?
Nurse -> Yes. When the pouch leaks, change it right away. Don't leave it on. Clean the skin with plain warm water, no soap, no wipes with alcohol. Pat it all the way dry. If you have any powder or a cream from before, use just a little before the new wafer.
Caller -> Plain water. Dry it all the way. Powder. I don't have any powder. I'll just do water and dry it.
Nurse -> That's fine. Make sure the wafer opening is cut right. Not too big. Just a little bigger than the stoma.
Caller -> I trace it. I use the little template.
Nurse -> Perfect. And with only three wafers, change only when it leaks, not on a schedule.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> Okay. I'll stretch them.
Nurse -> If you run out before Tuesday, call me. I'll find a way to get one to you.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Lorraine, there are a few warning signs. If you get a fever, if you see pus, if the stoma turns dark or purple, or if you have no output for a day and your belly swells or you vomit, call us right away.
Caller -> Fever. Pus. Dark stoma. No output with swelling. Okay. I know that list. My surgeon gave it to me.
Nurse -> Good. You're well prepared.
Caller -> I try. It's been eight months and I'm still getting used to it. It's a lot.
Nurse -> It is. How are you doing with it emotionally?
Caller -> Better. I was embarrassed at first. Now I've got a sense of humor. I named it Gerald.
Nurse -> Ha. Gerald.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> He's very dramatic. He makes noises at the worst times. Meetings. Church.
Nurse -> Ha. We all know a Gerald.
Caller -> I do. He's my coworker too.
Nurse -> Ha. Well, I'm glad you have a sense of humor.
Caller -> It saved me.
Nurse -> Do you need anything else? Bags? Wipes?
Caller -> Okay. I've got a notebook now. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Alright.
Caller -> I have plenty of bags. I'm all set on those. Just the wafers and the paste.
Nurse -> Alright. The supplies should come in the next two or three days.
Caller -> I think the line cut out for a second. Are you still there?
Nurse -> Yes, I'm here.
Caller -> Okay. I'll watch for the truck.
Nurse -> Anything else I can help with?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thank you, Lorenzo.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care.
Caller -> Bye.

Caller -> She's awake. She's sitting on the kitchen chair. She's shaky. She's sweating. I checked her sugar. It's forty eight.
Nurse -> Forty eight. Okay. Can she swallow?
Caller -> Yes. She's talking to me. She's mad at herself.
Nurse -> Do you have juice or something sweet in the house?

Nurse -> Go ahead. I'll stay on the line.

Nurse -> Give her half a cup. Let her sip it. Don't rush it.
Caller -> Odette, drink this. Drink. Okay. She's drinking. She says it's too sweet.
Nurse -> That's good. Teodor, how did this happen?
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> She has two pens. The Lantus and the, the mealtime one. They look the same. She grabbed the wrong one first and then dialed twenty without looking. No. She grabbed the right one but she dialed twenty instead of ten. I'm not sure. She says she just dialed it wrong.
Nurse -> And the Lantus is once a day at bedtime?
Caller -> Yes. Once a day. At bedtime. Ten units. She took it about forty minutes ago.

Nurse -> Good. Now, how's she looking? Any confusion, slurred speech?

Nurse -> Got it. How long since she started the juice?
Caller -> Maybe ten minutes. No, five. It's been a few minutes.

Nurse -> Of course. Let me say it slower.
Caller -> She says better. A little. Less shaky.
Nurse -> Good. Tell me when it's fifteen minutes.
Caller -> I'm looking at the microwave clock. Hold on. Okay. It's been fifteen. I'm checking. Okay. It says ninety two. Ninety two.
Nurse -> That's much better. But the Lantus is long acting. Twenty units is double what she needs, so her sugar can drop again in the next hours. I want her to eat something with protein and carbs now. A sandwich or crackers with peanut butter.
Caller -> I have peanut butter crackers. She likes those.
Nurse -> Perfect. Then recheck again in an hour, and set an alarm to check every two hours tonight. Stay with her. Don't leave her alone.
Caller -> Every two hours. Stay with her. I'm not sleeping anyway. I'll set my phone.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call clinician now, and they'll call you about whether to adjust anything.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Should I call an ambulance?
Nurse -> Not right now, since she's recovering. But if she can't swallow, if she won't wake up, or if she has a seizure, call nine one one right away.
Caller -> Can't swallow. Won't wake. Seizure. Nine one one. Okay. I have my phone right here.
Nurse -> And I'll send a nurse out tomorrow morning to go over the pens with both of you.
Caller -> That would help. We need a system. Something so she can't mix them up.
Nurse -> The nurse will help. Different pen colors, labels, and a place for each.
Caller -> I'm so angry at myself. I should have been paying attention.
Nurse -> It's not your fault, Teodor. Mix ups happen. You caught it fast. That's what matters.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Check on her now. How's her color?
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.

Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> Yes. Thank you, Lorenzo.

Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Ginevra.
Caller -> Hi, Ginevra. It's Genoveva Wolcott. I'm calling about my son. Pascal Wolcott. Just a check in about his asthma.
Nurse -> Hi, Genoveva. Good to hear from you. How's Pascal doing?
Caller -> Pretty well. Pretty well. A couple of little things. I wanted to make sure they're normal.
Nurse -> Sure. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> April ninth, twenty twenty. He turned six in the spring.
Nurse -> Perfect. And your number?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one one nine.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me about his controller. Is he still doing it twice a day?
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> Yes. The fluticasone. Forty four micrograms. Two puffs in the morning, two at night, with the spacer. I'm very strict. He did it this morning.
Nurse -> Great. And the rescue inhaler? The albuterol?
Caller -> Okay. I've got a notebook now. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Alright.
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> He needed it twice this week. Wednesday evening was the last one. Two puffs. He was coughing after soccer practice.
Nurse -> Did the albuterol help?
Caller -> Right away. Within five minutes. He went back to playing. He's got a lot of energy.
Nurse -> That's good. What about at night? Is he waking up coughing?
Caller -> Once. On Sunday. He coughed for a minute and went back to sleep. That's all. Just the once.
Nurse -> Okay. Any wheezing right now? Fast breathing? Using his belly to breathe?
Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> No. He's playing with his trains. He's breathing totally normally. No sounds at all.
Nurse -> Wonderful. Any colds, runny nose?
Caller -> A little sniffle at the beginning of the week. Gone now.
Nurse -> Good. Has anything changed at home? Pets, dust, smoke?
Caller -> We got a new rug. And my husband's been burning candles. Maybe it's the candles.
Nurse -> Candles can bother some kids. Maybe skip them for a while and see.
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> I'll tell him. He won't like it. He loves his pumpkin spice.
Nurse -> Ha. A sacrifice for the cause.
Caller -> One sec. My phone is making that beeping sound.
Nurse -> No worries, I'll wait.
Caller -> I'll make him.
Nurse -> Now, how is Pascal doing with the spacer?
Caller -> Good. I do it with him. He breathes in slow. We count.
Nurse -> Let me check technique with you. When he uses the spacer, he puts the puff in and breathes in slowly, and holds his breath for about ten seconds before breathing out. Is that what you do?
Caller -> I appreciate you being patient with me.
Nurse -> Not a problem at all.
Caller -> We hold for about five. Is ten better?
Nurse -> Ten is ideal if he can. Count out loud together. And after the controller inhaler, have him rinse his mouth and spit. That keeps the medicine from causing thrush.
Caller -> Rinse and spit. We forget that sometimes. I'll put a cup by the sink.
Nurse -> A cup by the sink is a great trick.
Caller -> Okay. And what do I do about gym class? He's allowed to run, right? The teacher says maybe he shouldn't.
Nurse -> He can absolutely do gym. Exercise is good for him. Give him the rescue inhaler before gym if his doctor's plan says so, and make sure the teacher knows where it is.
Caller -> It's in his backpack. And the school nurse has a spare.
Nurse -> Perfect. Make sure the school has a copy of his asthma action plan. The green, yellow, red one.
Caller -> I gave them one in September. I'll check they still have it.
Nurse -> Good. And please call us if he needs the rescue inhaler more than twice a week, or if he has trouble breathing, or if the cough wakes him more. If his lips turn blue or he can't talk, call nine one one.
Caller -> More than twice a week. Trouble breathing. Blue lips. Nine one one. Okay. I have it on the fridge.
Nurse -> Great. I'd like to check in with you again next week to see how the week went.
Caller -> That would be nice. Thank you. Call anytime in the afternoon.
Nurse -> Will do. Anything else?
Caller -> Just one thing. He asked if he can get a dog. I said ask the nurse.
Nurse -> Ha. Sneaky. Dogs can bother asthma for some kids, but not all. Let's talk to his doctor first.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell him you said we'll see.
Nurse -> Perfect. We'll see.
Caller -> He'll be thrilled. He thinks that's a yes.
Nurse -> Ha. Parents know that one.
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> Thank you so much, Ginevra.
Nurse -> Anytime. Bye, Genoveva.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Okay. Is she conscious? Talking to you?
Caller -> Yes, yes. She's talking. She says she's fine. She keeps saying I'm fine, I'm fine, I just sat down.
Nurse -> Did she fall, do you think?
Caller -> I don't know. I wasn't here. She says she sat down on purpose. But she's on the floor, in front of the fridge. And the chair is across the room. So I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. Did she hit her head?
Caller -> She says no. I don't see any blood. Or a bump. Her hair is, I don't want to touch her. I don't think so.
Nurse -> Did she pass out? Or did she black out, even for a moment?

Caller -> Two hours. Okay. I can stay. I don't have another route until four.

Nurse -> Tell her to wait. Is she able to move her legs, both arms? Without pain?
Caller -> Can you hear me okay? The signal's a little weak.
Nurse -> I can hear you fine.
Caller -> Hold on. Opal, can you wiggle your toes? She's wiggling. Both feet. She says that's fine. She can move her arms.
Nurse -> Good. And her color? Is she pale or sweaty?
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> Sorry, I just dropped my pen.
Nurse -> That's all right.
Caller -> I think the line cut out for a second. Are you still there?
Nurse -> Yes, I'm here.

Nurse -> Pelican Bay Home Health, this is Ansgar.
Caller -> Hi, Ansgar. It's Anders Kowalczyk. I'm a patient. I have the heart failure. I wanted to call about my weight. It's up.
Nurse -> Hi, Anders. Okay. Let me get your date of birth first.
Caller -> June eighth, nineteen seventy one.
Nurse -> June eighteenth, nineteen seventy one. Got it.
Caller -> No, June eighth. The eighth. Not the eighteenth. Just eight.
Nurse -> My apologies. June eighth, nineteen seventy one. Is that right?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> That's it. People mishear it all the time.
Nurse -> Thank you. Now, tell me about the weight.
Caller -> I weighed this morning. Two hundred fourteen. Last Saturday I was two hundred ten. So four pounds. In two days.
Nurse -> Okay. Two hundred fourteen this morning. What happened between Saturday and now?
Caller -> Honestly? Pizza. A whole weekend of pizza. My nephew's birthday. And chips. And then Sunday we had ham. I know. I know. I should have known better.
Nurse -> It happens. How are your ankles?
Caller -> Puffy. A little. Both of them. I can see the sock marks. And my shoes feel tight.
Nurse -> And your breathing?
Caller -> I'm a little winded on the stairs. I have to stop on the landing. That's new. Usually I go up without thinking about it.
Nurse -> Okay. At rest, are you short of breath? Lying flat?
Caller -> No. When I'm sitting, I'm fine. I slept on one pillow. No chest pain, nothing like that.
Nurse -> Good. Are you taking your furosemide?
Caller -> Yes. Forty milligrams every morning. I took it this morning, at seven.
Nurse -> Have you taken anything else for the swelling?
Caller -> No. Just that.
Nurse -> And your number, in case I need to call back?
Caller -> Okay. I've got a notebook now. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Alright.
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one eight six.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anders, a four pound gain in two days is more than we like. I'm going to send a message to the clinician with your weight and your symptoms.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Do you think they'll change my water pill?
Nurse -> They might. That's their decision. I'll also schedule a nurse visit tomorrow to check your weight, your lungs, and your swelling.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. In the morning?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call with a window. Probably morning.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be here. I work from home on Wednesdays.
Nurse -> In the meantime, weigh yourself every morning. After you use the bathroom, before you eat, same scale, same clothes. Write it down. If you gain more than two pounds in a day, or five pounds in a week, call us.
Caller -> Every morning. Same scale. Write it down. Two in a day, five in a week. Okay. I have a log. It's on the fridge.
Nurse -> Great. Now the food. Keep your salt low. That means skipping the pizza, canned soup, deli meat, chips. And keep your fluids to what the doctor told you.

Nurse -> Don't beat yourself up. One weekend. Just get back on track.

Nurse -> Ha. A good wife.
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> The best. She's hiding the chips.
Nurse -> Ha.
