Caller -> Chest pain. Bad breathing. Fainting. Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> Any questions?
Caller -> Can I ask you to hold for a moment? The kettle is going.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> Just one. Can I still walk? I walk the dog every morning. Should I stop?
Nurse -> Short, slow walks are fine. Stop if you get winded or dizzy.
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> Okay. Slow. He pulls, but I'll hold him.
Nurse -> What kind of dog?
Caller -> Sorry, I lost my train of thought.
Nurse -> That's okay. We were just getting started.

Caller -> One sec. My phone is making that beeping sound.
Nurse -> No worries, I'll wait.
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> Kind of sleepy. He's in his chair. He keeps nodding off. He's not out of it. He answers me. But more tired than usual.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a blood pressure cuff?
Caller -> I think the line cut out for a second. Are you still there?
Nurse -> Yes, I'm here.
Caller -> Sorry, somebody's at the door. Hang on a second.
Nurse -> No problem, I'll hold.
Caller -> Yes. I took it. Hang on. It was a hundred sixty eight over ninety six. That's high for him.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Is he having a headache, chest pain, vision changes?
Caller -> No. No headache. No chest pain. He says he's just sleepy.
Nurse -> Good. What's his date of birth, Magnus?
Caller -> Sorry, I lost my train of thought.
Nurse -> That's okay. We were just getting started.
Caller -> September seventeenth, nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Sorry, somebody's at the door. Hang on a second.
Nurse -> No problem, I'll hold.
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> Six one zero, five five five, zero one zero three.
Nurse -> Got it. Here's what I want you to do. Do not give any more from that bottle. Keep the bottle and the discharge paper together, in a bag, so we can show the pharmacy. Don't throw anything away.
Caller -> Don't give any more. Bottle and paper together. Okay. I'll put them in a bag right now.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call clinician about the blood pressure and the wrong tablet. They'll tell you what to do about the hydralazine.
Caller -> Okay. Does he need to go to the hospital?
Nurse -> That's for the clinician. Right now he's alert and not having chest pain, so we're watching. I'll also call the pharmacy to find out what was dispensed.
Caller -> I called them already. They said they'd look into it. But they didn't sound sure.
Nurse -> I'll follow up directly. And I'm sending a nurse to see him this afternoon.
Caller -> This afternoon. Okay. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you. Probably one to three.
Caller -> I appreciate you being patient with me.
Nurse -> Not a problem at all.
Caller -> I'll be here. I'm working remotely.
Nurse -> Magnus, call nine one one if he has chest pain, a severe headache, confusion, weakness on one side, or if he's hard to wake.
Caller -> Chest pain. Bad headache. Confused. One side weak. Hard to wake. Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Do you know what hydroxyzine is for?
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> It's an allergy pill, right? It makes you sleepy. That's why I'm nervous.
Nurse -> That's right. One tablet is usually not dangerous, but it can make him drowsy. That's why we're checking him.
Caller -> Okay. I've got a notebook now. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Alright.
Caller -> Okay. That's what I thought.
Nurse -> Don't beat yourself up. The labels are very similar. Pharmacies mix these up more than people know.
Caller -> Sorry, I lost my train of thought.
Nurse -> That's okay. We were just getting started.
Caller -> I'm just glad I caught it.
Nurse -> You did. Anything else?
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> No. That's it. Thank you, Estelle.
Nurse -> The clinician will call you within fifteen minutes.
Caller -> I'll keep my phone close.
Nurse -> Take care.

transcript:
Nurse -> Evergreen Home Health, this is Magdalena.
Caller -> Hi, Magdalena. It's Berenice Dunmore. I'm calling about my husband, Hollis Dunmore. I need to order supplies for his tube feeding.
Nurse -> Hi, Berenice. I can help. Let's go through what you have. What are you running low on?
Caller -> Everything, honestly. I should have called last week. I've been so busy.
Nurse -> Busy with Hollis?
Caller -> With Hollis, with the house, with my daughter's wedding in the spring. I keep forgetting what day it is.
Nurse -> That's what lists are for. We'll build one.
Nurse -> That's all right. We'll go item by item. Start with the formula. How many cans?
Caller -> I have four. Four cans of the formula. The Jevity. It's what he takes. Four left in the cupboard.
Nurse -> Is the cupboard cool and dry? Not near the stove?
Caller -> It's the bottom shelf in the pantry. Dark and cool. I rotate them, oldest in front.
Nurse -> You're better organized than you think.
Nurse -> And how many does he use in a day?
Caller -> Five. He gets five cans a day. So four is, what, less than a day.
Nurse -> It's under a day. We'll make sure it comes soon. What about the feeding bags?
Caller -> Sorry, I just dropped my pen.
Nurse -> That's all right.
Caller -> I have two. I wash them. The nurse said I can reuse them for a few days. But I'm on the last two.
Nurse -> Okay. And the extension set? The little tube that connects to the button?
Caller -> One. I have one. The other one cracked. I threw it out.
Nurse -> Okay. And the syringes? The sixty milliliter ones for flushing.
Caller -> One syringe. It's the only one. The plunger sticks. It's been sticking for a week.
Nurse -> Is it the rubber part that sticks, or the whole thing?
Caller -> The rubber part. It drags and I have to push hard. I'm afraid I'll push too hard and it'll pop off.
Nurse -> Don't force it. Stop using it if it drags. Is there any other syringe in the house?
Caller -> A smaller one, from the pharmacy. For the pills.
Nurse -> Use that for medicines only, and I'll get you proper flushing syringes.
Nurse -> That one needs replacing, too. How about the gauze for around the tube site?
Caller -> Almost out. I have maybe two pieces. The little split ones. I've been cutting regular gauze to fit.
Nurse -> That can leave loose threads near the opening, so I'd stop.
Caller -> I see. I didn't know. I thought it was the same.
Nurse -> Okay. Don't cut the regular gauze. We'll send the split ones.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Let's ask about the site. How does it look?
Caller -> It's, there's a little pink bit of skin around the hole. Pink, like a raised bit. It doesn't hurt him. It doesn't bleed.
Nurse -> Any drainage? Any leaking from around the tube?
Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> No. It's dry. Clean. No smell.
Nurse -> Any fever? Vomiting?
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> No. No fever. No throwing up. He tolerates the feeds. He's very good.
Nurse -> How long does each feeding take?
Caller -> About an hour. He sits up the whole time in the recliner. I make him stay upright for another hour after.
Nurse -> Exactly right.
Nurse -> Good. That pink tissue is probably granulation tissue. A nurse will look at it. Can I have his date of birth?
Caller -> March third, nineteen fifty one.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Six one five, five five five, zero one nine zero.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm going to order the formula, the feeding bags, extension sets, syringes, and the split gauze. I'll order extras of each so you don't run low again.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. That would help. I'd love not to think about it for a few weeks.
Nurse -> We'll have it delivered Thursday.
Caller -> Thursday. That's, what's today? Wednesday. So tomorrow. Okay. Good. I'll be home all day.
Nurse -> Does the delivery driver need to ring, or is there a gate?
Caller -> No gate. Just ring the bell twice. Hollis can't hear it, but the dog can.
Nurse -> Four cans won't last until tomorrow. How are you going to cover tonight and tomorrow morning?
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> I have a few cartons of the other kind. The vanilla. From the hospital. I could give that.
Nurse -> Is that the same formula?
Caller -> No. The hospital gave us a different one. A shake. But he's had it.
Nurse -> I'd rather not switch without asking. Let me check with the dietitian, or have the nurse call you back tonight. In the meantime, the four cans should cover this evening and tomorrow's early feeds.
Caller -> Okay. I'll stretch it. I'll do the last can in the morning.
Nurse -> And to be clear, the dietitian or the nurse will call you tonight if there's anything to change.
Caller -> Tonight. Okay. I'll answer the phone even if it's a number I don't know.
Caller -> Is it okay if I dilute it a little, to make it last?
Nurse -> No, please don't dilute it. Give him the usual amount. Ask me if you're short.
Caller -> Okay. I won't.
Nurse -> Good. If you're short, call me back, and I'll arrange something.
Caller -> I will. Thank you. I feel better already.
Nurse -> Berenice, you mentioned a question about flushing. What was that?
Caller -> Yes. I don't remember how often to flush. The paper said before and after but I do it only after. I think. Am I doing it wrong?
Nurse -> Let's go over it. You flush with sixty milliliters of water before every feeding, and again after. And before and after any medicine. That keeps the tube from clogging.
Caller -> Before and after. Sixty. Each time. And the medicines too. Oh, I've been missing the before.
Nurse -> That's okay. Start doing both from now on. And wash the syringe and the bag in warm soapy water after each use. Let them air dry.
Caller -> Warm soapy water. Air dry. I do that already. I put them on a towel by the window.
Caller -> Sometimes I forget and the bag sits in the sink overnight. Is that bad?
Nurse -> Rinse it well in the morning and wash it again. If it smells, throw it away.
Caller -> Smell test. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now for the tube site. Clean around it once a day with warm water, no peroxide, no alcohol. Pat it dry and put a clean split gauze under the tube.
Caller -> Warm water. Dry. Split gauze. Okay. I'll stop cutting the other kind.
Nurse -> Yes. Use the split ones as soon as they arrive. Berenice, call us if you see drainage or the redness spreading, a fever, vomiting, if the tube clogs and won't clear, or if the tube comes out.
Caller -> Drainage. Redness. Fever. Vomiting. Clog. Tube out. I'm writing it. I have the list from before. I'll add the clog part.
Nurse -> If the tube comes out, that's urgent. The hole can start to close in an hour or two. Call right away.
Caller -> Okay. Right away. I'll put the number on the fridge. Again.
Caller -> The magnet fell off. I keep sticking it back on.
Nurse -> Ha. Try the freezer door. Magnets love the freezer.
Caller -> Ha. I'll move it.
Nurse -> Good. I'll also send a nurse on Friday to look at the site and watch you do a flush, so we can be sure it's right.
Caller -> Friday. Okay. Is that in the morning?
Nurse -> Probably. The scheduler will call you.
Caller -> Should I have him ready, or dressed, or anything?
Nurse -> Just as he is. Maybe have his chair clear so she can reach the tube. She'll want to see the site in good light.
Caller -> I'll open the curtains.
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> I'll be here. Hollis gets up late, so any time is fine.
Nurse -> Perfect. How is he doing otherwise? Is he comfortable?
Caller -> He's good. He's in his chair watching the football. He's yelling at the screen. It's his team.
Nurse -> Does he talk back to the referees?
Caller -> He does. In full sentences. He taught the dog to bark at fumbles.
Nurse -> Ha. I love that.
Nurse -> Ha. Who's he rooting for?
Caller -> The Titans. He's been a fan since before they were the Titans. When they were the Oilers.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a long time.
Caller -> Fifty years. He's got the jersey. It doesn't fit him anymore.
Nurse -> Ha. But he wears it anyway.
Caller -> Every Sunday. Over his pajamas.
Nurse -> That's wonderful.
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> It's the little things. I'm learning that.
Nurse -> How are you doing, Berenice? It's a lot to manage.
Caller -> I'm okay. I'm tired. I do everything. The feeds, the flushes, the laundry. But I wouldn't have it any other way. I just want him home.
Nurse -> He's lucky to have you.
Caller -> I'm lucky to have him. Fifty one years in March. He proposed at a bowling alley.
Nurse -> A bowling alley! Did he roll a strike?
Caller -> A gutter ball. He says that's why I said yes. I felt sorry for him.
Nurse -> Ha. A wonderful story.
Nurse -> You're doing a beautiful job. Do you have help? Family, friends?
Caller -> I also have a church group. They offered to sit with Hollis so I can go to the store.
Nurse -> Take them up on it. You deserve an hour to yourself.
Caller -> My son comes Saturdays. And a neighbor brings casseroles. I can't eat that many casseroles.
Nurse -> Ha. Freeze a few.
Caller -> I have. The freezer is full of casseroles.
Nurse -> Any chance of a tuna one? Just kidding.
Caller -> I'll bring you one. They're all macaroni, I think.
Nurse -> Ha. You're sweet.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good problem.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little scattered today.
Nurse -> That's completely understandable.
Caller -> It's a blessing, I know. I shouldn't complain.
Nurse -> It's okay to be tired. Please tell the nurse on Friday if you need more help. We have resources.
Caller -> Thank you for saying that. Nobody asks me how I'm doing. They all ask how Hollis is.
Nurse -> That happens to caregivers all the time. You matter in this too.
Caller -> I will. Thank you. That means a lot.
Nurse -> Anytime. Is there anything else you need today?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Oh, the tape. Do you send tape?
Nurse -> We'll add the paper tape to the order.
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> Perfect. Thank you.
Caller -> I can't thank you enough. Truly. Before you all came, I was doing this alone with a binder from the hospital.
Nurse -> You were doing it well. We just fill in the gaps.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care, Berenice.
Caller -> You too. Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Seabrook Home Health, this is Valentina.
Caller -> Valentina, hi, it's Annalise Quimby. My father-in-law is Sylvester Quimby. He fell. He hit his head on the tub. He's bleeding.
Nurse -> Okay, Annalise. Is he awake? Is he talking to you?
Caller -> He's awake. He's sitting on the bathroom floor. He's talking. He's, he keeps saying the same thing.
Nurse -> What is he saying?
Caller -> He keeps saying, did I fall? Did I fall? And I tell him yes and then he says it again.
Nurse -> Okay. Where is he bleeding?
Caller -> Above his ear. The left side. It's a cut. I'd say two inches. It's bleeding a lot. I have a towel on it. It's soaked.
Nurse -> Annalise, I'm going to ask you to call nine one one right now. Put me on speaker, or have someone else call while we keep talking.
Caller -> Oh god. Okay. Okay. Hold on. Greg! Greg, come here! Call nine one one! Dad fell! Hit his head!
Nurse -> Is Greg calling?
Caller -> He's on it. He's calling. Okay. I'm still here.
Nurse -> Good. Press a clean towel firmly on the cut. Don't lift it to peek. If it soaks through, put another one on top, and keep pressing.
Caller -> Pressing. Firm. Okay. It's coming through. I'm putting another one on.
Nurse -> That's right. Keep pressing. Is he on any blood thinners?
Caller -> Yes. Warfarin. He takes it every evening. Five milligrams. He took it last night.
Nurse -> Okay. That's very important. The paramedics need to know that. Tell them right away.
Caller -> Warfarin. I'll tell them. Greg! Tell the dispatcher he's on warfarin!
Nurse -> Annalise, does he have a headache?
Caller -> He says his head hurts. He says it's a bad one. A headache, behind his eye. It wasn't there before he fell.
Nurse -> Has he vomited? Did he pass out, even for a second?
Caller -> No. No vomiting. He didn't pass out. I heard the thump and I ran in and he was awake. He was sitting up already.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep him still. Don't let him stand or walk around. Keep him lying down, or sitting against the wall if that's more comfortable. Don't move his neck.
Caller -> Wait, say that again? I missed the first part.
Nurse -> Of course. Let me say it slower.
Caller -> He's against the wall. He wants to get up. I'm telling him no. Dad, stay. Stay put.
Nurse -> That's right. Give him nothing by mouth. No water, no food, no pills.
Caller -> No pills. He has his evening pills on the counter. Do I give him anything?
Nurse -> No. None of them. Especially not the warfarin. Don't give him any of his medicines until the doctors say so.
Caller -> No pills. Okay. I'm putting them away. Not yet. Hold on, I'm pressing. I can't. Okay. Greg's got the pills.
Nurse -> Good. Tell me when the dispatcher says they're on the way.
Caller -> Greg says they're sending an ambulance. They said ten minutes. Ten minutes.
Nurse -> Perfect. Stay with him. What's his date of birth, Annalise? For the paramedics.
Caller -> December fifteenth, nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> And the best number to reach you?
Caller -> Two oh six, five five five, zero one nine eight. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now so they know what's happening.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Please.
Nurse -> Is the bleeding slowing at all?
Caller -> I don't know. Hold on. I can't look. If I lift it, it'll start again. The towel's heavy.
Nurse -> Don't lift. Just keep the pressure steady.
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> Okay. I'm leaning on it. He's wincing.
Nurse -> I know. It hurts, but it's important. Talk to him. Keep him awake. Ask him his name, where he lives.
Caller -> Dad, what's your name? Sylvester. Where do you live? Dad? He says Cedar Street. That's right. And he said the year. He said nineteen... no, he said the wrong year.
Nurse -> What year did he say?
Caller -> He said twenty ten. It's twenty twenty six.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics that, too. He's confused about the date.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> I will. I'll tell them everything.
Nurse -> Does he have any allergies or other health conditions you can tell them? Heart problems? Diabetes?
Caller -> He has atrial fibrillation. That's why the warfarin. And high blood pressure. No diabetes. No allergies I know of.
Nurse -> Good. Tell them all that. Is there a list of his medicines?
Caller -> On the fridge. A printed list. Greg is grabbing it for them.
Nurse -> Perfect. Annalise, are you hurt? Did you fall?
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> No. I'm fine. I'm just scared. My hands are shaking. I'm covered in his blood.
Nurse -> That's okay. You're doing great. Wash up after they take over, and wear gloves if you have them.
Caller -> I'll wash. I don't have gloves.
Nurse -> It's fine. Keep going.
Caller -> I hear something outside. Is that the sirens? Hold on. Greg, is that them?
Nurse -> Take your time. I'm here.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> Yes, yes, they're pulling up. Greg's going to the door. Okay. Here they come.
Nurse -> Good. Tell the paramedics the warfarin and the wrong date. They'll take it from here.
Caller -> I will. Thank you. Thank you, Valentina.
Nurse -> Go ahead. We'll follow up with the family.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Evergreen Home Health, this is Magdalena.
Caller -> Good afternoon. I'm calling from a law office. I need to request some records for a case we're working on.
Nurse -> I'm on the clinical line. Records requests go through our medical records department.
Caller -> Okay. Can you transfer me, or give me a direct line?
Nurse -> I can't transfer from here. The number is on our website under medical records.
Caller -> Is there anything I can do over the phone? Our client is a former patient. We have a signed release.
Nurse -> I can't discuss any patient or confirm whether someone was a patient. The records department can process your authorization.
Caller -> I understand. Do they accept it by fax or by email?
Nurse -> I'm not sure which they prefer. Their page lists the options.
Caller -> Okay. And how long does it usually take?
Nurse -> I don't know. It's not something I handle. They can tell you.
Caller -> I see. Is there someone I should ask for?
Nurse -> Just ask for medical records. They'll direct you.
Caller -> Alright. This is my third call today. Everybody keeps sending me somewhere else.
Nurse -> Ha. I'm sorry. It's the right place, I promise. I just can't be the one to help.
Caller -> I know. It's the nature of the work. Hospitals are the worst.
Nurse -> Ha. I can imagine.
Caller -> Well, thank you. I'll look at the website.
Nurse -> Good luck.
Caller -> Thanks. Have a good afternoon.
Nurse -> You too. Bye.

Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> Honestly pretty good. Better than I have in a while. I wanted to tell somebody, so I'm telling you.
Nurse -> That's wonderful to hear. What do you think made the difference?
Caller -> A lot of little things. I'll get to it. Don't let me ramble.
Nurse -> Ramble away. I have time.
Nurse -> I'm glad. What's your morning glucose been running?
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> I've been writing it down every day. I add them up on Sundays. The average this week was one eighteen. Last week was one twenty five. Before that I was in the one forties.
Nurse -> That's a nice trend. Are you taking your metformin?
Caller -> The doctor said the number I want to see is the A1C, right? That's the three month one.
Nurse -> Right. That comes from a blood test. The next one is due soon, and we'll go over it Friday.
Caller -> Okay. I'm a little afraid to see it. But I think it will be better.
Nurse -> With these numbers, I'd expect an improvement.
Caller -> Yes. Five hundred milligrams. Twice a day. With breakfast and with dinner. I took it this morning.
Nurse -> Any stomach upset with it?
Caller -> A little at first. Not anymore. I take it with food like you said.
Caller -> I thought about stopping it because of that. Then I read you shouldn't stop without asking.
Nurse -> Exactly. Always call first. I'm glad you did not.
Caller -> I called your office and a nurse told me to take it with food. Same advice.
Nurse -> Good. Any other medicines?
Caller -> Just my blood pressure one and a baby aspirin. Nothing new.
Nurse -> Any over the counter things, vitamins, supplements, herbal teas?
Caller -> A multivitamin and chamomile tea at night. That's it. I Googled the tea and it said fine.
Nurse -> Chamomile is okay for most people. Mention it to the doctor.
Caller -> I will.
Nurse -> Any dizziness with the blood pressure one?
Caller -> No. It's been steady. I check it at the pharmacy on Saturdays. They have a machine.
Nurse -> Good habit.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what you've changed. You said you're doing better.
Caller -> I'm walking. Twenty minutes every morning after breakfast. Around the neighborhood with my sister. And I stopped the soda. I was drinking three a day. Now it's sparkling water with lime.
Caller -> We go past the bakery, which is cruel. The smell is everything.
Nurse -> Ha. A test of willpower.
Caller -> I walk faster past it.
Nurse -> Any pain when you walk? Calf cramps, anything?
Caller -> No. A little tired in the last five minutes. That's all.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Three sodas a day is a big sugar load.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little scattered today.
Nurse -> That's completely understandable.
Caller -> I know. I was embarrassed to tell the doctor. Now I'm proud of myself.
Nurse -> Doctors have heard it all. Honestly, they love when patients change something.
Caller -> That's what my sister said. She dragged me to the last visit.
Nurse -> Sisters are useful.
Caller -> She's very bossy. But she's right about eighty percent of the time.
Nurse -> You should be. Any symptoms? Thirst, urinating a lot?
Caller -> No. That's gone. I used to get up three times a night. Now once.
Nurse -> That's a good sign your sugars are steadier.
Caller -> I sleep better. I haven't had coffee after noon, either. My sister's rule.
Nurse -> Any problems with your feet? Numbness, burning, sores?
Caller -> The tingling. In my toes. Mostly the big toes. At night when I'm lying in bed. It's been there a few months. It's not painful. Just a pins and needles feeling.
Nurse -> Okay. Is that the same or worse than last time?
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> About the same. Maybe a tiny bit more when I'm tired.
Nurse -> Does it keep you from sleeping?
Caller -> No. I notice it, then I fall asleep. I put a pillow under my feet and it settles.
Nurse -> Good trick.
Nurse -> Any cuts, sores, blisters, or color changes on your feet?
Caller -> No. I look every night, like you told me. I use a mirror from the bathroom. They look fine. No sores. And my vision's fine. I got new glasses in the fall, but nothing's changed.
Nurse -> Good. Keep doing exactly that. Do you wear shoes and socks around the house?
Caller -> Sorry, I lost my train of thought.
Nurse -> That's okay. We were just getting started.
Caller -> Socks, yes. Shoes mostly. I have the soft slippers for the bedroom.
Nurse -> What kind of shoes? Closed toe, with room?
Caller -> Sneakers. A half size bigger, my sister made me. They're ugly but comfortable.
Nurse -> Ugly and comfortable is exactly what we want.
Nurse -> Good. Now, supplies. How are your test strips?
Caller -> Wait, before the strips, can I ask about Thanksgiving? It's coming up and I'm nervous.
Nurse -> Of course. What are you worried about?
Caller -> The pie. And my mother's stuffing. Everything is carbs. I don't want to ruin the progress.
Nurse -> One holiday meal won't undo it. Eat a normal plate, go for a walk after, and don't skip breakfast to save room.
Caller -> A walk after. My sister will love that. She wants everyone on a family walk.
Nurse -> It's a good tradition. Start the pie with a small slice.
Caller -> A small slice. And no seconds. I'll try. No promises on the stuffing.
Nurse -> Ha. Honest.
Caller -> I'm glad you asked. I have fifteen left. That's about two weeks.
Nurse -> Do you test only in the morning, or other times, too?
Caller -> Just mornings. Once in a while after dinner if I'm curious.
Nurse -> That matches your plan. Keep doing that.
Nurse -> I'll order more right now. Do you need lancets or the control solution?
Caller -> Can you hear me okay? The signal's a little weak.
Nurse -> I can hear you fine.
Caller -> No, I'm fine on lancets. I have a whole box. I just need strips.
Nurse -> Then it's strips. I'll have them sent.
Caller -> Thank you. That'll come before I run out?
Nurse -> It should. Usually three days. If it's late, call me.
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> I will. I'm good at nagging.
Nurse -> Does your sister nag you, too?
Caller -> Oh, constantly. She texts me a picture of a salad every morning.
Nurse -> Ha. Accountability.
Caller -> Accountability with lettuce.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a skill.
Caller -> I also nagged the pharmacy until they found my old prescription. Persistence, that's my superpower.
Caller -> My sister says it's my only one.
Nurse -> Ha. Now, your appointment. What did you want to ask?
Caller -> I have a visit Thursday. At ten. But my daughter has a recital that morning and I want to go. Can we move it to Friday?
Nurse -> Let me look at the schedule. Friday at ten is open. I can move you.
Caller -> Friday at ten. Perfect. Yes, please.
Nurse -> It's done. Friday instead of Thursday.
Nurse -> You'll get a reminder call Thursday afternoon.
Caller -> Thursday afternoon. I'll be at the recital, but I'll see the phone after.
Caller -> Thank you so much. You're the best.
Nurse -> Will your sister drive you Friday, or will you walk?
Caller -> She'll walk over. She lives four blocks away. We'll have tea and she'll sit in on the visit.
Nurse -> She's welcome to. Bring your glucose log and your meter.
Caller -> I always do. I keep them in a little blue bag so I don't forget.
Nurse -> Anytime. A recital, how fun. What does she play?
Caller -> I should tell you, I wore a hat to her last one and blocked the whole row. I'm leaving it at home.
Nurse -> Ha. Your row will thank you.
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> The violin. She's eleven. She's been practicing the same piece for a month. I know every note. I could play it in my sleep.
Caller -> It's a Suzuki piece. Book two. Gavotte. I'll hum it for you if you want.
Nurse -> I'll pass this time. I'll hear it in my dreams.
Caller -> Ha. You and me both.
Nurse -> Ha. A proud mom.
Nurse -> When is the recital, exactly?
Caller -> Thursday at ten, at her school. It's in the gym. Folding chairs. Everybody's grandmother is there.
Nurse -> The best audience.
Caller -> I'm so proud. She's terrible. But she's trying. Ha.
Caller -> She's got a teacher who says she has an ear. I only have ears for wrong notes.
Nurse -> Ha. We've all been there.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the best kind of music.
Caller -> It really is.
Nurse -> Josephine, a couple of reminders for you. Check your feet every day, like you're doing, with the mirror. Wear socks and shoes. And if you see any sore, blister, or a color change, call us right away.
Caller -> Sore. Blister. Color. I will. I'll call the same day.
Nurse -> Good. And keep logging your morning sugars. Call if you get a reading over three hundred, or under seventy.
Caller -> Three hundred or seventy. Okay. I have a sticky note on the meter. It says that.
Nurse -> Great. And call us any time you have questions. About the strips, the log, your toes, anything.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Percival. I really appreciate how you all treat me.
Caller -> Oh, and one more thing, does the agency do holiday hours? Just so I know who to call if something comes up.
Nurse -> The line is open every day, all hours, including holidays.
Nurse -> It's our pleasure. You're doing the work.
Caller -> I used to think nobody cared about the small stuff. Then I got you all.
Nurse -> The small stuff is the big stuff. It adds up.
Caller -> I'm trying. One day at a time.
Nurse -> Is your mood okay? Sometimes managing a condition gets heavy.
Caller -> It's good. Actually the best in years. I started painting again. Watercolors.
Nurse -> That's lovely. What do you paint?
Caller -> Birds, mostly. Cardinals. They come to the feeder and I can't resist.
Nurse -> I'd love to see one.
Caller -> I'll show you Friday. I'll bring the cardinal.
Nurse -> That's how it works.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let you go. Have a good day.
Nurse -> You too. Bye, Josephine.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Octavia.
Caller -> Hello, yes, hello. This is Barnaby Stroud. I'm calling about my wife, Wilhelmina Stroud. She's in pain and we're both here.
Nurse -> Hi, Barnaby. Hi, Wilhelmina. Can you both hear me?
Caller -> I can. Wilhelmina, can you hear her? She can hear you. She's right here on the speaker.
Nurse -> Wonderful. Wilhelmina, tell me about the pain, if you're able.
Caller -> She's able. She just doesn't like to complain. Wilhelmina, tell her. No, you tell her.
Nurse -> Take your time, both of you.
Caller -> It's in her hip and her back. The bones. Her bones hurt.
Nurse -> Wilhelmina, how bad is it, zero to ten?
Caller -> She says a five. A five. Wilhelmina, tell her. Five.
Nurse -> A five. And is that all the time, or comes and goes?
Caller -> It comes and goes. It's worse when she turns over. It's worse in the evening.
Caller -> She was a nurse herself. Forty years. She always said patients should speak up. Now look at her.
Nurse -> Ha. The hardest patients are the nurses.
Caller -> She's the worst. She corrects the aide.
Nurse -> Okay. What has she taken for it today?
Caller -> The oxycodone. Five milligrams. She's had it twice today. Once at nine, once at one o'clock.
Nurse -> Every four hours as needed, is that the order?
Caller -> Yes. Every four hours as needed. It's on the bottle. She wants another one but it's only, what, it's six now, so it's been five hours. So she can have it.
Nurse -> Yes, that's more than four hours since one. She can have it now if she needs it.
Caller -> One sec. My phone is making that beeping sound.
Nurse -> No worries, I'll wait.
Nurse -> Take it slow with the water, and have her sit up a bit.
Caller -> She's propped on three pillows. I know how.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I'll get it. Wait. Let me finish. The other thing is the constipation.
Caller -> Hold on, there's a noise in the background. That's the television. Barnaby, turn it down.
Caller -> I am turning it down. Can't hear a thing.
Nurse -> No problem. I'll wait.
Nurse -> Go ahead.
Caller -> She hasn't gone in two days. She's uncomfortable. Her belly is tight. She's been straining.
Nurse -> Is she on anything for that?
Caller -> The softener. The docusate. A hundred milligrams every morning. She had it this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she nauseated? Vomiting?
Caller -> No. No nausea. She's been eating. A little. Toast and soup.
Caller -> A little soup. A few crackers. Her sister's coming Saturday with the casserole.
Nurse -> Tell her sister to bring the prune juice, too.
Caller -> Ha. She has a case already.
Nurse -> That's good. Barnaby, I'd like to get her date of birth.
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> July third, nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number?
Caller -> Three oh three, five five five, zero one five four.
Nurse -> Got it. Wilhelmina, I'm going to ask Barnaby a couple of questions about how you're feeling. Is that okay?
Caller -> She's nodding. She says yes.
Nurse -> Perfect. So here's my plan. I'm going to send a message to our clinician about the pain and the constipation. They may want to add a stronger bowel medicine.
Caller -> Okay. That would help. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'll send the nurse to see her tomorrow morning, to check her belly and go over her medicines. Is that all right?
Caller -> I'll send the nurse tomorrow morning. Okay. That's fine. I'll be here. We're always here.
Nurse -> Okay. Barnaby, I'll go over dosing. Give the oxycodone no sooner than every four hours, and write down the time of every dose. And keep giving the docusate every morning.
Caller -> Every four hours. Write it down. And the docusate every morning. Yes. Wilhelmina, did you hear? She says she can't hear. Hold on.
Caller -> Is it the phone or her ears? Her hearing aid is on the dresser.
Caller -> Barnaby, get it. No, the right one. The one with the little tail.
Nurse -> I'll hold.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> I'm turning the speaker up. Can you hear me now? Can you hear her?
Nurse -> Yes, I hear you.
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> Okay. She says thank you.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Wilhelmina. A few comfort things. A warm pack on the sore spot, wrapped in a towel. Change her position slowly. Offer prune juice and sips of fluids through the evening.
Caller -> Warm pack. Slow turns. Prune juice. We have prune juice. We have a whole case. Her sister brought it.
Caller -> Do we have a warm pack? We have the one from the hospital with the blue gel. Wilhelmina, where's the blue one?
Caller -> It's in the freezer. That's the cold one. You want the warm one.
Nurse -> The gel packs can work both ways, microwaved briefly in a damp towel. Check the temperature on your wrist first.
Caller -> Wrist first. Okay.
Nurse -> Ha. That's helpful.
Caller -> I think the line cut out for a second. Are you still there?
Nurse -> Yes, I'm here.
Caller -> She hates it. But she'll drink it.
Nurse -> A little at a time. Half a cup.
Caller -> Half a cup. Okay. I'll warm it a bit. She likes it warm. She says that's the secret.
Nurse -> Ha. Whatever works.
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> Wilhelmina says she wants to tell you something.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> She says thank you for being so kind. She says you all are angels.
Nurse -> That's very sweet. Tell her she's the angel.
Caller -> She says forty years of nights and weekends, and the one thing she learned is that kindness costs nothing.
Nurse -> She's right. I'll remember that.
Caller -> She says no, she's a cranky old lady. Ha. She's laughing.
Nurse -> Ha. A cranky angel is the best kind.
Caller -> She wants me to tell you she used to work the night shift at the county hospital. Third floor.
Nurse -> I bet she has stories.
Caller -> She does. Not for the phone.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> Yes. She always had a sense of humor. Even now.
Nurse -> It's good to laugh.
Caller -> Barnaby, did I give her the pill? No. Wait. I haven't yet. I'll do that.
Nurse -> Go ahead and give it. I'll wait.
Caller -> Wait, say that again? I missed the first part.
Nurse -> Of course. Let me say it slower.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. I'm getting the bottle. It's in the drawer. Five milligrams. One tablet.
Nurse -> That's the dose. With a little water.
Caller -> With water. I'm bringing it. Wilhelmina, here. Swallow. Good. She took it.
Nurse -> Wonderful. What time is it?
Caller -> Six oh five. I'll write it. Six oh five. Oxycodone.
Nurse -> Perfect. The next one is no earlier than ten.
Nurse -> Ten in the evening, to be clear.
Caller -> Ten tonight. Understood.
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> No earlier than ten. Got it.
Nurse -> Call us if the pain isn't better in an hour, or if she's very sleepy, or if she can't have a bowel movement by tomorrow night.
Caller -> If the pain stays, if she's sleepy, if no bowel movement by tomorrow night. Okay.
Nurse -> Anything else I can do?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. We're all set. Thank you so much, Octavia.
Caller -> One more. Do we need to call tomorrow's nurse to confirm?
Nurse -> No. She'll call you before she comes with a time window.
Caller -> Wonderful. Thank you.
Nurse -> Anytime. Take care of each other.
Caller -> We will. Goodnight.
Nurse -> Goodnight.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Raphael.
Caller -> Hi, Raphael. It's Emmerich Kettering. I'm calling about my mother. Rosalind Kettering. She's not sleeping. I'd like to ask about getting a sleeping pill.
Nurse -> Hi, Emmerich. Tell me how long this has been going on.
Caller -> Three nights now. She's up at two, three in the morning. I hear her in the kitchen. Opening cabinets. Making tea she doesn't drink.
Nurse -> Is that normal for her?
Caller -> Can I ask you to hold for a moment? The kettle is going.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> No. She's always slept like a rock. Eight hours. She used to nap in the car.
Caller -> My father used to say she could fall asleep at a rock concert.
Nurse -> Ha. A talented sleeper.
Nurse -> Has anything changed? Medicines, a move, a loss?
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> Nothing I know of. Same pills. Same house. Well. Her sister died in October. But that was two months ago. She seemed okay.
Nurse -> Were they close?
Caller -> Very. They talked every night at nine. The phone rings at nine and she still looks at it.
Nurse -> That's a hard habit to break.
Nurse -> I'm sorry about her sister. That could be part of it.
Caller -> Maybe. She doesn't talk about it. She just says she can't sleep.
Nurse -> Have you tried anything?
Caller -> Melatonin. Three milligrams. For a week. And a warm bath. She says the bath is nice but it doesn't help.
Nurse -> Okay. Any pain? Any falls?
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> No pain. No falls. She walks around holding the counter. I'd hear if she fell. I'm in the next room.
Nurse -> Good. What sleeping pill were you thinking of?
Caller -> I looked it up. Zolpidem. Five milligrams at bedtime. The older folks get the lower dose. My neighbor takes it.
Nurse -> I understand. I can't start a new medicine myself. That has to come from her doctor. And I want to be careful with that one in older adults. It can cause confusion and falls.
Caller -> Oh. I didn't know that.
Nurse -> Many people don't. I'll send a message to her doctor about the sleep trouble and your request, and let them decide.
Caller -> I just want her to rest. I'm tired too, to be honest. I keep one ear open all night.
Nurse -> That's exhausting. We'll help find a plan for both of you.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. That makes sense.
Nurse -> Can I have her date of birth?
Caller -> Sorry, somebody's at the door. Hang on a second.
Nurse -> No problem, I'll hold.
Caller -> April twenty eighth, nineteen forty seven.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> Six four six, five five five, zero one four zero.
Nurse -> Got it. In the meantime, there are a few things to try. Keep a regular bedtime and wake time, even on weekends. Avoid caffeine after noon, and keep naps short. Dim the lights an hour before bed. A warm drink, like milk or herbal tea, can help.
Caller -> Regular times. No caffeine. Short naps. Dim lights. Warm milk. Okay. She does have a coffee in the afternoon. She won't give it up.
Nurse -> See if she'd switch to decaf. Just after lunch.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> I'll try. She'll complain.
Nurse -> Ha. A bit.
Caller -> I appreciate you being patient with me.
Nurse -> Not a problem at all.
Caller -> I'm good at complaints. I'm her son.
Nurse -> Ha. And for safety at night, put a night light in the hall and the bathroom, keep the path clear, and lock the outside doors so she can't wander out.
Caller -> Night lights. Clear path. Lock the doors. We have a deadbolt. I'll turn it before bed.
Nurse -> Good. Is she confused at other times? Forgetting names, losing track of the day?
Caller -> Can you hear me okay? The signal's a little weak.
Nurse -> I can hear you fine.
Caller -> A little. Forgetful. It's gotten a bit worse. But not crazy. She knows me.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll mention that to the doctor, too.
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> I appreciate that.
Nurse -> I'll call you tomorrow afternoon to let you know what they say.
Caller -> Tomorrow afternoon. Great. I'll be at work but I'll answer.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else?
Caller -> Okay. I've got a notebook now. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Alright.
Caller -> No. I feel better having asked. I was scared to ask.
Nurse -> Never be scared to ask.
Caller -> I won't. Thank you, Raphael.
Nurse -> Take care, Emmerich.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Juniper Ridge Hospice, this is Pilar.
Caller -> Hi, Pilar. It's Imogen Radcliffe. My dad is Barnard Radcliffe. He can't stop throwing up. Nothing is staying down.
Nurse -> Okay, Imogen. I'm sorry. How long has this been going on?
Caller -> I'm sorry for how I sound. I haven't slept and I've been cleaning up since seven.
Nurse -> You sound like someone doing a hard job. Go ahead.
Caller -> Since this morning. Since about seven. I've counted six times. Six. The last one was twenty minutes ago.
Nurse -> What's coming up? Food, liquid, anything unusual?
Caller -> Just liquid. Yellow, kind of. Watery. He hasn't eaten since yesterday. There's no blood. I checked. It's not red and it's not dark.
Nurse -> Does he complain of heartburn or a sour taste?
Caller -> He said it tastes bitter. He keeps asking for water, and then it comes right back.
Nurse -> Good. Does he have an anti-nausea medicine?
Caller -> The ondansetron. The little one that melts on the tongue. Four milligrams. Every eight hours as needed.
Nurse -> Has he taken it today?
Caller -> Twice. At eight, and then at noon. It came back up both times. I could see it in the bowl. Mostly dissolved but it came back.
Nurse -> Did he swallow anything else with it? Other pills?
Caller -> The morning ones were with it. Everything came up together. I couldn't tell you what was what.
Nurse -> That's okay. The clinician will sort out the medicine list.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he in pain?
Caller -> No. No pain. He's just sick and weak. His mouth is so dry. His lips are cracked.
Nurse -> Is he awake and answering you?
Caller -> Yes. He's tired. He's lying on his side. He keeps closing his eyes. But he answers.
Nurse -> Is he lying on his side with his head up a bit, or flat?
Caller -> Flat on his side. I'll add a pillow.
Nurse -> Yes, please. That helps with the vomiting.
Nurse -> Does he have a fever? Belly swelling?
Caller -> I haven't taken his temperature. His belly looks the same. It's soft.
Nurse -> When was his last bowel movement?
Caller -> Yesterday. A small one. Normal.
Nurse -> Any belly pain when you press gently?
Caller -> He doesn't flinch. He just looks tired.
Nurse -> Okay. Imogen, can I have his date of birth?
Caller -> January twenty sixth, nineteen forty two.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Five oh five, five five five, zero one zero two.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now. When a person keeps vomiting up the dissolving tablet, they often switch to a different form, like a suppository or an injection.
Caller -> Okay. Please. I hate seeing him like this.
Nurse -> I know. For now, don't give him any more of the dissolving tablet. Wait for the clinician's call.
Caller -> No more. Okay. How long will that be?
Caller -> Is it normal for this to happen? He's been fine for weeks.
Nurse -> It can happen with illness at this stage. It doesn't mean you did anything wrong.
Caller -> I keep thinking I missed something.
Nurse -> You didn't. You called at the right time.
Nurse -> Probably within fifteen minutes. And I'm also sending a nurse to your house. She should be there within two hours.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, give him nothing by mouth for an hour. After that, offer ice chips, or tiny sips of water, one teaspoon at a time. Keep his head raised on pillows, and moisten his mouth with a swab.
Caller -> Nothing for an hour. Then ice chips. Head up. Swab. Okay. I have the swabs.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep a bowl and a towel near him.
Caller -> I have a bowl. It's right here.
Nurse -> Put a towel under his chin as well. And a cool washcloth on his forehead helps some people.
Caller -> A cool cloth. Yes. I'll get one.
Nurse -> Good. If he vomits again, note the time and what it looks like.
Caller -> I will. I'm writing it on the back of an envelope.
Nurse -> Fine. Is anyone with you?
Caller -> My husband's here. He's helping. He's cleaning up.
Caller -> Our kids are at school. I'll tell them when they get home, if it's still bad.
Nurse -> That's up to you. We can help with that conversation if you want.
Nurse -> Good. You don't have to do it alone.
Caller -> No. It's okay. We're managing.
Nurse -> The clinician will call you soon. Please keep the line free.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Pilar.
Caller -> Should I call my brother? He's out of state.
Nurse -> It's a good idea to keep him posted. Maybe after the clinician calls, so you have more to tell him.
Caller -> After the call. Okay. That makes sense.
Nurse -> Take care. Call back if anything changes.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cedar Hollow Home Care, this is Blanca.
Caller -> Hi. Hello. Blanca. It's Orville Beckwith. I'm calling about my wife, Marisol Beckwith. I'm not saying there's something wrong. I'm not saying there's nothing wrong, either.
Nurse -> Okay, Orville. Let's figure it out together. What made you call?
Caller -> I'm bad at this. I don't want to say the wrong thing and have you think she's worse than she is.
Nurse -> Just tell me what you saw and heard. I'll sort it out.
Caller -> She was, I wouldn't say she wasn't dizzy this morning. When she stood up. But then she wouldn't say she was. You know how she is.
Nurse -> Okay. So I'm going to ask a simple question. Was Marisol dizzy this morning, yes or no?
Caller -> I think yes. But she says no. I don't think she'd admit it. So, I'd say probably. I don't know. I'm not going to say definitely.
Nurse -> Okay. So she may have been dizzy. She says no. That's fine.
Caller -> Right. I saw her hold onto the counter. That's what I saw.
Nurse -> Got it. Let's move on. Did she take her blood pressure pill this morning?
Caller -> Oh, she didn't not take it. I mean she took it. I watched her. She took it with her coffee. The lisinopril. Ten milligrams. Once a day.
Nurse -> So yes, she took it.
Caller -> One sec. My phone is making that beeping sound.
Nurse -> No worries, I'll wait.
Caller -> Yes. She took it.
Nurse -> Good. Does she have a headache?
Caller -> She wouldn't say she hasn't had one. But she hasn't mentioned one. Wait. That's confusing. She hasn't said anything about a headache. I asked her. She said her head is fine.
Nurse -> So no headache.
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> No headache. That's what she said. Yes.
Nurse -> Do you have a blood pressure cuff?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> We do. I took it a minute ago. A hundred thirty four over eighty two.
Nurse -> That's a reasonable number. What does she usually run?
Caller -> About that. A little lower, maybe. A hundred twenty something. It's never been what I'd call high.
Nurse -> Does the doctor have you both keep a log of the readings?
Caller -> She keeps it in a spiral notebook. Every morning. She's neater than me.
Nurse -> Okay. Any chest pain? Any falls? Shortness of breath?
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> No chest pain. No falls. She didn't fall. She held the counter and sat down. I'd say she's not short of breath. She's fine in that way.
Nurse -> Good. What's Marisol's date of birth?
Caller -> October tenth, nineteen fifty two.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Nine oh one, five five five, zero one eight seven.
Nurse -> Got it. Orville, is she able to come to the phone?
Caller -> She's in the shower. She'd say she can't. She'd say she's fine. But she's in the shower.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. I won't bother her. Here's what I'll do. I'll call you back this afternoon when she's out, and I'll ask her myself.
Caller -> That's smart. She'll tell you more than she'll tell me. Maybe. She might not.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll see. I'm also going to schedule a nurse to visit tomorrow, to check her blood pressure and ask how she's feeling.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. She'll say she doesn't need it. But I think she does.
Nurse -> It's a routine check. Don't worry about it.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> Orville, until then, here's something that will help. When she gets up from sitting or lying down, have her go slowly. Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute first. Use her walker or hold something steady. And if she feels lightheaded, sit right back down.
Caller -> Slow. Sit on the edge. Hold something. Sit back down. I'll tell her. She won't love it.
Nurse -> Tell her the nurse said. It works.
Caller -> Ha. Everybody says that. She doesn't listen to nurses either.
Nurse -> Ha. A tough customer.
Caller -> The toughest. Fifty five years I've been losing arguments.
Caller -> We met at a skating rink. She pushed me and I fell. That was the first argument.
Nurse -> Ha. And you still married her.
Caller -> I got up. That's the lesson.
Nurse -> Fifty five years. Congratulations.
Caller -> Okay. I've got a notebook now. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Alright.
Caller -> Thank you. It's been an education.
Nurse -> Call us if she faints, has chest pain, a severe headache, or if the dizziness gets worse. If it's an emergency, call nine one one.
Caller -> Faints. Chest pain. Bad headache. Worse dizziness. Nine one one. I'll write it down.
Nurse -> Great. Anything else?
Caller -> I think the line cut out for a second. Are you still there?
Nurse -> Yes, I'm here.
Caller -> No. I don't think there's nothing else. I mean, that's all.
Nurse -> Ha. Perfect.
Caller -> Thank you, Blanca.
Nurse -> Talk to you this afternoon.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Aspen Grove Home Health, this is Nikolai.
Caller -> Hi, Nikolai. It's Ximena Torregrosa. I'm the aide for Lawrence Ostrander. I need supplies for his dressing changes.
Nurse -> Hi, Ximena. What do you need?
Caller -> Everything for the sore on his tailbone. I'm running out. I should have called yesterday, but I was waiting on his daughter to say.
Nurse -> That's okay. Let's go through it. Start with the foam dressings.
Caller -> His daughter keeps saying to wait for the nurse's visit, and then the nurse is on a different route. It's a whole thing.
Nurse -> Next time, call the line directly. You don't have to wait for anyone.
Caller -> I have four. The big square ones with the adhesive. I change one every other day, and when it gets soiled, so four is maybe a week. Maybe less.
Nurse -> Okay. And the wound wash? The saline spray?
Caller -> One bottle. It's about half full.
Nurse -> And gloves?
Caller -> None. I used the last pair this morning. I have a bag of the kitchen ones, but I don't want to use those.
Nurse -> Right. Don't use the kitchen gloves for wound care. I'll get you proper ones.
Caller -> Wait, say that again? I missed the first part.
Nurse -> Of course. Let me say it slower.
Caller -> Thank you. I've been washing my hands extra. But I need the real gloves.
Nurse -> That's good practice. Wash for twenty seconds, before and after, even with gloves.
Caller -> Twenty seconds. I sing happy birthday twice.
Nurse -> Ha. The classic.
Nurse -> What about tape, or barrier film?
Caller -> The dressings have the adhesive. I don't use tape.
Nurse -> Any skin tearing when you take the foam off?
Caller -> Not now. I peel it back slow, like a bandage, low and slow. The old nurse showed me.
Nurse -> That's the right way.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, how does the wound look today?
Caller -> That's the other reason I called. This morning, when I took off the dressing, there was more fluid than usual. It was soaked. The whole center of the foam was wet and yellowish. Not green. It was wetter than the last few days.
Nurse -> Okay. Was there a smell?
Caller -> No smell. I smelled it. Nothing. Just the regular smell of the cleanser.
Nurse -> And the skin around it, is it intact, or any open spots nearby?
Caller -> Intact. Just the one sore. The skin next to it is dry and flaky, though. I put the barrier cream on the outside edge only.
Nurse -> Good. Not inside the wound.
Nurse -> Any fever? Does he feel warm?
Caller -> I took his temperature this morning, he was normal. And he doesn't feel hot. He's cold, actually. He always has cold hands.
Caller -> I put socks on his hands at night. He says it looks silly, but they're warm.
Nurse -> Ha. A caregiver's trick.
Nurse -> Good. What about the edges? Are they red? Is the redness spreading?
Caller -> A little pink around the edge. The same pink as before. It's not spreading. I drew a circle with a marker last week, like the nurse showed me, and it's inside the circle.
Nurse -> That's an excellent technique. Thank you for doing that.
Caller -> Sure. The nurse taught me. I learned a lot from her.
Nurse -> Is he in more pain than usual?
Caller -> He says no. He says he doesn't feel it. He has the numbness. He doesn't feel much below the waist.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me have his date of birth.
Caller -> June twenty first, nineteen forty three.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one one seven.
Nurse -> Got it. Ximena, I'm going to order the foam dressings, the wound wash, and a couple of boxes of gloves.
Caller -> Oh, perfect. Thank you.
Nurse -> I can have them to you this evening.
Caller -> This evening? That's great. I'll be here until eight.
Nurse -> The driver will call before coming. Is that okay?
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> Yes. Call me on the number I gave you.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'm also going to message the wound care nurse about the extra drainage so she can decide whether to see him sooner.
Caller -> Yes, please. I thought that's what you'd say.
Nurse -> Until then, keep doing what you're doing. Turn him every two hours, and use the pillows to keep pressure off the tailbone. Keep the dressing clean and dry.
Caller -> Every two hours. Pillows. Keep it dry. I have a timer on my phone. I turn him at the top of every even hour.
Nurse -> What do you do at night, when you're not there?
Caller -> The night aide takes over at eight. I leave her a note with the turning times and where the pillows go.
Nurse -> A handoff note. That's excellent.
Nurse -> That's great. How's his skin in other places? Heels, hips?
Caller -> Fine. I check them every time. They're pink and they go back to normal when I press. The heels are floated on a pillow.
Nurse -> Beautiful. You're doing excellent care.
Caller -> Thank you. It's the part of the job I like.
Caller -> Some of the other aides don't like wounds. I don't mind. It's just a body doing its best.
Nurse -> That's a lovely way to put it.
Nurse -> How long have you been doing this work?
Caller -> Eleven years. Before that I worked in a bakery. I like being useful in a different way.
Nurse -> Bakers and caregivers get up early.
Caller -> Ha. Both of us.
Nurse -> I can tell. Now, if you smell anything bad, if he gets a fever, if the redness spreads past your circle, if there's much more fluid, or if the wound gets bigger or darker, call us right away.
Caller -> Smell. Fever. Redness past the line. A lot more fluid. Bigger or darker. I'll watch for all that.
Nurse -> Great. Is he eating well?
Caller -> Pretty good. He likes the protein shakes. I give him one at ten and one at three. And he eats a decent lunch.
Nurse -> Is he drinking water too?
Caller -> A glass at every meal and one at bedtime. He says it makes him go to the bathroom, so he fights me.
Nurse -> Keep encouraging it. It helps healing.
Nurse -> Good. Protein helps wounds heal.
Caller -> That's what the nurse said. I buy the chocolate ones. He won't drink the vanilla.
Nurse -> Ha. A man of taste.
Caller -> He says the vanilla tastes like a candle.
Caller -> I tried mixing the two. He tasted it and said, Ximena, you're cheating.
Nurse -> Ha. He's not fooled.
Nurse -> Ha. Fair.
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> He's a funny man. He used to be a high school shop teacher. He's got stories about every kid.
Nurse -> I bet he does.
Caller -> He tells me one every day. Yesterday it was about a boy who built a canoe in the parking lot.
Nurse -> Ha. Did it float?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little scattered today.
Nurse -> That's completely understandable.
Caller -> It sank in the pond. They all clapped anyway.
Nurse -> That's the best kind of story.
Caller -> He says it's the most successful failure of his career.
Nurse -> Ha. I love that.
Caller -> Sorry, somebody's at the door. Hang on a second.
Nurse -> No problem, I'll hold.
Caller -> Me too. Okay. Anything else you need from me?
Caller -> I should tell you, his wife passed in the spring and he still sets two plates for dinner. I don't say anything.
Nurse -> That's gentle of you.
Caller -> I sit and have tea with him. It feels right.
Nurse -> No, I think we're set. The driver will call this evening. Call me if there's a problem.
Caller -> I'll leave the porch light on in case it's dark.
Nurse -> Perfect. Thanks, Ximena.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Nikolai.
Nurse -> Thank you, Ximena. Take care.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Tidewater Pediatric Home Health, this is Hortensia.
Caller -> Hi. This is Callum Whitcombe. I'm calling about my daughter, Juniper Whitcombe. It's just a check in. She has the reflux.
Nurse -> Hi, Callum. Good to hear from you. How is Juniper?
Caller -> She's good. She's great. I just, I get nervous. My wife went back to work on Monday so it's me during the day.
Nurse -> I can hear you're a little nervous. That's normal on your first week alone.
Caller -> I keep checking on her every ten minutes while she naps. She's fine every time.
Nurse -> That's a big change. Let me start with her date of birth.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little scattered today.
Nurse -> That's completely understandable.
Caller -> July thirtieth, twenty twenty six. She's four months.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number for you?
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> Nine one eight, five five five, zero one two one.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me about the spit-up.
Caller -> She spits up a little after most feeds. Like a spoonful. Sometimes more. It's milky. It comes out the side of her mouth. She doesn't seem upset about it. She just smiles.
Nurse -> Is it forceful? Does it shoot out?
Caller -> No. It just dribbles. It's not projectile. I know what projectile looks like, I watched a video.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. Any blood? Green color?
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> No. It's white or a little yellow, like the formula. No fever. I took her temperature this morning. It was normal.
Nurse -> Good. How's her weight?
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> We weighed her at the pediatrician yesterday. Fourteen pounds six ounces. Up from fourteen pounds even two weeks ago.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. She's gaining well.
Caller -> Okay. I've got a notebook now. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Alright.
Caller -> The doctor said so too. But I still worry.
Nurse -> It's natural. How often is she feeding?
Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> Every three hours. Five ounces. Formula. She finishes it all. She sleeps through most of the night, maybe wakes once.
Nurse -> That's a great schedule. How many wet diapers a day?
Caller -> Six, seven. She's very wet. I'm changing her a lot.
Nurse -> Perfect. Let me go over some tips for the reflux. After she eats, keep her upright for about twenty minutes. Burp her halfway through the bottle and again at the end.
Caller -> Upright, twenty minutes. Burp halfway. Okay. I've been burping at the end. Not halfway.
Nurse -> Try halfway. It often reduces the spit-up. And avoid bouncing or lots of tummy time right after a feed.
Caller -> Okay. No bouncing. My wife loves bouncing her. I'll tell her.
Nurse -> Ha. A little fun after twenty minutes is fine.
Caller -> She giggles when she's bounced. It's the best sound.
Nurse -> It is. Enjoy it.
Caller -> Okay. Does she need to sleep on an incline? I read that online.
Nurse -> No. Please keep her flat on her back in a crib. No wedges, no pillows. That's the safest.
Caller -> Flat on her back. Right. That's what the pediatrician said. I was just checking.
Nurse -> Good. It's the safest way, even with reflux.
Caller -> Okay. I'm glad I asked.
Nurse -> Call us if she starts vomiting forcefully, if the spit-up looks green or has blood, if she has fewer wet diapers, a fever, or if she refuses to feed.
Caller -> Forceful. Green or bloody. Fewer diapers. Fever. Refusing. Okay. I'll put it on the fridge.
Nurse -> Great. I'd like to check in with you again next week to see how she's doing and how you're doing.
Caller -> That would be great. I'd appreciate it. Call me at this number.
Nurse -> Will do. How are you holding up, Callum?
Caller -> I'm okay. I'm tired. Her sleep is good, but I'm the one who's up. I don't know why.
Nurse -> New dads often are. Are you eating?
Caller -> Cereal. Mostly cereal.
Nurse -> Ha. Try to add some protein. And take a break when your wife is home.
Caller -> Sorry, somebody's at the door. Hang on a second.
Nurse -> No problem, I'll hold.
Caller -> I will. She makes me. She gives me the baby carrier and tells me to take a walk.
Nurse -> Take the walk. It helps.
Caller -> Sorry, I lost my train of thought.
Nurse -> That's okay. We were just getting started.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Hortensia. I feel better.
Nurse -> You're doing a good job already.
Caller -> Thanks, I needed to hear that.
Nurse -> Anytime. Congratulations, Dad.
Caller -> Thank you. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Gladstone Home Health, this is Cordelia.
Caller -> Hi, Cordelia. It's Mervin Calloway. M E R V I N. I'm a patient. I had my toe taken off last week. And I think there's something going on with it.
Nurse -> Hi, Marvin. I'm sorry to hear that. Okay. Let me bring up your chart. Marvin Calloway?
Caller -> Mervin. With an E. But that's all right. Everyone gets it.
Nurse -> Okay, Marvin. Tell me what's going on with the toe.
Caller -> It's nothing, probably. I kept telling myself that. For two days.
Nurse -> You did the right thing calling.
Caller -> My neighbor made me. She said, Mervin, pick up the phone.
Caller -> Wait. Mervin. It's not a big deal. Go on. Please go on.
Nurse -> Alright. What's happening with the toe, Marvin?
Caller -> The toe is draining and it, it smells a little.
Nurse -> It's draining and it smells.
Caller -> A little. Not a lot. It started yesterday. It was dry before. Today the dressing was wet through, yellowish.
Nurse -> Did anything happen to the dressing? Did it get wet, or did you bump the foot?
Caller -> I bumped it on the coffee table on Saturday. Not hard. I yelped. Biscuit ran out of the room.
Nurse -> Okay. That could have irritated it.
Nurse -> Okay. How much drainage? Is it soaked?
Caller -> The gauze was wet. About the size of a, a half dollar. Maybe bigger. I changed it this morning and by lunch it was wet again.
Nurse -> What color was the fluid? Clear, yellow, green, brown?
Caller -> Yellow. Pale yellow. Like weak tea.
Nurse -> Any thick or pus-like material?
Caller -> No. Thin. Runny.
Nurse -> Any bleeding?
Caller -> No. No bright blood. Just that thin, yellowish stuff.
Nurse -> Okay. Any pain?
Caller -> A four. A four out of ten. It aches. It's a throbbing ache. It was a two last week. It got worse yesterday.
Nurse -> Does it keep you up at night?
Caller -> Some. I wake up around three, adjust the pillow, and go back to sleep. It's not terrible.
Caller -> It kind of pulses with my heartbeat when I'm sitting still. Like a little drum.
Nurse -> That's helpful to know. I'll pass it on.
Nurse -> Does anything make it better or worse?
Caller -> Raising the foot helps. When I put it down on the floor the throbbing starts.
Nurse -> That's useful. Elevation is good.
Nurse -> Do you have a fever?
Caller -> I took it an hour ago. Ninety nine point six. So a little warm.
Caller -> I use the digital one. It beeps. It beeped twice, so I did it again to be sure.
Nurse -> And both were the same?
Caller -> Both the same. Ninety nine point six.
Nurse -> Okay. Any chills? Shaking, sweats?
Caller -> No chills. I felt kind of warm last night. No shaking.
Nurse -> Did you take anything for it, like acetaminophen?
Caller -> Nothing. I didn't want to hide a fever. The nurse said not to cover it up.
Nurse -> That's a smart instinct.
Nurse -> Any redness going up the foot or the leg? Any red streaks?
Caller -> I looked. I used the mirror. It's red around the edge of the dressing, but no streaks. Nothing climbing up. Just the, around the wound.
Nurse -> Okay. Are you taking an antibiotic?
Caller -> Yes. The cephalexin. Five hundred milligrams. Four times a day. I'm on day five of ten. I took one at noon.
Nurse -> Good. Have you missed any doses?
Caller -> No. I have an alarm. Seven, noon, five, and ten. I haven't missed one.
Nurse -> Excellent. What's your date of birth, Mervin?
Caller -> Wait, could you say that again? The line broke.
Nurse -> What is your date of birth, Mervin?
Caller -> Got it. May fourteenth. I'll say it slow.
Caller -> May fourteenth, nineteen sixty four.
Nurse -> May fourteenth, nineteen sixty four. Thank you. And a number?
Caller -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one zero three.
Nurse -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one eight three. Is that right?
Caller -> No, no. Zero one zero three. The number ends in zero one zero three. Not eight. Zero.
Nurse -> Zero one zero three. Got it. Sorry about that.
Caller -> No problem. It's a bad connection. I keep dropping out. Can you hear me okay?
Nurse -> Do you want to move indoors and call back?
Caller -> No, no. It's cold but the signal's better. I'll stay put.
Nurse -> Alright. Tell me if you drop out.
Nurse -> I can. A few words are cutting out, but I'm getting most of it.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I'm on the porch because it's the only place I get a signal.
Nurse -> I'll keep my questions short then.
Caller -> I appreciate it. It's windy, too. You might hear the chimes.
Caller -> Hang on. There they go.
Nurse -> Ha. I can hear them. Pretty.
Nurse -> Ha. A porch phone call. Are you warm enough?
Caller -> I used to sit out here every evening before the surgery. Watching the street. It's my spot.
Nurse -> It sounds like a nice spot.
Caller -> I'm bundled. I have a blanket and a coffee. It's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Mervin, let's talk about the dressing. How are you changing it?
Caller -> Once a day. I wash my hands. I take the old one off, I look at it, I put a new one on. I use the gauze and the paper tape. And the, the nurse said to wrap it with the rolled gauze.
Nurse -> Do you use any ointment under the gauze?
Caller -> Just what they gave me at the hospital. It's the white stuff in the tube. A thin layer.
Nurse -> That's right. Only a thin layer.
Nurse -> How many rolls of gauze do you have?
Caller -> I have three. Three rolls. I'm using one a day, so that's three days.
Caller -> I could stretch it by using the tape more. But I don't want to.
Nurse -> Don't stretch it. Use what you need.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll order more. I'll send plenty.
Caller -> Thank you. I appreciate that.
Nurse -> Mervin, I'm going to send a message to the wound clinician about the drainage and the smell, so they can decide if they want to change anything.
Caller -> Okay. That's good. I was hoping somebody would look at it.
Nurse -> And I'm scheduling a nurse visit for tomorrow, so she can look at it in person.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Great. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a window. Probably in the morning.
Caller -> I'll be around. I'm not going anywhere. I can't, with the foot.
Nurse -> Ha. That's true. In the meantime, change the dressing once a day or any time it gets soaked. Wash your hands first. Keep your foot raised on a pillow when you're sitting. And keep the dressing dry.
Caller -> Once a day, or when it's soaked. Wash hands. Foot up. Keep it dry. Okay. I'll cover it when I shower.
Nurse -> And after the shower, change the dressing right away, even if it stayed dry.
Caller -> Right after. Okay. I'll have the clean one ready on the towel.
Nurse -> Do you shower?
Caller -> I sit on a stool and I put a plastic bag over the foot. With tape.
Nurse -> That's good. Make sure the bag is sealed all the way around.
Caller -> It is. I've done it a few times.
Nurse -> Great. Also, finish every dose of the antibiotic. Even if the toe looks better. Take it evenly spaced and with food.
Caller -> Every dose. Spaced out. With food. I take it with crackers or toast.
Nurse -> Perfect. Mervin, there are a few things to watch for. If your temperature goes to one hundred one or higher, if you get chills, if you see red streaks going up the foot, if the drainage gets heavy, or the pain gets worse, call us right away.
Nurse -> Does that make sense so far?
Caller -> It does. You're easy to follow, Cordelia. The last nurse talked so fast I wrote nothing down.
Caller -> A hundred one. Chills. Red streaks. Heavy drainage. More pain. Okay. I wrote it on a sticky note. It's on the coffee table.
Nurse -> Good. If you can't reach us, go to the emergency room.
Caller -> I will. My neighbor said she'd drive me if I need it.
Nurse -> What's her name, in case we need to reach her?
Caller -> Loretta. Across the street. She has a green door.
Nurse -> We'll make a note of it.
Nurse -> That's great. It helps to have a ride.
Caller -> She's a good neighbor. She brought me soup.
Caller -> She also brought a casserole, but I haven't touched it. It has olives. I hate olives.
Nurse -> Ha. A hazard of casseroles.
Caller -> I'm politely hiding it in the freezer.
Nurse -> Ha. What kind?
Caller -> Chicken and rice. With too much pepper. But I ate it.
Caller -> I love pepper, though. I just can't taste much since the cold.
Nurse -> Ha. Then Loretta did the right thing.
Nurse -> Ha. That's what neighbors are for.
Caller -> Yes. And she's checking on my cat when I'm in bed. His name is Biscuit.
Nurse -> Is it hard being home alone?
Caller -> A little. I'm not used to sitting. I used to drive a delivery truck. Now I'm watching the same four shows.
Nurse -> That's a big change.
Caller -> It's driving me nuts. But I'll get through it. I just want to walk again.
Nurse -> Biscuit. I like that.
Caller -> He's got a bad attitude. But he's a good boy.
Nurse -> Ha. Cats and attitudes.
Caller -> He's an orange tabby. He sits on my foot. The good foot.
Nurse -> Ha. Keep it that way.
Caller -> I do. I don't want him near the bad one.
Caller -> He tried to sniff the dressing once and I about jumped through the roof.
Nurse -> Good reflexes. Keep the cat away from the wound for now, and wash your hands if he's been on the foot.
Nurse -> Good plan. Is there anything else I can help with?
Caller -> No, that's it. Oh, wait. Can I drive?
Nurse -> Not yet. Not until the surgeon says. Which foot?
Caller -> When do you think I could? Roughly.
Nurse -> That's for the surgeon to say. They'll know when the wound has healed.
Caller -> Okay. I'll ask at the follow up. It's the twentieth.
Caller -> The right. The driving foot. Ha.
Nurse -> Does your insurance cover a ride service to appointments?
Caller -> I think so. I'll ask. Loretta says she'll drive me but I hate to impose.
Nurse -> The scheduler can help check that. Ask at the visit tomorrow.
Nurse -> Then definitely not. Let the neighbor drive.
Caller -> Okay. I figured. I'll behave.
Caller -> Can I ask one more silly thing? Is it okay to elevate the foot above my heart?
Nurse -> Slightly above is fine while you're lying down. Not hanging it down is the main thing.
Caller -> Okay. Pillows then.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself, Mervin. We'll see you tomorrow.
Caller -> I will. And thank you for not rushing me. I know you've got other calls.
Nurse -> You're not rushing me. You're one of my calls today.
Caller -> Thank you, Cordelia. Bye.
Caller -> Oh, one more thing, sorry. Is it normal for it to itch around the edges?
Nurse -> Mild itching can be part of healing, but tell the nurse tomorrow. Don't scratch it.
Caller -> I'll keep my hands off.
Nurse -> Bye, Mervin.
