transcript:
Nurse -> Gladstone Home Health, this is Cordelia.
Caller -> Hi, Cordelia. It's Evander Prescott. My mother is Hildegard Prescott. She's out of her seizure medicine. She's been out for two days.
Nurse -> Okay, Evander. Thank you for calling. Which medicine is it?
Caller -> I should have called Monday. I kept thinking the pharmacy would figure it out.
Nurse -> You called today. That counts.
Caller -> Levetiracetam. Five hundred milligrams. Twice a day. Morning and night. The last one was Sunday night.
Nurse -> And today is Tuesday. So she's missed Monday morning, Monday night, and this morning.
Caller -> Three doses. Yes. Three doses. And tonight's is due now.
Nurse -> How long has she been on it?
Caller -> Six years. Since her stroke. She has never missed it. Not once, until now.
Nurse -> That makes me want to fix this quickly.
Nurse -> What happened with the refill?
Caller -> The pharmacy says it's out of refills and needs a new authorization from the doctor. They said they sent a request Friday. Nobody answered. I called the doctor's office today and I got voicemail.
Caller -> I left two messages. The recording said the office closes at five and reopens at eight. It's after nine.
Nurse -> Right. That's why I'll use the after hours line.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to take over on that. First, how is your mother right now?
Caller -> She's okay. She's in her chair. She seems okay. This morning she had a moment though. She stared at the wall for maybe ten seconds. Didn't answer me. Then she was fine.
Nurse -> Has she been sleepier than usual today?
Caller -> A little. She napped after lunch for two hours. That's long for her.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll pass that on too.
Nurse -> Is she talking normally? Following conversation?
Caller -> Yes. She asked me what's for dinner. She's irritated I forgot the salt.
Nurse -> Ha. A good sign.
Nurse -> A staring spell. Did her eyes move, her mouth, her hands?
Caller -> Her lips were doing a little smacking thing. Just for a second. Then she blinked and said what? She didn't remember it.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she had a full seizure? Shaking, falling, losing consciousness?
Caller -> No. No convulsions. She hasn't fallen. She's been sitting most of the day.
Nurse -> Does she use a walker or a cane?
Caller -> A walker. It's next to her chair. I put it within reach.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Good. What's her date of birth, Evander?
Caller -> February eighth, nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> And a number?
Caller -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one two eight.
Nurse -> Is that your cell?
Caller -> Yes. I'll keep it on the table next to me and on loud.
Nurse -> Got it. Missing seizure medicine can be risky, so I want to act quickly. I'm going to call the pharmacy right now and ask if they can release a few doses while we get authorization.
Caller -> Oh, thank God. Please. I'd drive there but I don't have a car tonight. Mine's in the shop.
Caller -> What if the pharmacy refuses? Because they said no authorization, no pills.
Nurse -> Pharmacists can sometimes give an emergency supply for a medicine like this. I'll ask.
Caller -> Okay. I didn't know that.
Nurse -> We'll work something out. I'm also going to contact the neurologist's office. They should have an after hours line.
Caller -> I tried. It just rings.
Nurse -> I have a different number. And I'll page our on-call clinician so we have someone who can authorize a short supply tonight.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I was so scared to call. I thought you'd tell me to go to the ER.
Caller -> Is it dangerous that she's missed three doses?
Nurse -> It raises the risk of a seizure, which is why I'm taking this seriously. It doesn't mean one will happen.
Caller -> Okay. That's honest. Thank you.
Nurse -> It's possible, if we can't get the medicine tonight. Let's see what we can do first. Evander, in the meantime, stay with her. Don't leave her alone, and keep her away from stairs, the stove, and the bathtub. If she has a seizure, lay her on her side, put something soft under her head, and time it.
Caller -> Stay with her. Away from stairs and the stove. If she seizes, on her side, time it. Okay. I have the clock on the wall.
Nurse -> Don't put anything in her mouth.
Caller -> No. Nothing in her mouth. I remember that from the video.
Nurse -> Good. And call nine one one if a seizure lasts more than five minutes, if she has more than one in a row, if she has trouble breathing afterward, or if she's hurt.
Caller -> Over five minutes. More than one. Trouble breathing. Hurt. Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> Say it back to your wife too, so you both know.
Caller -> I will. I'll write it on the fridge. She'll add her own notes.
Nurse -> Is anyone else with you?
Nurse -> How many kids do you have?
Caller -> Two. Six and nine. They love their grandma. The nine year old reads to her at night.
Nurse -> That's sweet.
Caller -> My wife is here. She's putting the kids to bed. She's watching mom for a minute.
Nurse -> Good. Keep your phone close. I'll call you back within thirty minutes.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. Thank you, Cordelia. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> You did the right thing by calling.
Caller -> She's the one who raised me and now I'm the one on the phone. It's strange.
Nurse -> It is. And you're doing a good job.
Caller -> I almost waited till morning. My wife made me call.
Nurse -> Tell your wife she's right.
Caller -> I will. Ha. Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Marigold Home Care, this is Sebastian.
Caller -> Hi, Sebastian. My name is Harlan Obregon. I'm calling about my neighbor. Tabitha Pomeroy. I'm not family. Her daughter asked me to check on her.
Nurse -> Hi, Harlan. Thanks for calling. Is everything all right?
Caller -> Oh, yes. Everything's fine. I just wanted to give you an update. The daughter is in Phoenix this week for work. And I told her I'd call you folks if anything came up. Nothing came up. But I said I'd report in.
Nurse -> That's very thoughtful. Tell me how she is.
Caller -> I'm retired, so I've got the time. I used to be a mail carrier. I walked this route for twenty six years.
Nurse -> Then you know every porch in the neighborhood.
Caller -> Every one. And every dog.
Caller -> Sorry, I lost my train of thought.
Nurse -> That's okay. We were just getting started.
Caller -> She's good. I went over at eight. She was up. She had her robe on. She'd made oatmeal and she ate it all. She was singing along to the radio. She asked me if I wanted breakfast.
Nurse -> That sounds wonderful. Did she seem steady on her feet?
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> Steady as ever. She walked me to the door. She uses the cane but she doesn't lean on it much.
Nurse -> Does she have a medical alert button, or a phone she keeps nearby?
Caller -> She wears a pendant around her neck. I saw it. She jokes that it's her necklace.
Nurse -> Ha. Good that she wears it.
Nurse -> Any falls? Any complaints? Pain, dizziness, anything new?
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> No falls. No complaints. I asked her straight out. She said, Harlan, I'm eighty four, everything hurts, nothing's new. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. That sounds like her.
Caller -> It does. She's got a sense of humor.
Nurse -> Did you happen to see her pills? Any trouble with her medicines?
Caller -> I looked at the organizer. The one with the days of the week. It's full. The daughter filled it Sunday before she left. Monday and Tuesday are empty, as they should be. Wednesday is today and that one's empty too. So she's taking them.
Nurse -> That's very helpful. Thank you.
Caller -> I didn't touch anything. I just looked.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Harlan, can I get your phone number, in case the nurse needs to reach you?
Caller -> Sure. Three oh three, five five five, zero one six nine. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Got it. Do you know Tabitha's date of birth, by any chance?
Caller -> Oh, no. No idea. I know she's in her eighties, and her birthday's in the spring, because she makes a cake and invites the whole street. But I don't know the date.
Nurse -> That's all right. I have it in her chart. Did you want to ask about something?
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> Yes. Her daughter said the nurse comes on Thursday. I wanted to confirm that's still happening. And whether I should do anything. Like be there, or leave the door unlocked.
Nurse -> Let me check the schedule. Yes, I see a visit on Thursday. The nurse will knock. Tabitha can let her in. You don't need to be there.
Caller -> Okay. That's good. I'll tell her.
Nurse -> I'll message the visiting nurse and let her know you checked in, and I'll pass along your number in case she wants to reach you.
Caller -> That's fine. I'd be glad to help.
Nurse -> Thank you. Harlan, if you notice anything that worries you, call us any time. A fall, if she seems confused, if she skips meals, anything unusual. And if it's an emergency, call nine one one.
Caller -> Fall. Confused. Skipping meals. Anything off. And nine one one for an emergency. Okay. I've got your number on my phone now.
Nurse -> Great. Do you know whether she has any visitors this week besides you?
Caller -> The pastor comes Friday. And the lady across the street brings the paper. She's well looked after.
Nurse -> And the daughter calls her every day?
Caller -> Every evening at six. Tabitha puts it on speaker so I can say hi through the window. It's a whole routine.
Nurse -> That's good to hear.
Caller -> We look out for each other on this street. There are six of us who've lived here over thirty years.
Nurse -> That's a great neighborhood.
Caller -> It is. We have a barbecue every Fourth of July. Tabitha makes the potato salad.
Nurse -> Ha. Can't beat that.
Caller -> Tabitha's husband used to work the grill. He passed a few years back. Now the whole street takes turns.
Nurse -> That's a lovely way to keep it going.
Caller -> She won't share the recipe. I think it's mustard.
Nurse -> Ha. The secret ingredient.
Caller -> Anyway. Sorry, I'm talking too much.
Nurse -> Not at all. I appreciate the call.
Caller -> I wasn't sure it was okay to call, since I'm not family.
Nurse -> It's always fine to call. We just can't share her chart, but we can listen and pass things along.
Caller -> That's all I wanted.
Caller -> Sorry, I just dropped my pen.
Nurse -> That's all right.
Caller -> Well, I'll let you go. Thanks, Sebastian.
Nurse -> Thank you, Harlan. Take care.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

Nurse -> Briar Hill Home Health, this is Anselmo.
Caller -> Hi, Anselmo. This is Winifred Larkin. I'm a patient. I have a question about my insulin. I can't remember if I took it last night.
Nurse -> Hi, Winifred. Okay. Let's work through it. Which insulin?
Caller -> I know it's silly. I've been taking it for nine years. I should know.
Nurse -> Nine years of nightly habit means you do it without thinking. That's exactly why it's easy to lose track.
Caller -> The Levemir. The long one. Fourteen units. At bedtime. Every night.
Nurse -> Do you keep the pen in the refrigerator or at room temperature?
Caller -> The one in use is on the nightstand. The spare pens are in the fridge door.
Nurse -> That's right. The one in use is fine at room temperature.
Nurse -> Okay. And you're not sure you took it last night.
Caller -> I'm not sure. My daughter was here. She says she saw me do it. She says I took it at ten, and I said good night. But I don't remember. I remember sitting on the bed with the pen in my hand. And then I remember the morning.
Nurse -> Were you tired, or distracted? Was the television on?
Caller -> The television was on. A baking show. She had the remote. We were talking about her son's soccer game.
Nurse -> That would do it.
Nurse -> Hmm. Do you see the pen? Is the counter on it? Can you tell how many units you dialed?
Caller -> I have it. It's right here. It's got the little window. It shows a zero. It always goes back to zero after I inject. So that doesn't tell me anything.
Nurse -> Right. It resets. Is there a log? A notebook where you write the doses?
Caller -> I'm supposed to write it. I wrote it Monday. I didn't write Tuesday. Last night is Tuesday. So I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. What did your sugar read this morning?
Caller -> Two twelve. Fasting. Normally I'm a hundred forty or so.
Nurse -> That's higher than usual. Is it high enough to suggest you missed the dose? It could be. It could also be from something you ate.
Caller -> Wait, say that again? I missed the first part.
Nurse -> Of course. Let me say it slower.
Caller -> I had a piece of cake at the church thing. And ice cream. I know. I know.
Caller -> It was Gloria's retirement party. I couldn't say no. Nobody says no to Gloria.
Nurse -> Ha. One piece of cake and a scoop of ice cream isn't a crime.
Nurse -> Ha. That could do it.
Caller -> Can you hear me okay? The signal's a little weak.
Nurse -> I can hear you fine.
Caller -> It could. So it might not be the insulin. I just don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. How are you feeling today? Thirsty, tired, urinating a lot?
Caller -> A little thirsty. I've had two glasses of water already. Not too bad. I'm a little tired but I always am.
Caller -> Is that the sugar? Or the salt from the soup?
Nurse -> Could be either. Keep sipping water and we'll see how the readings look.
Nurse -> Any nausea, vomiting? Any confusion, or trouble thinking?
Caller -> No. No, I'm clear. I did the crossword. I'm clear as a bell.
Nurse -> How did you do?
Caller -> Finished it. Even the one about the Roman emperor.
Nurse -> Impressive.
Nurse -> Good. Winifred, can I get your date of birth?
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> September ninth, nineteen fifty.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one three two.
Nurse -> Got it. So here's the thing. I can't tell you for sure whether you took it. Your daughter says yes, you say you don't remember. We can't solve that over the phone.
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> That's what I figured. What do I do?
Nurse -> Please do not take an extra dose now to make up for it. If you did take it last night, a second dose could drop your sugar a lot.
Caller -> No extra. Okay. I wouldn't have.
Nurse -> For tonight, take your regular fourteen units at bedtime, unless the clinician tells you otherwise. I'm going to message them and ask.
Caller -> Regular dose tonight. Unless they say. Okay. And I'll write it down. I'll write the time.
Nurse -> Good. And from now on, write down every dose, every night, right when you take it. Even before you put the pen away.
Caller -> I'll put the notebook on the pillow so I can't forget. Right on the pillow.
Caller -> I'll put a pencil on a string, too. Like at the bank.
Nurse -> Ha. A good idea.
Nurse -> That's smart.
Caller -> Sorry, I just dropped my pen.
Nurse -> That's all right.
Caller -> Thank you. My daughter bought me a pill alarm too. It beeps. I turn it off and then I forget.
Nurse -> A good tool, as long as you don't snooze it.
Caller -> I snooze everything.
Nurse -> Ha. Don't turn it off until you've written it in the notebook.
Caller -> That's a good rule. I'll do that.
Nurse -> I'm messaging the clinician now about the two twelve and the unsure dose.
Caller -> Yes. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll send a nurse to see you this afternoon. She can look at the pen log, check your sugar, and go over a plan with you.
Caller -> This afternoon. Okay. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call. Probably between two and four.
Caller -> Okay. I've got a notebook now. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Alright.
Caller -> I'll be home. I'm not going anywhere. My daughter's coming at five. She'll be so relieved.
Nurse -> Winifred, keep checking your sugar before meals and at bedtime. Drink water through the day. And call us if it's over three hundred or under seventy.
Caller -> Before meals and at bedtime. Water. Over three hundred or under seventy. Okay. I'll check at lunch.
Nurse -> Perfect. Also, call nine one one if you get confused, can't stop vomiting, have trouble breathing, or faint.
Caller -> Confused. Vomiting. Breathing. Faint. Nine one one. I have a sticker on the phone with the number.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have someone who can check on you tonight?
Caller -> One sec. My phone is making that beeping sound.
Nurse -> No worries, I'll wait.
Caller -> My daughter. She calls at nine. And the neighbor across the hall pops in.
Nurse -> What's the neighbor's name?
Caller -> Mr. Delacroix. He's ninety one and he checks on me. It's backwards, but it works.
Nurse -> Ha. We take what we get.
Nurse -> Great. You have a good support system.
Caller -> I do. I'm lucky. I just hate being a burden.
Nurse -> You're not a burden. You called. That's exactly what we want.
Caller -> Thank you for saying so.
Caller -> My daughter wants me to move in with her. I keep saying no. I like my own kitchen.
Nurse -> That's a family decision. We can help you think through safety at home.
Caller -> I'd appreciate that. Maybe the nurse can talk to her too.
Nurse -> Is there anything else you want to talk about?
Caller -> I don't think so. Just that I'm embarrassed. A grown woman who can't remember her own insulin.
Nurse -> It happens to everyone. Try not to be hard on yourself.
Caller -> My late husband used to give me my shots. I never worried when he was here.
Nurse -> That's a big adjustment. You're doing better than you think.
Caller -> Thank you. I miss him every night at bedtime.
Nurse -> I'm sure. That routine carries a lot of memory.
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> Okay. I'll try. Thank you, Anselmo.
Caller -> One more. When the nurse comes, should I have the pen and the log out?
Nurse -> Yes. Put the pen, the notebook, and the meter on the table where she can see them.
Caller -> I'll set it all out. Like a tea party.
Nurse -> Ha. A very clinical tea party.
Caller -> I'll use the good cups for the pencils.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Talk to you later today.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Bayview Pediatric Home Care, this is Ingeborg.
Caller -> Hi, Ingeborg. This is Philomena Ashcroft. I'm calling for my daughter. Linnea Ashcroft. I need to order nebulizer supplies.
Nurse -> Hi, Philomena. Okay, let's see what you need. How many neb vials do you have left?
Caller -> I counted six. Six vials. I thought we had more. She's had a cold since Sunday and we've been using them.
Nurse -> Okay. And the mask?
Caller -> Can I ask you to hold for a moment? The kettle is going.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> The mask is cracked. I have one. It's the little elephant one. It cracked at the edge where the strap goes. I've been holding it on her face with my hand.
Nurse -> Don't use a cracked mask. It can leak the medicine. Do you have a spare?
Caller -> No. That's the only one. She doesn't like the other kind. The fish one. She screams at the fish.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll send the elephant. What about the tubing?
Caller -> I appreciate you being patient with me.
Nurse -> Not a problem at all.
Caller -> One set. It looks okay. A little cloudy. I'd like a spare.
Nurse -> Sure. We'll send an extra. How is Linnea doing today?
Caller -> Much better. She had the cough, the wet cough, with the cold. She's still got it, but it's looser. She's eating. She's playing with her dolls.
Nurse -> Has she needed a treatment today?
Caller -> Twice since last night. Once at bedtime and once this morning at six. She was coughing hard at six.
Nurse -> Did it help?
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> Yes. She settled right away. She went back to sleep.
Nurse -> Is she wheezing right now? Breathing fast?
Caller -> Wait, say that again? I missed the first part.
Nurse -> Of course. Let me say it slower.
Caller -> No. She's breathing normally. No wheezing. I'm listening. She's humming. She hums when she plays.
Nurse -> Good. Philomena, what's her date of birth?
Caller -> February fourteenth, twenty twenty three. She's three. A Valentine's baby.
Nurse -> Happy early birthday. And a number?
Caller -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one two five.
Nurse -> Got it. I'll order the neb vials, two child masks, and an extra tubing set.
Caller -> Two masks. Yes. Thank you. I'll keep one for the car.
Nurse -> Smart. We'll have them delivered tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. I'll be home. Is there a time?
Nurse -> The driver will call before. Will you have enough vials for tonight?
Caller -> Six. Yes. If she needs one at bedtime and one in the morning, that's two. Plenty.
Nurse -> And since the mask is cracked, how will you give the treatment tonight?
Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> I'll hold the mask on with my hand like I have been. Or use the blow-by. Is that okay?
Nurse -> A cracked mask isn't ideal. Try to hold it as snug as you can. If you can't get a good seal, call me and we'll figure it out.
Caller -> Okay. I'll call.
Nurse -> Let's go over cleaning, too. After every treatment, rinse the cup and the mask with warm soapy water, shake them out, and let them air dry on a clean towel. Don't use a cracked mask.
Caller -> Warm soapy water. Air dry. I do that. Mostly. Sometimes I just rinse and leave it on the counter.
Nurse -> Soap and air dry is better. Germs can grow in a wet cup.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be better about it.
Nurse -> Call us if her breathing gets fast or hard, if a treatment doesn't help, or if she has a fever of one hundred two or higher. If her lips turn blue, call nine one one.
Caller -> Fast breathing. Treatment doesn't help. A hundred two. Blue lips, nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> Great. Does she have a thermometer?
Caller -> Yes. The ear one. We use it a lot.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else you need?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Oh, can I ask? She keeps taking the mask off and trying to put it on her doll. Is that a problem?
Nurse -> Ha. Not at all. It can help her get used to it. Let her put it on the doll first.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> That's what the other nurse said. She calls it the doll doctor game.
Nurse -> Ha. Let her be the doctor.
Caller -> She's very serious about it. She has a stethoscope. She listens to my chest and tells me I have a cold.
Nurse -> Ha. A good diagnosis.
Caller -> She's not wrong. I do have a cold.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself too.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> I will. Thanks, Ingeborg.
Nurse -> Bye, Philomena.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Octavia.
Caller -> Octavia, it's Ingrid Vandenberg. My husband is Cornelis Vandenberg. I think this is it. I think he's dying. His breathing is different. It stops for a long time and then it starts again.
Nurse -> Ingrid, I'm here with you. Take a breath. I'm going to help you through this. Where is Cornelis right now?
Caller -> I'm trying. I'm so sorry. I don't know why I'm apologizing.
Nurse -> You don't need to. This is a lot. Go slowly.
Caller -> He's in the hospital bed. In the living room. I'm sitting next to him. I'm holding his hand.
Nurse -> Good. Is anyone else in the house?
Caller -> No. Just me. My son is on his way. He's driving from Tulsa. He'll be here in about forty minutes.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what you're seeing. The breathing first.
Caller -> It's, he takes a few breaths, loud ones, deep, and then he stops. For a long time. I count. It's twenty seconds. Twenty five. I think he's gone, and then he takes another one. It's awful.
Nurse -> That pattern is called Cheyne-Stokes. It's common near the end of life. It's frightening to watch, but he isn't struggling.
Caller -> I read the booklet you gave us. It said this might happen. But reading is different from seeing.
Nurse -> It is very different. I'm here.
Caller -> Is he in pain? He doesn't look like he's in pain. His face is smooth. He's not moaning.
Nurse -> It sounds like he's comfortable. Is there any sound when he breathes?
Caller -> Yes. A wet sound. Like a rattle. Like gurgling in the back of his throat. It's been going on for an hour. It's getting louder.
Nurse -> That's the secretions that gather in the throat. He can't clear them anymore. It sounds worse than it feels to him. We have medicine for that in the comfort kit.
Caller -> The kit. The box in the refrigerator.
Nurse -> Yes. Can you bring it to him?
Caller -> I'll get it. Hold on. I have to let go of his hand. Don't hang up.
Nurse -> I'll be right here.
Caller -> Okay. I'm in the kitchen. I have the box. I'm going back.
Nurse -> Good. Ingrid, is he waking up at all? Does he respond to your voice?
Nurse -> When did he last eat or drink anything?
Caller -> Yesterday morning. A few spoonfuls of applesauce. Nothing since, not even water.
Nurse -> That's expected too. He isn't hungry or thirsty now.
Caller -> He hasn't opened his eyes since this afternoon. He doesn't squeeze my hand. I said his name just now and nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you looked at his legs and feet? What color are they?
Caller -> I lifted the blanket. His knees are blotchy. Purple and white, like marble. His feet are cold. Cold and a little bluish.
Nurse -> Those changes are normal at this stage. The body is slowing down. Ingrid, does he have a DNR?
Caller -> Yes. It's on the refrigerator. We signed it months ago. We don't want the ambulance. He told me. He wants to be home. He said, Ingrid, no machines.
Nurse -> Then you're doing exactly what he asked. Let me ask for his date of birth to be sure I have the right chart.
Caller -> I keep wondering if I should call the ambulance anyway. Just in case.
Nurse -> I understand the urge. He asked for comfort at home, and that's what we're giving him. If you ever want to talk about that, I'm here.
Caller -> No. I know what he wanted.
Caller -> March eleventh, nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> And your number, in case we get cut off?
Caller -> Nine one eight, five five five, zero one six three.
Nurse -> Got it. Now let's give him the medicine. Open the comfort kit. Do you see a small bottle of morphine with an oral syringe?
Caller -> Yes. It says morphine concentrate. And there's a syringe. It's in a bag.
Nurse -> The order is five milligrams every two hours as needed. That's a quarter of a milliliter on the syringe. Draw it up to the first mark, the quarter mark.
Caller -> Okay. I'm drawing it. It's, I'm shaking. Okay. It's at the line.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now lift his upper lip a little and squirt it slowly in the pocket under his tongue, or between his cheek and gum. A little at a time.
Caller -> Under the tongue. Okay. His mouth is open. I'm doing it. Slowly. A little. Okay. A little more. That's all of it.
Nurse -> Beautiful. That's five milligrams of morphine. It will ease any air hunger and keep him comfortable.
Nurse -> Take a moment. Watch his face.
Caller -> His forehead is smooth. His jaw is relaxed. He looks like he does when he's napping.
Nurse -> That's what we hope to see.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Should I write the time?
Nurse -> Yes. What time is it?
Caller -> Five twenty. No, five twenty three.
Nurse -> Write five twenty three. Morphine, five milligrams. Now, the other bottle. Do you see small drops? It says atropine.
Caller -> Yes. A little white bottle with a dropper. Atropine. One percent.
Nurse -> Give him two drops under the tongue. Tip his head back just a little first.
Caller -> Two drops. Okay. One. Two. Done. They went in. He didn't react.
Nurse -> Good. That dries the secretions. It takes about fifteen to twenty minutes to work. The rattle may soften.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. And again in how long?
Nurse -> The atropine can be repeated every four hours as needed. The morphine every two hours. Write both down.
Caller -> I wrote them. Morphine five twenty three. Atropine five twenty five.
Nurse -> Perfect. You did great, Ingrid.
Caller -> Is there anything I did wrong? I was so slow with the syringe.
Nurse -> Nothing. You did it exactly right, step by step.
Caller -> I'm just glad I'm doing something. I felt so helpless.
Nurse -> You're doing everything right. Now let's make him more comfortable. Can you raise the head of the bed, or add pillows behind his head and shoulders?
Caller -> The bed has a button. Let me. There. It's up a bit.
Nurse -> Good. Turn him gently onto his side with a pillow at his back. That helps the fluid drain from the throat.
Caller -> Won't it hurt him to move him?
Nurse -> Gentle turning shouldn't hurt, and the morphine is on board. Move him slowly and support his head.
Caller -> He's so light. I can do it. Okay. He's on his left side. His mouth is hanging open.
Caller -> He used to carry me over the threshold. Every anniversary, until his back gave out.
Nurse -> A romantic. I love that.
Nurse -> That's fine. Moisten his mouth and lips with one of the pink swabs and a little water. And lip balm.
Caller -> I have the swabs. I'm doing it. Okay. His lips are so dry. I'm putting the balm.
Nurse -> Lovely. Now talk to him. Hearing is the last sense to go. Tell him you're here, tell him it's all right.
Caller -> I'm here, Cor. I'm right here. Gerrit's on his way. You're not alone. It's all right. You can rest. I love you.
Nurse -> That's perfect. He can hear you.
Caller -> I'm going to put on his music. The Sinatra. He loves the Sinatra.
Nurse -> That's a lovely idea. Keep it soft.
Caller -> I'll turn it down low. There. Fly me to the moon.
Nurse -> He'd approve.
Caller -> Do you think so? Really?
Nurse -> I do. Everything you say matters to him.
Caller -> I told him for fifty nine years to stop leaving his socks on the floor. I'd give anything to find one now.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a beautiful thing to say.
Caller -> I mean it.
Nurse -> I know. Ingrid, the pauses in his breathing, the rattle, the cold, the blotchy skin, those are all expected at this stage. They don't mean he's suffering. They mean his body is winding down.
Caller -> Okay. I'm trying to remember that.
Nurse -> Say it back to me if it helps. What do the pauses mean?
Caller -> They're normal. His body is winding down. He's not in pain.
Nurse -> That's right.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now so they know, and I'm sending a nurse to be with you. She should be there within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. Thank you. Please hurry.
Nurse -> She's on her way. I'll make sure of it.
Caller -> Okay. What do I do until then?
Nurse -> Stay with him. Hold his hand. Keep talking. If the rattle gets louder, you can turn him a little more. If he seems restless or the breathing looks labored, you can give another dose of morphine in two hours. Or call me sooner.
Caller -> Two hours. Five twenty three. So seven twenty three.
Nurse -> Or sooner if I tell you to. Stay on the phone with me if you like.
Caller -> Can I? Can you stay on?
Nurse -> As long as you need.
Caller -> I've never done this before. Not with anyone.
Nurse -> You're doing it beautifully. Most families haven't, and no one is ever ready.
Caller -> Thank you. I don't want to be alone.
Nurse -> You're not. I'm right here. Tell me about Cornelis.
Caller -> He was a carpenter. He built this house. Every cabinet. Every door. He built the crib for our first baby. He hand cut the dovetails.
Nurse -> That sounds like a craftsman.
Caller -> He taught our grandson to hold a chisel. They built a birdhouse last summer. It's on the porch.
Nurse -> Then a piece of him is on the porch.
Caller -> Yes. I'll sit there tomorrow.
Caller -> He was. He fixed everyone's porches. He never charged the widows.
Nurse -> That's a good man.
Caller -> The best. I'm so lucky.
Nurse -> Does he have a favorite chair, or a favorite spot he'd want to be near?
Caller -> The window. He likes the morning light. The bed is by the window. I arranged it that way.
Nurse -> You thought of everything.
Nurse -> Ingrid, our social worker and our chaplain will reach out to you in the morning, if you'd like. They can help with whatever comes next.
Caller -> I'd like that. Yes. Our pastor is coming too. I'll call him once Gerrit gets here.
Nurse -> That's a good plan. Call back at any hour tonight. Even if you only want to hear a voice. I'll stay with you until the nurse arrives.
Caller -> Thank you. I think the rattle is softer. Or maybe I'm used to it. Hold on. Let me listen.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> It's softer. It really is. And the pauses are about the same. He's breathing slowly. It's peaceful.
Nurse -> That's what we hope for.
Caller -> I think I can hear the car. Is that Gerrit? Hold on. Yes. Headlights. He's here.
Nurse -> Good. Let him in. The nurse will be there soon too.
Caller -> Okay. I'm going to the door. Thank you, Octavia. Thank you for being with me.
Nurse -> Take your time. Turn on a light on the porch for him.
Caller -> The porch light is on. I left it on for him.
Nurse -> It's been an honor, Ingrid. I'm right here if you need me.
Caller -> Will you write down everything for the other nurse? So I don't have to explain it all again?
Nurse -> Yes. I'll note the doses and times. She'll have it all when she walks in.
Caller -> I know. Bye for now.

Nurse -> Bayview Pediatric Home Care, this is Ingeborg.
Caller -> Good afternoon! I'm calling on behalf of a research group. We're doing a short survey about home health services in the area. Do you have ten minutes?
Nurse -> I'm sorry, this is our clinical line. We're here for families and patients. I'm not able to take surveys.
Caller -> I understand. It's very short. Just a few questions about how you find new patients and which vendors you use.
Nurse -> I'm not the right person for that. I'm a nurse.
Caller -> Is there a manager or an administrator I could speak to?
Nurse -> The administrative office handles that. Their number is on our website.
Caller -> Wonderful. And would they be available now?
Nurse -> I don't know their schedule. The website lists their hours.
Caller -> Okay. Is there a name, so I can ask for someone specific?
Nurse -> I can't give names. Ask for the office manager.
Caller -> I see. Okay. Well, we do offer a gift card for participation. Twenty five dollars.
Nurse -> That's generous, but I really can't help from this line. We need to keep it open for patients.
Caller -> Of course. I'll try the main number. I'm sorry for the interruption.
Nurse -> That's all right. Good luck with your project.
Caller -> Thank you. You've been very polite. Most people just hang up.
Nurse -> Ha. I understand. It's a tough job.
Caller -> It is. Have a lovely afternoon.
Nurse -> You too. Bye.

not_applicable.reason: Market research survey request; no patient or clinical content.

transcript:
Nurse -> Crescent Home Health, this is Leopoldo.
Caller -> Hi, Leopoldo. This is Yolanda Beauchamp. I'm the aide at Maple Court, the group home. I'm calling with the weekly update on Ambrose Whitlock.
Nurse -> Hi, Yolanda. Good to hear from you. How is Ambrose this week?
Caller -> Good. Really good. He's in a great mood. He's been singing in the van. He picked all the music last Sunday.
Nurse -> Any particular reason for the good mood?
Caller -> He got a new friend in the house. And his sister visited Sunday with a birthday cake. Early, but she couldn't wait.
Nurse -> Ha. A cake for no reason.
Nurse -> Ha. A music man. Before we start, can I get his date of birth?
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> April third, nineteen ninety two. He turned thirty four in the spring.
Nurse -> Perfect. And the best number to reach you?
Caller -> Sorry, I lost my train of thought.
Nurse -> That's okay. We were just getting started.
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one five two. That's the house line. Someone's always by it.
Nurse -> Great. Let's start with his medicines. Any changes?
Caller -> No changes. The baclofen. Ten milligrams. Three times a day. Morning, lunch, bedtime. He had lunch today at noon and took it. Nothing missed this week.
Nurse -> Does he swallow his tablets whole, or crushed in applesauce?
Caller -> Whole, with water. He doesn't like applesauce. He says it's baby food.
Nurse -> Ha. Whole is fine.
Nurse -> And his weight?
Caller -> We weighed him on the chair scale Thursday. One forty eight. He's been one forty seven, one forty eight for a month. Steady.
Nurse -> Good. How's his eating? Sleeping?
Caller -> Eating great. He clears his plate. He loves Taco Tuesday. He's sleeping through the night. He's been going to bed at nine and waking at six. And he's doing PT three times a week. Monday, Wednesday, Friday. The therapist's been happy.
Nurse -> Wonderful. What about his skin? Anywhere red, or sore? Under his bottom, his back, his heels?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little scattered today.
Nurse -> That's completely understandable.
Caller -> I checked at bath time. Nothing. His skin is clear. No red spots. No marks. The cushion's holding up. Well. That's my question.
Nurse -> Go ahead.
Caller -> Sorry, I just dropped my pen.
Nurse -> That's all right.
Caller -> The cushion on his chair. It's the gel one. It's got a dent in the middle. Like it's flattening. He says it's fine, but I think it needs a look.
Nurse -> That can mean it's worn. I'm going to message the therapist and ask her to check it at the next visit.
Caller -> Oh, great. Thank you. I didn't want to wait for a red spot.
Nurse -> That's exactly right. What about spasms? Any change?
Caller -> He has them. His legs. Mostly in the morning when he wakes up. It's mild. The same as always. A few minutes and they settle. Nothing worse.
Nurse -> Good. That sounds stable. Let me go over skin care. Help him shift his weight, or lean forward, every hour in the chair. Check his skin at every bath. And keep the cushion dry and smooth.
Caller -> Every hour. We do that. We set a timer on the van and the kitchen. Everybody's trained. We check the skin. Yes.
Nurse -> Excellent. And if a spot stays red for more than half an hour, or the spasms get worse, or he stops eating well, call us.
Caller -> Red more than half an hour. Spasms worse. Not eating. Okay. I'll write it in the log.
Nurse -> Perfect. How are the other residents?
Caller -> Okay. I've got a notebook now. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Alright.
Caller -> Everyone's good. We have a new housemate, Gerald. He just moved in. He and Ambrose are friends already. They watch baseball together.
Nurse -> How many residents are at Maple Court now?
Caller -> Six, with Gerald. Two aides on days, two on nights. It's a good ratio.
Nurse -> That's wonderful.
Caller -> Ambrose says Gerald knows more about the Rangers than anyone. He's been teaching him the players.
Nurse -> Ha. A good friend.
Caller -> They're inseparable. We eat dinner together. We've started a movie night on Fridays.
Nurse -> That sounds like a good house.
Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> It's a happy house. I'm really lucky to work there.
Nurse -> The residents are lucky to have you.
Caller -> I've been there eight years. I started as a night aide. Ambrose was the second person I met on my first shift.
Nurse -> And he's still teaching you baseball.
Caller -> Ha. Yes. I'm a Padres fan. He doesn't let it go.
Caller -> Sorry, somebody's at the door. Hang on a second.
Nurse -> No problem, I'll hold.
Caller -> I like to think so. Okay. That's all I have. Anything else you need?
Nurse -> No, that's perfect. Thank you for the thorough update.
Caller -> I keep a notebook. Every shift writes in it. When I call, I read from the last seven days.
Nurse -> It shows. This is one of the clearest updates I get.
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> Of course. I'll call next week.
Nurse -> Sounds good. Take care, Yolanda.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Crescent Home Health, this is Leopoldo.
Caller -> Hi. It's Rosalinde Haverford. I'm calling about my brother. Quentin Haverford. He just had his medicine changed and I want to make sure we're doing it right.
Nurse -> Hi, Rosalinde. Tell me what changed.
Caller -> I drove over right after work. He's been on his own most of the week and he's not great about reading labels.
Nurse -> That's what family is for. Go ahead.
Caller -> His doctor called yesterday. Because of his liver. They said to stop the ibuprofen. And use Tylenol instead. But with a limit. I wrote it down, but I'm not sure I understood.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's go through it. What did they say about the Tylenol?
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> Acetaminophen. Five hundred milligram tablets. As needed. No more than four a day. That's what I wrote.
Nurse -> That sounds right. That's two grams in a day. Has he taken any yet?
Caller -> One sec. My phone is making that beeping sound.
Nurse -> No worries, I'll wait.
Caller -> No. Not yet. He's only had the ibuprofen. And that's the other thing. This morning, before I came over, he took two. Two ibuprofen. Two hundred milligram each. He said he hadn't read my text.
Caller -> He doesn't check his phone. It's in the junk drawer half the time.
Nurse -> Ha. Maybe we move it.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. When was that?
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> About eight. So maybe ten hours ago.
Nurse -> And how's he feeling?
Caller -> His stomach is upset. He says it's a gnawing feeling. Not terrible. A little queasy. He had toast and it settled some.
Nurse -> Is he drinking? Any heartburn, burning in the chest?
Caller -> Water, mostly. A little heartburn. I gave him a glass of milk.
Nurse -> That's fine for now.
Nurse -> Has he vomited? Any black stools, or blood in the vomit?
Caller -> No vomiting. I asked about the stools. He says they're normal. Brown. He's been checking since I said it.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring. Rosalinde, can I have his date of birth?
Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> January nineteenth, nineteen seventy four.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Can you hear me okay? The signal's a little weak.
Nurse -> I can hear you fine.
Caller -> Five oh five, five five five, zero one three four.
Nurse -> Got it. So the ibuprofen is stopped. For someone with liver disease, those pain pills can cause bleeding and kidney trouble. Two tablets once isn't likely to cause a problem, but he shouldn't take any more.
Caller -> No more ibuprofen. Okay. What about Advil, and aspirin? And Aleve?
Nurse -> Same group. No Advil, no Aleve, no aspirin, unless the doctor says. They can all upset his stomach and bleed.
Caller -> I appreciate you being patient with me.
Nurse -> Not a problem at all.
Caller -> I'll clear the cabinet. He has a whole shelf.
Caller -> There's Advil, Motrin, the store brand, three kinds of headache powder. It looks like a pharmacy.
Nurse -> Put them in a bag and out of sight. You can ask the doctor about disposal.
Nurse -> Good. For pain, only the acetaminophen, up to four of the five hundred milligram tablets in twenty four hours. Read the labels on cold medicines too, because many have acetaminophen hidden in them.
Caller -> Hidden acetaminophen. Okay. NyQuil, probably.
Nurse -> Yes. Some of those. Check for the word acetaminophen on the box.
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> I'll read every box. I'll make a list.
Nurse -> I'm going to message the clinician about the ibuprofen he took this morning, so they're aware.
Caller -> Yes. Thank you. I wasn't sure whether to call.
Nurse -> You did the right thing. Watch him for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, severe belly pain, or yellowing of the skin. If you see any of that, call us right away. If it's severe, call nine one one.
Caller -> Black stools. Blood. Bad belly pain. Yellow skin. Nine one one if it's bad. I'll tell him to tell me.
Nurse -> I'll call you tomorrow to check on his stomach and see how the new pain plan is going.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. That would help.
Nurse -> Is his pain controlled right now?
Caller -> He says a three. It's his back. He'll start the acetaminophen tonight.
Nurse -> Good. Space the tablets out, and don't take more than four total in the day.
Caller -> I'll set alarms. I'll write each dose on the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Do you live nearby, Rosalinde?
Caller -> Twenty minutes. I come by after work and on weekends. His wife left a few years ago.
Nurse -> It sounds like you're his anchor.
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> He's stubborn, you know. He never reads anything.
Caller -> He's the youngest. He thinks he's thirty. He's fifty two.
Nurse -> Ha. Some of us never age.
Nurse -> Ha. That's why he has a sister.
Caller -> That's what I tell him. Thank you, Leopoldo.
Nurse -> Anytime. Talk to you tomorrow.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Silverleaf Home Care, this is Marisol.
Caller -> Marisol, hi, this is Thibault Fontaine. My mother is Eulalia Fontaine. She's really sick. She has a fever and she's confused and she's breathing fast.
Nurse -> Okay, Thibault. Stay with me. Is she awake?
Caller -> Sorry. I'm sorry. I got up when I heard her calling and I just ran in. I haven't even put shoes on.
Nurse -> That's fine. Shoes can wait. Stay with her.
Caller -> She's awake. Sort of. She's in bed. She's shaking. She's talking but it doesn't make sense. She keeps asking for my father. He died years ago.
Nurse -> Is she looking at you when you talk? Following you with her eyes?
Caller -> Sometimes. Then she drifts. She looks past me at the wall.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you taken her temperature?
Caller -> Yes. A hundred and three point two. I did it twice.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have a catheter?
Caller -> Yes. The Foley. It's been in about three weeks. The bag has cloudy urine. Dark. It smells bad. And there's very little. Almost nothing since last night.
Caller -> The nurse changed it last Tuesday, I think. No, Thursday. It's in the chart on the wall.
Nurse -> It's okay. The paramedics will see it. We have the chart too.
Nurse -> Is the tubing kinked, or the bag lower than her body?
Caller -> The bag is hanging on the side of the bed. The tubing looks straight. I didn't touch it.
Nurse -> Good. Leave it as it is.
Nurse -> Okay. How is she breathing?
Caller -> Fast. She's panting. Like she ran a mile. I counted, I think it's over thirty a minute.
Nurse -> Do you have a blood pressure cuff?
Caller -> I do. Hold on. It says eighty eight over fifty two. That's low, right? That's low for her. She runs about one thirty.
Nurse -> Thibault, I want you to call nine one one right now. This sounds like a serious infection. She needs the hospital.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Should I hang up and call? Or do you call?
Nurse -> Don't hang up on me. I'll stay on the line while Natalie calls.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I won't.
Nurse -> You call, on another phone if you have one, or put me on speaker and call from your cell. Is anyone else in the house?
Caller -> My wife's here. Natalie! Natalie! Call nine one one! It's Mom. It's an emergency!
Nurse -> Good. Is she calling?
Caller -> Yes. She's on it. She's on the phone with them.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep your mother lying down, on her back, with her legs raised a little on a pillow. Don't give her anything to eat or drink.
Caller -> Lying down. Legs up. Nothing to eat or drink. Okay. I'm putting a pillow under her feet.
Nurse -> Is her skin clammy? Cold? Is she sweating?
Caller -> Yes. Cold and sweaty. Clammy. She's pale. She's shivering under three blankets.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she confused about where she is?
Caller -> She thinks it's nineteen seventy something. She asked me why the kids aren't at school. She doesn't know who the president is. She knows my name though. She said Thibault. Then she said it was my brother's name.
Nurse -> Okay. That's new confusion. That's important. Tell the paramedics that. Thibault, what's her date of birth?
Caller -> August twenty third, nineteen forty.
Nurse -> And the best number for you?
Caller -> Five oh five, five five five, zero one zero nine.
Nurse -> Thank you. Grab her medicine list and anything for the paramedics. And the catheter bag, with the urine in it. Don't empty it.
Caller -> I'll get the list. It's on the fridge. Natalie! Get the list on the fridge! And leave the bag!
Nurse -> Is the front door unlocked, and the light on?
Caller -> Natalie's already there. She's holding the door. The dog is barking. She put him in the bathroom.
Nurse -> Good thinking.
Caller -> Yes. I'll unlock it. Natalie, go turn on the porch light.
Nurse -> Good. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now so they can notify the hospital.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. What if she gets worse before they come?
Nurse -> If she stops responding or her breathing slows or stops, tell the dispatcher right away. They'll talk you through it.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Natalie says they're sending an ambulance. Six minutes.
Nurse -> While you wait, loosen the blankets a little if she's too hot, but don't let her get cold.
Caller -> She's shivering. I'll leave two on. She's pulling at them.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Nurse -> Perfect. Stay with your mother. Hold her hand. Talk to her.
Caller -> Mom, I'm here. Help's coming. You're okay. She squeezed my hand. She's looking at me.
Nurse -> That's good. She knows you're there.
Caller -> I'm so scared. I thought it was just a cold she had.
Nurse -> Infections can fool us. She seemed fine yesterday?
Caller -> She was tired. She was sleeping a lot. I thought it was the weather. I should have called yesterday.
Nurse -> You're calling now. That's what matters.
Nurse -> You're doing the right thing. Getting her to the hospital is the right thing.
Caller -> I hear a siren. Is that them? Yes, it's them. Natalie's at the door.
Nurse -> Go with them. We'll let the hospital know she's coming.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> Go. We'll be thinking of you both.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Juniper Ridge Hospice, this is Genevieve.
Caller -> Hi, Genevieve. It's Beatrix Wren. I'm calling about my husband, Thaddeus Wren. No emergency. I just wanted to give you a little update and ask a couple of things.
Nurse -> Hi, Beatrix. I'm glad you called. Let me get his date of birth first.
Caller -> November seventh, nineteen thirty six. He's almost ninety. He says he's ninety already.
Nurse -> And the best number?
Caller -> Six one five, five five five, zero one one one.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me how he's been.
Caller -> I think he's fine. I think. It's hard to know what's normal now.
Nurse -> That's what I'm here for. Let's walk through it.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little scattered today.
Nurse -> That's completely understandable.
Caller -> Quiet. Peaceful, mostly. He's sleeping more. He sleeps most of the day now. He wakes up for a bit around lunch and again in the evening. He tires out fast. Even sitting up for a meal wears him out.
Nurse -> That's common. How's his eating?
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> Less. A lot less. Half a bowl of soup. A few bites of mashed potatoes. He used to love steak. Now he pushes it away. I made him a custard yesterday, and he ate that. He likes the custard.
Nurse -> Does he have trouble swallowing, or cough when he drinks?
Caller -> No. He swallows fine. He just doesn't want much.
Nurse -> That fits. His appetite is quieting.
Nurse -> That's okay. Small favorites are fine. Is he in any pain?
Caller -> No. No pain. He says he's comfortable. He rests his hand on his chest sometimes, but he says it's habit. He's not short of breath. He breathes easy.
Nurse -> Good. Is he sleeping well at night?
Caller -> Yes. He takes the lorazepam. The half milligram. At bedtime. He took it last night. He goes right to sleep.
Nurse -> Any problems with the medicine? Too drowsy in the morning?
Caller -> No. He wakes up at his regular time. He's just slow.
Nurse -> Does he know you and the family when he's awake?
Caller -> Always. He teases me about my hair. He says I look like a dandelion.
Nurse -> Ha. A sign of a clear mind.
Nurse -> Good. Now, you said you had a couple of questions?
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> Yes. Our grandchildren are coming. Two of them. Eight and eleven. For the holidays. They arrive Thursday. And I don't know how to prepare them. They haven't seen him in a few months. He looks so different. He's lost so much weight.
Nurse -> That's a thoughtful concern. How much do they know?
Caller -> Their mother told them he's very sick. But they don't understand what hospice is. The eleven year old asked if he's going to die at Christmas.
Caller -> I nearly dropped the phone. Her mother was laughing and crying at the same time.
Nurse -> Children say what the rest of us are thinking.
Nurse -> Oh. That's a hard question. What did you say?
Caller -> I said I didn't know. And that grandpa loves them and wants to see them.
Nurse -> That's a good answer. Children usually do better with honest, simple words. You can tell them he's very tired and his body is getting weaker, and that he still loves hearing about their day.
Caller -> Weaker and tired. Loves hearing about their day. Okay. I like that.
Nurse -> Let them decide how close to get. Some kids want to climb on the bed. Some want to wave from the door. Both are fine.
Caller -> What if they cry? What if the little one cries and upsets him?
Nurse -> Crying is okay. Tears show love. He may even be comforted by it.
Caller -> I never thought of it that way.
Caller -> The little one will climb on the bed. The eleven year old will hang back.
Nurse -> That's very typical. I'm also going to ask our social worker to call you. She is wonderful with children, and she can give you words to use and activities to do with them.
Caller -> Oh, that would be wonderful. Yes. Please.
Nurse -> I'll message her today.
Caller -> Thank you. That takes a weight off.
Nurse -> What was your other question?
Caller -> It's a silly one. He wants a little wine. A glass of red. With dinner on Christmas Eve. Is that all right? I know he's on the medicine. I didn't want to do anything wrong.
Nurse -> It's not silly at all. A sip or a small glass is fine if he wants it and can swallow safely. It can make him sleepier, so give it earlier in the evening, not right before the lorazepam.
Caller -> Earlier. With dinner. Not at bedtime. Okay. He'll be so happy. He's been talking about his Cabernet.
Nurse -> Then let him have his Cabernet.
Caller -> He used to make his own, in the garage. Twenty bottles every fall. The neighbors lined up.
Nurse -> A winemaker. I bet it was good.
Caller -> It was terrible. But he was proud.
Nurse -> Ha. The best kind.
Caller -> I'll get a nice bottle. I haven't bought a bottle in a year. We'll all have a toast.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely. Let him sleep when he wants, offer small favorite foods and sips, and keep visits short and quiet. Don't push him to eat.
Caller -> No pushing. Short visits. I understand. Honestly it's a relief to hear someone say it's okay.
Nurse -> Many families feel they need permission to let things be simple. You have it.
Caller -> Thank you. I'll write that down: let things be simple.
Nurse -> It is okay. You're doing a beautiful job, Beatrix.
Caller -> I don't feel like it. I feel like I'm barely hanging on.
Nurse -> That's very common. Are you sleeping? Eating?
Caller -> A little. My daughter's coming Wednesday and she'll help. The church ladies have been bringing food. I have about nine casseroles.
Nurse -> Does she know the plan for comfort and the medicines?
Caller -> She does. She was a nurse's aide in college. She's calm in a crisis, thank goodness.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a lot of casseroles.
Caller -> I'm freezing them in little portions.
Nurse -> Ask someone to bring something other than a casserole. Fruit, soup, bread.
Caller -> Ha. I'll mention it at church. They mean well.
Nurse -> Good. Take care of yourself too. And I'll have the nurse come Monday as scheduled. She'll check his comfort and talk with you.
Caller -> Monday. Okay. That's the one at ten?
Nurse -> Is the morning still best for you, with the grandchildren around?
Caller -> Mornings are quiet. They sleep late. It's perfect.
Nurse -> Yes. The usual time.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> Wonderful. I'll have the coffee ready.
Nurse -> Beatrix, call us any time if his breathing changes, if he has any pain, or if you just need to talk. Day or night.
Caller -> I will. I have the number on the fridge. It's magnetized. Right next to his photo from the Navy.
Nurse -> Navy? Tell me.
Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> He was a radioman on a destroyer. In the fifties. Korea. He still can Morse code. The grandchildren love it. He taps it on the table.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Maybe he can teach them a few letters.
Caller -> Sorry, I lost my train of thought.
Nurse -> That's okay. We were just getting started.
Caller -> He already did. The eight year old can spell his name.
Nurse -> Ha. A new skill.
Caller -> He taps the dot dash on the arm of the chair when he's thinking. I think it's his way of talking when he's too tired to speak.
Nurse -> That's beautiful.
Caller -> Yes. Okay. I'll let you go. Thank you, Genevieve.
Nurse -> Anytime, Beatrix. Take care.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Northstar Home Health, this is Colleen.
Caller -> Hi, Colleen. It's Dorothea Lindqvist. I'm calling about my husband, Harald Lindqvist. I need to order oxygen supplies. And there's a storm coming. I'm nervous.
Nurse -> Hi, Dorothea. I'm glad you called before it hits. Let's go through what you have. Start with his portable tanks.
Caller -> I called the supplier too, but their line was busy and then it said all agents were assisting other customers.
Nurse -> Everyone's calling about the storm. I can reach them through a different line.
Caller -> I have two. Two full ones. They're the little silver ones on the cart. I checked the gauge this morning. They're both in the green.
Nurse -> Do you remember how many hours each one gave you last time?
Caller -> Four and a half, I think. I wrote it on the tank with a marker. Four and a half hours at two liters.
Nurse -> That matches what the supplier says. Good record keeping.
Nurse -> Good. And the concentrator, the big machine, is it working well?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> Yes. It hums along. We've had it a year. No problems. But if the power goes out, then what?
Nurse -> Do you clean the filter on the back?
Caller -> Every Sunday. I rinse it and let it dry. The tech showed me. It's a little gray sponge.
Nurse -> Perfect. That keeps it running well.
Nurse -> That's what we'll talk about. First, supplies. Nasal cannulas?
Caller -> I have one spare. The one he's wearing is about two weeks old. I should change it. I have the one spare.
Nurse -> Change it every two weeks, or sooner if it's dirty or he's been sick.
Caller -> I'll change it tonight. I'll put the new one on and keep the old one out of sight.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll send more. And the humidifier bottle? Does he use distilled water?
Caller -> Yes, the humidifier bottle. And I'm out of the distilled water. The jug. I used the last of it yesterday.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll send that too. Dorothea, how is Harald right now?
Caller -> He's sitting in his chair. He's doing the crossword. He's okay. He seems okay. I took his oxygen with the little finger clip. It said ninety three.
Caller -> He's very stubborn about the stairs. I told him to sleep in the den this week but he refuses.
Nurse -> It might be worth a conversation. At least until the storm passes.
Caller -> I'll try. He says the den couch is too soft for his back.
Nurse -> Ninety three on his two liters. That's right where we like him. Is he short of breath at all?
Caller -> Only on the stairs. We have the bedroom upstairs, and he's been using the stairs. He stops halfway. Catches his breath. Then he goes on. It's mild. It's the same as last week.
Nurse -> Does he rest between flights of stairs or push through?
Caller -> He rests. He holds the rail and breathes in through his nose, out through pursed lips. The therapist showed him.
Nurse -> That's exactly right.
Nurse -> Okay. Any chest pain? Fever? Increased cough?
Caller -> No. No fever. A little cough in the morning, with a bit of clear. The same as always.
Nurse -> Has the sputum changed color, thicker, yellow or green?
Caller -> No. Same as always. Clear, a little white. He clears his throat and goes on.
Nurse -> Good. What's his date of birth, Dorothea?
Caller -> March twenty ninth, nineteen sixty five.
Nurse -> And a number to reach you?
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> Five oh five, five five five, zero one five six.
Nurse -> Got it. Now the storm. What's the forecast?
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> The news says ice. Maybe a foot of snow. The power might go out for a day or two. Last time the lights were out for three days. We went to my sister's. But the roads will be closed.
Caller -> We had candles everywhere. Which I now realize was a terrible idea with the oxygen.
Nurse -> I'm glad you're thinking about it now. Flashlights this time.
Caller -> I'm buying fresh batteries today.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a legitimate worry. Here's what I'm going to do. I'll order the cannulas and the distilled water. And I'll message the oxygen supplier to ask for extra backup tanks before the storm hits.
Caller -> Oh, thank God. Yes. That's what I was hoping.
Nurse -> I'll order the cannulas and the distilled water.
Caller -> And the tanks? How many? Because two doesn't last long, right?
Nurse -> A full tank at two liters lasts about four to five hours. Two tanks is eight to ten hours. If the power's out for a day, you'd need more. I'll ask for at least four extra.
Caller -> Four extra. That would help.
Caller -> Will the tanks be heavy? I can lift about twenty pounds.
Nurse -> The small portable tanks are light. The bigger backup cylinders are heavier. The driver will set them where you need them.
Caller -> Oh good. By the concentrator, please.
Nurse -> I'll try to get them delivered tomorrow morning, before the storm.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Great. What time?
Caller -> If they can only come in the afternoon I'll understand. The roads are the roads.
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning, and I'll tell them it's urgent.
Nurse -> The driver will call you with a window. If it's snowing already, they might come earlier.
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> I'll be home. I'm always home.
Caller -> I haven't left the house for more than an hour since Harald came home from the hospital. I don't mind. It's just how it is.
Nurse -> That's a lot to carry. Do you have help?
Caller -> My sister, when the roads are clear. And Mr. Henderson, like I said.
Nurse -> Now let's go over the outage plan. If the power goes out, the concentrator stops. Switch Harald to a full tank at two liters right away. Write down the time you switched. And only use the tank as long as the power is out. When the power returns, switch back.
Caller -> Switch to a tank. Two liters. Write down the time. Switch back when the lights are on. Okay. Where do I write it?
Nurse -> Do you know how to tell if a tank is empty?
Caller -> The needle goes to the red area. And the hissing stops. He's learned to watch the needle.
Nurse -> Switch to a new tank before it hits the red, not after.
Nurse -> On a notepad next to the concentrator. I'll have the nurse bring a log sheet.
Caller -> Okay. I have a notepad. I'll write it there.
Nurse -> Perfect. And the tanks, how do you turn them on?
Caller -> There's a key. On the top. A wrench. I turn it a quarter turn. And then the dial. Harald knows how. He's done it before.
Nurse -> Good. Keep the wrench tied to the tank, so it doesn't get lost.
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> It's on a string. The nurse put it there.
Nurse -> Great. Let's talk safety. In the cold, people use space heaters, fireplaces, candles. Oxygen and flames don't mix. No smoking, no open flames, and keep the oxygen at least six feet from the stove, the candles, and the fireplace.
Caller -> Six feet. We have a gas stove. And a fireplace. He sits near the fireplace. I'll move him.
Nurse -> Please do. And no candles near the tanks. Use flashlights.
Caller -> Flashlights. I have a good one. And the battery lantern.
Nurse -> Keep one flashlight right by his chair, and one in the bedroom, so no one is fumbling in the dark.
Caller -> Two flashlights. By his chair and by the bed. I'll tape them down so they don't wander.
Nurse -> Good. And if the power's out and it's cold, dress him in layers, rather than using a heater near the oxygen.
Caller -> Layers. Blankets. Okay.
Nurse -> Dorothea, call nine one one if he has severe shortness of breath, his lips turn blue, he becomes confused, or if the oxygen runs out and he can't breathe.
Caller -> Severe breath. Blue lips. Confused. Oxygen out. Nine one one. If the roads are closed will they come?
Nurse -> They will try. Call early, don't wait until it's an emergency. Tell them he's on oxygen and the road conditions.
Caller -> Early. Tell them oxygen. Okay.
Nurse -> And keep your address and the nearest cross street written by the phone. The dispatcher will ask.
Caller -> I'll write it on a card. And I'll put his medicine list next to it.
Nurse -> Is there a neighbor who could help in the storm?
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> The Hendersons next door. They have a generator. They offered to let us plug in the concentrator if we need.
Nurse -> That's a wonderful offer. That could be your backup. Run an extension cord. Make sure it's a heavy duty one.
Caller -> I'll ask Mr. Henderson. He knows about cords. He's an electrician.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's a big help.
Caller -> He's wonderful. He fixed our furnace last year for free. He wouldn't take a dime.
Nurse -> Neighbors like that are priceless.
Caller -> I feel much better. I was up half the night worrying.
Nurse -> Anxiety before a storm is natural. A plan is the best medicine.
Caller -> My husband says I worry enough for both of us.
Nurse -> Ha. A good team.
Nurse -> Of course you were. But you've got a plan now.
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> A plan. Yes. Write down the time. Switch to the tank. Henderson's generator. Nine one one if bad.
Caller -> I think I'll make a poster. Big letters. Taped to the wall by the concentrator.
Nurse -> A poster would be perfect. Short steps in large print.
Nurse -> That's it. Anything else?
Caller -> What about his medicines? If we can't get out to the pharmacy?
Nurse -> Do you have at least a week's supply of his regular medicines?
Caller -> I think so. I'll check tonight. I'll put them in a bag.
Nurse -> Check tonight. If you're short on anything, call us tomorrow.
Caller -> I keep his medicines in a plastic tub in the pantry. I'll go through it after dinner.
Nurse -> Check the dates too. Anything expired, set aside and tell the nurse.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Colleen. You're a lifesaver.
Caller -> I'm going to the store now for water and batteries. Before the crowds.
Nurse -> Go. Tell Harald we said hello.
Caller -> I will. He likes you all. He says the Northstar nurses are the only ones who listen.
Nurse -> Anytime. Stay warm.
Caller -> I made a pot of soup. Enough for a week. If the power goes out, I'll heat it on the camp stove.
Nurse -> Use the camp stove outside or in a well ventilated spot, away from the oxygen.
Caller -> Garage with the door open. I know. Thanks.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Tidewater Pediatric Home Health, this is Hortensia.
Caller -> Hi, Hortensia. This is Soledad Quintanilla. I'm calling about my son, Mateo Quintanilla. He has the ear infection. And I have a question about his amoxicillan.
Nurse -> Hi, Soledad. Amoxicillin, is that the pink liquid?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm in the car, in the school pickup line. The kids are loud.
Nurse -> No problem. I can hear you fine.
Caller -> Yes, the pink one. It says amoxicillan on the bottle. The pharmacy label. Four hundred milligrams in five milliliters. And he takes five milliliters twice a day.
Nurse -> Okay. And what day is he on?
Caller -> Day four. Of ten. He's had it since Friday. He had a dose this morning, at eight.
Nurse -> Good. How's his ear?
Caller -> Sorry, I lost my train of thought.
Nurse -> That's okay. We were just getting started.
Caller -> Much better. He was crying Thursday night. He kept pulling at it. Now he doesn't touch it. He says it doesn't hurt. Maybe a little when I press behind the ear.
Nurse -> That's a good sign. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> I took it before I called. Ninety nine point one. Normal. He had a hundred and one on Friday.
Nurse -> Good. Any vomiting, diarrhea, rash, hives?
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> No. His stomach's fine. He's eating. No spots. Nothing. He's a little cranky, but that's him.
Nurse -> Is he sleeping through the night?
Caller -> Mostly. He wakes up once and comes into our bed. That's been going on since the ear started.
Nurse -> That's understandable.
Nurse -> Okay. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> October twelfth, twenty twenty one. He's five.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Four one four, five five five, zero one one zero.
Nurse -> Got it. What was your question?
Caller -> Okay. I've got a notebook now. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Alright.
Caller -> He feels so much better. Can I stop the medicine? He hates it. He fights me every time. I have to hold his nose. I feel terrible.
Nurse -> I understand, Soledad. But please keep going for all ten days. If you stop early, the infection can come back, and sometimes it comes back stronger.
Caller -> All ten. Even though he's fine.
Nurse -> Yes. The ear can still have infection even when it stops hurting. The medicine needs the full course to clear it out.
Caller -> Okay. I figured you'd say that. I just hoped.
Nurse -> Ha. Of course. Let's make it easier. Do you use the oral syringe that came with it?
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> I use a spoon. A teaspoon. Because the syringe makes him gag.
Nurse -> A kitchen teaspoon isn't accurate. A real teaspoon is five milliliters, but kitchen spoons vary. Please use the syringe, but squirt it slowly into the side of his cheek, not at the back of the throat. Shake the bottle first. And give it with a little food, like applesauce or a cracker.
Caller -> Syringe. Slow. In the cheek. Shake it. With food. Okay. I can try that. He might gag less.
Nurse -> A sticker or a small treat afterward can help too.
Caller -> He loves stickers. I'll give him a dinosaur one.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> What if he spits some out?
Nurse -> If he spits out a little, don't repeat the dose. If he throws up within fifteen minutes, call us.
Caller -> One sec. My phone is making that beeping sound.
Nurse -> No worries, I'll wait.
Caller -> Okay. Fifteen minutes. Call you.
Nurse -> And call us if he gets a fever of one hundred two or higher, a rash, if he vomits and can't keep it down, or if the ear pain gets worse.
Caller -> A hundred two. A rash. Vomiting. Ear pain worse. Okay.
Nurse -> I'll call you in two days to see how he's doing and whether he's taking it.
Caller -> Two days. That's Wednesday. Okay. Call after four. I pick him up from school.
Nurse -> After four on Wednesday. Got it.
Caller -> Thank you so much. You made me feel less guilty.
Nurse -> No guilt. You're doing a good job. It's hard to give medicine to a five year old.
Caller -> He told me yesterday he was going to throw it out the window. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. Kids are creative.
Caller -> His teacher says he told her the medicine is poison. I was mortified.
Nurse -> Ha. He's testing you. Stay calm and consistent.
Caller -> Sorry, somebody's at the door. Hang on a second.
Nurse -> No problem, I'll hold.
Caller -> Oh, he's very creative. He drew a picture of me with a giant spoon.
Nurse -> Ha. Hang that on the fridge.
Caller -> It's already there.
Nurse -> Take care, Soledad.
Caller -> Bye. Thanks again.
