transcript:
Nurse -> Silverleaf Home Care, this is Marisol.
Caller -> Hi. Hello. This is Lucian Ferreira. I'm calling about my aunt. Ruth. Ruth Delaney, I think. Or Dulaney. I always get that wrong. D E L A, I think.
Nurse -> Hi, Lucian. I'm Marisol. I should tell you that I can't confirm whether someone is our client. But tell me what's going on and I'll help however I can.
Caller -> I know, I know. I'm sorry. I didn't know who else to call. I looked up home health agencies in her zip code and started at the top.
Nurse -> Then you've called the right place. Go on.
Caller -> Sure, sure. I understand. She's, my aunt lives alone. In Milwaukee. I'm in Phoenix. I've called her every day for two years. Every morning at nine. And she didn't answer yesterday. Or today. It just rings.
Nurse -> Does it go to voicemail, or just ring and ring?
Caller -> Just rings. She doesn't have voicemail. She says it's for people with nothing to say.
Nurse -> Ha. A woman of principle.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she ever missed a day before?
Caller -> Never. Not once. She picks up on the second ring. Even when she was in the hospital, she took the call. That's why I'm scared.
Caller -> She says the second ring is for being polite. The first is too eager.
Nurse -> I like her already.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there anyone nearby who could check on her? A neighbor?
Caller -> Yes. Mrs. Abernethy next door. She went over this morning. She knocked and nobody answered. She said the lights are on. All of them. And the newspaper is still on the porch from yesterday.
Nurse -> Does Mrs. Abernethy have a key?
Caller -> She doesn't. My aunt never gave anyone a key. She's very private.
Caller -> She doesn't even tell me what's wrong when she's sick. I find out from my mother, a month later.
Nurse -> Some people guard their privacy fiercely. It doesn't mean they don't love you.
Nurse -> Okay. When did you last talk to her?
Caller -> Sunday. Four days ago. She sounded a little off, honestly. She was, I don't know, wobbly. Her voice. Maybe slurred, a little? Or maybe she was tired. She said she was fine.
Nurse -> What do you mean by wobbly?
Caller -> Like she was out of breath. Or her words ran together. I can't say for sure. I thought maybe she'd had a glass of wine. She doesn't drink much, though.
Caller -> I keep replaying it. She said she had a headache, I think. Or a tired head. Something about her head.
Nurse -> That's helpful. I'll pass it along to the nurse.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Does she have any health conditions that you know of?
Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> High blood pressure. And the sugar. Diabetes, I think. And she had a fall in the spring. She uses a cane. I'm not clear on everything. She keeps it private.
Nurse -> Do you know if she takes insulin, or pills for the sugar?
Caller -> No idea. I know there's a pill box on the kitchen table. The big one with the lids.
Nurse -> Okay. The nurse will look at that too.
Nurse -> That's fine. Lucian, do you know her date of birth?
Caller -> I think the line cut out for a second. Are you still there?
Nurse -> Yes, I'm here.
Caller -> No. No, I should. It's in June, I think. She's in her eighties. I don't have the date. I could ask my mother. She's her sister.
Nurse -> Don't worry about the date. What's the address?
Caller -> Twelve forty three, Maple. Maple Avenue. No, Maple Street. It's near the library.
Nurse -> Is it a house or an apartment? Is there a doorbell or a gate?
Caller -> A little brick house. Blue door. A doorbell that doesn't work. You have to knock hard.
Nurse -> Got it. Blue door. Knock hard.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me look up that address. Do you have a number for you?
Caller -> Sorry, I lost my train of thought.
Nurse -> That's okay. We were just getting started.
Caller -> Four one four, five five five, zero one eight two. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Got it. I can't share what's in our records, but the address is enough for me to act on. For Ruth Dulaney, is that spelled D U L A N E Y?
Caller -> Dulaney. Maybe. It could be. She says it Dulaney. But the mail says Delaney. I honestly don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. That's close enough for me to take it from here. I'll send a nurse to her house this afternoon to check on her.
Caller -> Oh, thank God. Today? This afternoon?
Nurse -> Yes. Today. I'll also call you back within two hours to let you know what we find.
Caller -> What if she's at the hospital? Would you be able to tell me?
Nurse -> The nurse will check. If she's been taken somewhere, we'll find out what we can.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. Thank you. I'll keep my phone on loud.
Nurse -> Lucian, if the nurse can't get in, we may ask the police to do a welfare check. Is that okay with you?
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> Yes. Yes, please. Whatever you need to do.
Nurse -> I'll note that we have your permission. Do you want the police to call you directly?
Caller -> Yes. Same number. Any time of day. I'm not sleeping anyway.
Nurse -> Good. In the meantime, ask Mrs. Abernethy to go back and knock again. Call out her name. Look in the windows if she can do it safely. If she sees your aunt on the floor, or hears her calling for help, call nine one one right away.
Caller -> Knock. Call out. Look in the windows. If she's on the floor, nine one one. I'll call Mrs. Abernethy right now.
Nurse -> Good. Have her stay on the porch until the nurse arrives, if she's willing.
Caller -> She will. She's a good woman. She'll stand there all afternoon if I ask.
Nurse -> That's very kind of her.
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> I just hope I'm overreacting. I hope she's at the beauty parlor and forgot her phone.
Nurse -> Checking on someone you love is never an overreaction.
Caller -> My mother says that too. She says I get it from her.
Nurse -> That's possible. Let's find out.
Caller -> Does she go to a beauty parlor? She never mentioned one. Ha. I'm grasping.
Nurse -> It's okay to grasp. It means you care.
Caller -> She raised me. When my father left. She's like a mother.
Nurse -> Tell me about her.
Caller -> She was a school secretary for thirty one years. She knows every kid in the district. She still gets Christmas cards from people she hired in the nineties.
Nurse -> A pillar of the community.
Caller -> She is. She'd hate me saying so.
Nurse -> Then it makes sense you're worried.
Caller -> She makes the best kolaches. I haven't had one in two years because I can't get back there. I keep promising to visit.
Nurse -> There's time. Let's make sure she's okay first.
Caller -> I'll hold on to that. Thank you for not making me feel foolish.
Nurse -> Not at all.
Caller -> Yes. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm going to hang up now and get the nurse on her way. I'll call you in two hours or sooner.
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> Thank you. I appreciate it more than you know.
Caller -> Can I ask you something? Do you think I should get on a plane?
Nurse -> Let's see what the nurse finds first. If you want to start looking at flights, there's no harm.
Caller -> I'll look at flights. Just in case.
Caller -> Is there anything I should be doing besides calling the neighbor?
Nurse -> Keep your phone near you and try her number once more in a half hour. Someone might hear it ring, and a ring on the other side is information too.
Caller -> I'll set a timer.
Nurse -> Talk soon, Lucian.
Caller -> Bye. Thank you.

transcript:
Nurse -> Aurora Home Health, this is Benedikt.
Caller -> Hi, Benedikt. This is Corbin Brennerman. I'm calling about my father, Alistair Brennerman. He came home from the hospital Thursday. I need to go over his medicines because I think I made a mistake.
Nurse -> Hi, Corbin. Okay. Let's slow down and go through it. Do you have the discharge list in front of you?
Caller -> I do. Seven pages. They stapled the pharmacy printout to the back. And a sheet about blood thinners. I tried to read it all in the first night.
Nurse -> That's a lot for anyone. Don't worry about the pile. We'll go step by step.
Caller -> I do. And all the bottles. I've lined them up on the kitchen table. Eleven bottles. It's like a pharmacy.
Nurse -> Some of those may be old bottles from before the hospital.
Caller -> Most of them. I didn't want to throw anything out until someone told me.
Nurse -> Smart. We'll sort them tomorrow.
Nurse -> Perfect. Start with the new ones. What changed in the hospital?
Caller -> Before I start, they kept him four days. They said his heart rate was racing, up near a hundred and forty at one point. They shocked it back, I think. Cardioversion.
Nurse -> That's a big stay. You've been through a lot.
Caller -> They started a new blood thinner. Apixaban. Five milligrams. Twice a day. The paper says it replaces the warfarin.
Nurse -> Right. That's a big change. So the warfarin stopped.
Caller -> It's supposed to. The paper says discontinue warfarin. In a box, in bold. But here's the thing. I didn't read the paper carefully on Thursday. Friday I gave him the warfarin in the evening, because that's what he always took. I thought, well, he's on a new one too, but maybe both. And then Saturday evening I gave him both again. The warfarin and the apixaban.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. That's very important. When exactly did you give both?
Caller -> Saturday evening. Around seven. The warfarin three milligrams. The one pill. And the apixaban at the same time. It was his evening dose of the new one.
Nurse -> And he got warfarin on Friday evening too?
Caller -> Friday, yes. Just the warfarin on Friday. The apixaban was only supposed to start Saturday morning. Because the hospital said, wait for the INR to come down. I don't know. It's confusing. I read it again last night and I saw the box. And I stopped. I haven't given the warfarin since.
Nurse -> Okay. So Friday evening warfarin, then Saturday evening warfarin and apixaban together. And none since.
Caller -> Right. Sunday and today, just the apixaban. And the other pills.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there any bleeding? Bruising? Anything unusual?
Caller -> I checked him from head to toe last night. No bleeding. His gums are fine. No nosebleeds. A bruise on his arm from the IV, but that was there when he came home. Nothing new. He says he feels fine.
Nurse -> Good. Any black stools? Blood in the urine?
Caller -> He says the stools are normal. Brown. And the urine is yellow. He's careful about that. I asked.
Nurse -> Any headaches? Dizziness? Falls?
Caller -> No falls. He's steady with the walker. No headaches. A tiny bit of tiredness. He's seventy eight, he's tired.
Nurse -> Is he sleeping more than before the hospital, or the same?
Caller -> A bit more. He naps after lunch for an hour. He didn't do that before.
Nurse -> That's common after a hospital stay.
Nurse -> Okay. Corbin, can I have his date of birth?
Caller -> April second, nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Six one zero, five five five, zero one zero nine.
Nurse -> Thank you. Now let's go through the rest. Keep your list handy. What's the metoprolol?
Caller -> Metoprolol succinate. The extended release. Fifty milligrams. Once a day in the morning. It's unchanged from before. He took it this morning.
Nurse -> Good. Please don't crush it. And the water pill?
Caller -> Furosemide. Twenty milligrams. Once a day. The hospital lowered it. It used to be forty. But I want to make sure, because the old bottle at home says forty. It's the old bottle. And the new bottle says twenty.
Nurse -> Which are you using?
Caller -> The new one. Twenty. I put the old one in a drawer.
Nurse -> Good. Keep the old one away. And the cholesterol medicine?
Caller -> Wait, one more question about the furosemide. If he gains weight, do I give more?
Nurse -> No. Weigh him every morning and report a gain to us. Don't change the dose yourself.
Caller -> Don't change. Report. Got it.
Caller -> Atorvastatin. Forty milligrams. At night. No change. He took it last night.
Nurse -> Perfect. So the list is apixaban five twice a day, metoprolol succinate fifty daily, furosemide twenty daily, atorvastatin forty at night. And warfarin is stopped.
Caller -> Yes. That's what the paper says. Warfarin stopped. I should have been careful. I feel awful.
Caller -> If anything happens to him because of me, I'll never forgive myself.
Nurse -> Let's take one thing at a time. We have good steps to take today.
Nurse -> I understand. It's an easy mistake when there's so much paper. Where's the warfarin bottle now?
Caller -> On the table with the others. I'll put it away.
Nurse -> Please put it in a bag, away from the other bottles. Don't throw it out yet. The nurse will help you with it.
Caller -> In a bag. Away. Okay.
Nurse -> Corbin, here's what I'm going to do. I'm paging the on-call clinician now about the double blood thinner on Saturday. They may want a blood test to check how thin his blood is.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'm also going to call the pharmacy to confirm the discharge medicine list, so everything matches.
Caller -> That would be great. I'd feel better if somebody else looked at the list.
Nurse -> And I'm sending a nurse tomorrow. She'll go through every bottle with you, fill the pill organizer from the current list, and take the old warfarin out of the house.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What time?
Caller -> If I'm at the pharmacy when she comes, my dad can let her in. He's fine with the door.
Nurse -> I'd prefer you be there for the medication review, if you can.
Caller -> Then I'll stay. I'll get what I need by delivery.
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you. Probably the morning.
Caller -> I'll be here.
Nurse -> Until then, give no more warfarin. Give the apixaban twelve hours apart, morning and evening. Same times every day.
Caller -> Twelve hours apart. Morning and evening. Okay. Eight and eight.
Nurse -> Does he drink alcohol, or take any herbal supplements?
Caller -> A glass of wine on Sundays. No supplements. He thinks vitamins are a scam.
Nurse -> Ha. Fine. Keep the wine to that.
Nurse -> Eight and eight is good. Now, call us right away if he has bleeding that won't stop, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, a bad headache, or a fall where he hits his head. For any of those, call nine one one.
Caller -> Bleeding. Black stools. Vomiting blood. Bad headache. Head injury. Nine one one. I'm writing it down.
Nurse -> Stick the list on the fridge where everyone in the house sees it.
Caller -> Right next to the pizza magnet. It's the only magnet we have.
Nurse -> Also, a few safety things. Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor. No ibuprofen or aspirin. And fill the pill organizer only from the current list.
Caller -> Soft brush. Electric razor. No Advil. Pill organizer from the new list. Okay. I don't think he has an electric razor. I'll buy one.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Caller -> He's been shaving with a safety razor for fifty years. He'll complain.
Nurse -> Ha. Safety first.
Caller -> I'll tell him the nurse said.
Nurse -> Does he live with anyone else?
Caller -> No. He's alone since my mother passed. That's why I'm here.
Nurse -> It's good you could take the week.
Nurse -> Always works.
Caller -> Ha. Benedikt, can I ask you something? Am I a bad son?
Nurse -> Not at all. You're a son who's carrying a lot, and who caught the mistake and called. That's what a good caregiver does.
Caller -> I'm an accountant. I'm good with numbers. But these are different numbers. Milligrams and units, twice a day, with food, without food.
Nurse -> Ha. A different spreadsheet.
Caller -> I made one. A spreadsheet. It has the times and the doses and a checkbox.
Nurse -> Perfect. Bring it tomorrow. The nurse will love it.
Caller -> I'm just so tired. I took a week off work. I'm sleeping on his couch. I'm cooking. I'm doing the pills. I haven't been this stressed in my life.
Nurse -> That's a lot. Is there anyone who can help?
Caller -> My sister's coming Wednesday. She can take over the evenings.
Nurse -> Good. Share the medicine list with her. One person fills the organizer, and the other checks it. Two sets of eyes.
Caller -> Two sets of eyes. That's smart. I'll set it up that way.
Caller -> She's a pharmacist's assistant, my sister. She's going to enjoy catching my mistakes.
Nurse -> Ha. Siblings.
Nurse -> Does your father know what happened?
Caller -> I told him. He laughed. He said, Corbin, I've been on warfarin for ten years, I could have told you. I said, Dad, why didn't you? He said he thought the hospital knew best.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the kind of thing patients assume.
Caller -> He's a retired engineer. He thinks everything is a system. If the system says take it, he takes it.
Nurse -> Does he want to be involved in the medicine plan?
Caller -> He does, actually. He asked for a chart. He wants to tick them off himself. He says it's his heart, he'll count the pills.
Nurse -> That's great. Both of you checking is ideal.
Nurse -> The system needs a human check sometimes.
Caller -> Exactly. I'll be the human check.
Caller -> He's already making jokes about me being the pharmacist now.
Nurse -> Ha. You're the family pharmacist and the family chef.
Caller -> The chef is a stretch. Soup from a can.
Nurse -> The clinician will call you within the hour.
Caller -> Okay. I'll stay right by the phone.
Nurse -> Thank you for calling, Corbin. You did the right thing.
Caller -> Thank you for not making me feel stupid.
Caller -> I'll tell you, the hardest part was admitting it to my dad. He didn't judge me. He just said, thanks for catching it.
Nurse -> He sounds like a good man.
Caller -> He is. He built bridges for thirty five years. He knows all about redundancy.
Nurse -> Never. Take care.
Caller -> Should I tell the hospital about this? The cardiologist?
Nurse -> The clinician will handle that, and the nurse can bring it up tomorrow. You don't need to chase anyone down.
Caller -> Okay. That's a relief. One less thing.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Octavia.
Caller -> Octavia, it's Matthias Oyelaran. My father is Jonas Oyelaran. He's agitated. He's really agitated. He won't settle. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> Okay, Matthias. I'm here. Tell me what you're seeing.
Caller -> Sorry for calling so late. Early. I don't know what time it is anymore.
Nurse -> Any hour is fine. That's what we're here for.
Caller -> He's been like this since about midnight. Restless. He's pulling the sheets off. He keeps trying to sit up and swing his legs over. He tried to climb out of the bed twice. I had to hold him.
Caller -> He's strong. He was a boxer in his twenties. It took everything I had to keep him from standing.
Nurse -> That's a lot. Are you hurt?
Caller -> No. A scratch on my arm. I'm fine.
Nurse -> Is he talking?
Caller -> He's mumbling. He's talking to people. He keeps saying, Ruth, Ruth, come in, shut the door. My mother's name is Ruth. She's been dead for eleven years. And he's looking at the corner like she's standing there.
Caller -> It's frightening. I keep looking at the corner too. There's nothing there. But he's so sure.
Nurse -> That's normal for visitors to feel that. It's okay to be shaken.
Nurse -> Okay. That's very common near the end of life. It's called terminal restlessness. It's not dangerous for him in the way it feels to you. Has he had any medicine for it?
Caller -> The haloperidol. Half a milligram. Every six hours as needed. I gave it at one. It's three fifty now. It didn't help. He's the same.
Nurse -> Has he eaten or had anything to drink tonight?
Caller -> He had some juice around ten. Nothing since. He wouldn't take his pills.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll let the clinician know.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he in pain, do you think? Grimacing, moaning?
Caller -> No. His face is not in pain. It's more like worry. And his breathing is normal. Not fast. Not noisy. It's just that he can't stay still.
Nurse -> Good. When did he last have morphine?
Caller -> Nine last night. He hasn't needed any since. I asked him about pain and he shook his head.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he had a bowel movement? Is he able to urinate? Retention and constipation can make people restless.
Caller -> He has the catheter. The bag has some. And no bowel movement in three days. I told the nurse that on Monday.
Nurse -> Is the catheter bag draining well? Is the tubing kinked?
Caller -> It looks straight. It's draining. A small amount, dark yellow.
Nurse -> Thank you. That helps.
Nurse -> Okay. That could be adding to it. We'll tell the clinician. Matthias, I'm going to page the on-call clinician now. They'll call you back with orders.
Caller -> Is there something we can do about that tonight?
Nurse -> The clinician may order something. Don't give any laxative on your own.
Caller -> Understood.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'm also sending a nurse to be with you. She should be there within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. I'm so glad. I thought I'd have to do this alone till morning.
Caller -> My wife's asleep upstairs with the baby. I didn't want to wake her. She has to work tomorrow.
Nurse -> You can still wake her if you need a second pair of hands. It's a hard night.
Nurse -> You won't. Let me help with the next hour. First, safety. Is the bed at its lowest?
Caller -> No. It's up high. For my back, when I change him. Should I lower it?
Nurse -> Yes, lower it all the way down. And put pillows or a folded blanket on the floor next to the bed, in case he does get out. Keep the area clear. And stay with him. Don't leave him alone.
Caller -> Lower it. Pillows on the floor. Stay with him. Okay. I'm lowering it now. There. It's down.
Nurse -> Good. Now the room. Dim the lights and turn off the television. Speak softly. And don't argue with what he sees.
Caller -> The TV's already off. The lamp's on. I'll turn it low. I won't argue. I said to him, Dad, Mom's not here. That upset him.
Nurse -> It can. Try, I hear you, Dad. Everything's okay. You're safe. You don't have to agree.
Caller -> That sounds so simple. I couldn't think of it. I was just panicking.
Nurse -> Panic is normal. You're thinking just fine now.
Caller -> I hear you, Dad. Everything's okay. You're safe. Okay. He's calmer already. A little.
Nurse -> Good. Another thing: please don't give another dose of the haloperidol until the clinician calls. I want them to decide.
Caller -> No more until they call. Okay.
Nurse -> What's his date of birth, Matthias?
Caller -> June thirtieth, nineteen thirty nine.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Nine one eight, five five five, zero one seven zero.
Nurse -> Is that a cell? Will you hear it ring if you're by the bed?
Caller -> Yes. I keep it on loud.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Got it. Keep talking to him. Hold his hand. Sometimes touch helps.
Caller -> He's whispering something. I think he's praying. Or counting.
Nurse -> Let him. It may be soothing to him.
Caller -> I'm holding it. He squeezed. He said, my boy. He knows me.
Caller -> I haven't heard him say that in days. He's been so quiet.
Nurse -> It's a good moment. Hold on to it.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. He knows you're there.
Caller -> Yeah. Okay. He's lying back a little. His hands are still moving. But he's less wild.
Nurse -> Good. The clinician will call within about fifteen minutes. Keep your phone beside you.
Caller -> Should I wake my brother? He's across town. He'd want to be here.
Nurse -> That's your decision. If you want company, call him. A familiar voice can help.
Caller -> I'll call him after I hang up.
Caller -> It's on the bed. Right next to his hand. Thank you, Octavia.
Nurse -> I'm here. If he gets worse, call me right back.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Linden Park Home Care, this is Gwendolyn.
Caller -> Hello, dear. This is Hortense Ballard. I'm one of your patients. I call every Wednesday. Well, every Tuesday, because Wednesday you come. I'm confused today.
Nurse -> Hi, Hortense. It is Tuesday. Wednesday you have a visit. Is that what you wanted to confirm?
Caller -> Yes, that's it. Wednesday. At ten.
Nurse -> Let me look. Yes. Tomorrow at ten o'clock. It's on the schedule.
Caller -> Good. Good. I wrote it on the calendar, but I don't trust my own handwriting these days.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll be there. Hortense, how have you been?
Caller -> I've been all right. I had a good week. My great-grandson visited and we made cookies. Well, he made a mess and I supervised.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the best way.
Caller -> Can I ask you to hold for a moment? The kettle is going.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> Oh, fine. I'm ninety two. I'm never fine, but I'm fine. I had my blood pressure taken at the pharmacy. They have a machine. A hundred thirty eight over seventy eight. They gave me a little slip.
Nurse -> That's a nice number. Do you have any dizziness, or have you had any falls?
Caller -> No dizziness. No falls. I use my walker like a good girl. I don't go anywhere without it. Even to the mailbox.
Nurse -> Wonderful. Any pain?
Caller -> My knee. The right one. It's a dull ache. It's been there a few weeks. It's not terrible. It's worse after the stairs. I have the exercises where I go up and down two steps.
Nurse -> Is the knee swollen or red or warm?
Caller -> No. It looks like a knee. It's just old. It aches when the weather changes.
Nurse -> Okay. I'd like the nurse tomorrow to look at it. For now, here's what I'd suggest for the stairs. Do only as many as are comfortable, rest between sets, and don't push through pain. A warm pack on the knee for fifteen minutes can help afterward.
Caller -> A warm pack. I have a rice sock. I put it in the microwave. Is that all right?
Nurse -> That's perfect. Check the temperature first.
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> Oh, I always do. I burned myself once on a rice sock. Never again.
Nurse -> Do you have someone who checks on you during the day?
Caller -> My daughter calls at noon and my neighbor brings the paper. Between them I'm never alone for more than a few hours.
Nurse -> Ha. A hard lesson.
Caller -> The hardest. Could I skip the stairs on the bad days?
Nurse -> On the bad days, yes. Do the seated exercises instead. The nurse tomorrow will show you which ones.
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> Seated ones. Good. I like the seated ones.
Caller -> The ones with the little band. I do ten. Then I count to ten again to be sure I did ten.
Nurse -> Ha. Counting twice is fine.
Nurse -> Hortense, what's your date of birth? For the chart.
Caller -> September twenty first, nineteen thirty four. I always forget and then I remember.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> Nine oh one, five five five, zero one eight eight.
Nurse -> Thank you. How are the hearing aids?
Caller -> Sorry, I just dropped my pen.
Nurse -> That's all right.
Caller -> Wonderful! I can hear the birds. I haven't heard a bird in ten years. I cried. My daughter took me to the audiologist. She said, Mother, you need these. I said, I do not. And then I put them in and I heard a cardinal.
Nurse -> That's lovely. That must have been quite a moment.
Caller -> It was. The first thing I heard was the refrigerator. It hums. I'd forgotten.
Nurse -> Ha. The little things.
Caller -> And the clock. I had no idea my clock ticked. It's been ticking for fifty years.
Nurse -> It's wonderful how much we miss.
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> And I can hear you. Much better. I don't have to say what? three times.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. Hortense, call us any time if the knee swells, turns red, or if you feel dizzy or fall. Don't wait for Wednesday.
Caller -> Swells. Red. Dizzy. Fall. I'll call. I have your number on the phone with the big buttons.
Nurse -> Great. Anything else?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> No, dear. I just like to hear a voice. My friends are mostly gone. You're a nice voice.
Nurse -> Thank you, Hortense. So are you.
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> Oh, stop. I'm an old lady. Well. Thank you. I'll see you tomorrow at ten.
Caller -> Don't stop calling me. I like the company.
Nurse -> We'll keep calling. Tomorrow we'll see you in person.
Nurse -> See you then. Take care.
Caller -> Bye bye, dear.

Nurse -> Evergreen Hospice, this is Annelise.
Caller -> Hi, Annelise. It's Marisela Brightwater. My father is Gideon Brightwater. I need to restock his supplies. And I have a skin question.
Nurse -> Hi, Marisela. Sure. Let's start with the supplies. What are you low on?
Caller -> The briefs. The adult briefs. I have six left. I'm changing him four or five times a day. That's a day and a bit.
Nurse -> Okay. And underpads?
Caller -> Four. The blue ones, for the bed. They get used up fast.
Nurse -> Okay. What else?
Caller -> Is it okay if I put you on speaker? My hands are full.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> The mouth swabs. The pink ones on the sticks. I'm out. I used the last one this morning.
Nurse -> I'll get those to you right away. How is Gideon today?
Caller -> Thank you. I've been wetting my finger and rubbing his lips in the meantime. It's all I had.
Nurse -> That's fine. Water on a clean cloth works.
Caller -> I think the line cut out for a second. Are you still there?
Nurse -> Yes, I'm here.
Caller -> Sleeping. He sleeps most of the day. He opens his eyes when I talk to him. He takes a few sips from the straw. No food. But he's comfortable. No moaning.
Nurse -> That's what we want to hear. Tell me about the skin.
Caller -> Sorry, I just dropped my pen.
Nurse -> That's all right.
Caller -> When I changed him this morning I noticed his tailbone is pink. A pink patch. About the size of a half dollar. It's not open. It's not broken. It doesn't look like a bedsore. But it looks like the beginning of one.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it red or pink? Does it turn white when you press it and then pink again?
Caller -> It's pink. When I press, it goes white and then pink again. I think. I'm not sure. It might be a little darker in the middle.
Nurse -> Good observation. Does he seem to be in pain when you touch it, or when you turn him?
Caller -> No. He doesn't flinch. He doesn't wince. And there's no open spot, no blister.
Nurse -> Okay. Marisela, what's your father's date of birth?
Caller -> Sorry, give me a minute, he just stirred. Dad? Dad, it's okay. He's settling again.
Nurse -> Take all the time you need.
Caller -> Sorry, I keep going back and forth. It's been a long day.
Nurse -> I understand. Take a breath.
Caller -> December nineteenth, nineteen thirty seven.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Nine one nine, five five five, zero one nine four.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm going to order the briefs, the underpads, the mouth swabs, and a barrier cream. I'll order plenty so you don't run low.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. A cream. Yes. I didn't know about that.
Nurse -> We'll send it. I can have everything delivered this afternoon.
Caller -> This afternoon. Good. I'll be home. Is there a delivery window?
Nurse -> The driver will call before. And I'll message the hospice nurse about the pink skin so she looks at it on her next visit.
Caller -> Yes. Thank you. I wasn't sure if it was something I should worry about.
Nurse -> It's good that you noticed. Let's talk about what you can do now. Turn him gently every two hours, from one side to the other, and put a pillow behind his back and between his knees. That keeps pressure off the tailbone.
Caller -> Every two hours. Side to side. Pillows. I've been doing every three or four. I'll set a timer.
Nurse -> Every two is better. Keep his skin clean and dry. After a change, pat him dry, and put a thin layer of the barrier cream on the pink area when it arrives.
Caller -> Thin layer. Pat dry. Okay. I'll use plain petroleum jelly until the cream comes.
Nurse -> Just a thin layer, and only on the pink skin, not into any folds.
Caller -> Right.
Nurse -> That's fine for a few hours. Don't massage the pink area. Just pat.
Caller -> No massage. Got it.
Nurse -> Is the bed mattress an air mattress, or a regular one?
Caller -> Regular hospital mattress. The foam one. They said an air one if he gets a sore.
Nurse -> The nurse will look at that. Call us if the skin opens, turns dark red or purple, or he seems to be in pain when you move him.
Caller -> Opens. Dark red or purple. Pain. Okay. I'll check at every change.
Nurse -> Great. How are you holding up?
Caller -> Tired. But okay. My brother comes tonight. He'll sit with Dad so I can sleep.
Nurse -> Good. You need rest too.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> I know. I'm a nurse myself, a school nurse. I should know better. But it's different when it's your own dad.
Nurse -> It always is.
Caller -> Okay. Sorry about that. Go on.
Nurse -> Alright, thank you.
Caller -> I keep checking his skin like I'm in the office. I can't turn it off.
Nurse -> Ha. A professional hazard.
Caller -> Sorry, somebody's at the door. Hang on a second.
Nurse -> No problem, I'll hold.
Caller -> Yes. Thank you, Annelise. You made this easy.
Nurse -> Anytime. Take care.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Linden Park Home Care, this is Gwendolyn.
Caller -> Hi, Gwendolyn. This is Merrick Salazar. I'm calling about my wife, Odalys Salazar. She had her gallbladder out Monday. Two days ago. And she's in pain and I wanted to check if it's normal.
Nurse -> Hi, Merrick. Okay. Tell me about the pain.
Caller -> Sorry if I cut out. I'm in the garage, the signal in the house is terrible. Can you hear me okay?
Nurse -> A few words are dropping, but I'm following.
Caller -> It's at the, the cuts. The, the little incisions in her belly. She says a five. A five out of ten. It's, uh, it's sore and tight. Worse when she coughs or gets up.
Nurse -> Is it sharp or dull? Does it spread to her shoulder?
Caller -> Dull, mostly. Sometimes her right shoulder aches. The surgeon said that's from the gas they use.
Nurse -> That's right. That's normal and it should fade.
Nurse -> That's very common after this surgery. Is she taking anything for it?
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> The oxycodone. Five milligrams. Every six hours as needed. She took one at four. And she's taking Tylenol in between. The surgeon told her to.
Nurse -> Any constipation? That oxycodone can bind her up.
Caller -> A little. She hasn't gone since the surgery. She's drinking prune juice. Hateful stuff.
Nurse -> Ha. A good plan. Keep that up.
Nurse -> Good. Does she have a fever?
Caller -> Sorry, I just dropped my pen.
Nurse -> That's all right.
Caller -> I took it an hour ago. It was ninety nine point eight. A little warm. Not, not a fever, the sheet said under a hundred is okay.
Nurse -> Which thermometer?
Caller -> The ear one. The one with the beep.
Nurse -> Good. Consistent is what matters.
Nurse -> That's right. Under a hundred point four is normal after surgery. Any vomiting, or drainage from the incisions?
Caller -> No vomiting. She's eating soup. Crackers. The dressings are dry. There's no, nothing coming out. No red around them.
Caller -> She says her stomach feels bloated. She has a lot of gas. That's normal too, right?
Nurse -> Walking helps with that. A cup of peppermint tea might help.
Nurse -> Good. Can I get her date of birth?
Caller -> February twenty sixth, nineteen eighty one.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on.
Nurse -> Ha, no worries.
Caller -> Six one zero, five five five, zero one five zero.
Nurse -> Got it. She's walking?
Caller -> Sorry, somebody's at the door. Hang on a second.
Nurse -> No problem, I'll hold.
Caller -> Yes. She walks the hall every hour. With the, the pillow against her belly. She's doing good. She just, it hurts when she, when she stands up fast.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a normal amount of walking. Let me arrange the follow up.
Caller -> I think the line cut out for a second. Are you still there?
Nurse -> Yes, I'm here.
Caller -> I'll arrange a nurse to visit tomorrow to check the incisions and go over her medicines. Oh. Okay. Thank you. That helps.
Caller -> I'm learning a lot. I'm the one doing everything. She's the boss and I'm the assistant.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good arrangement.
Nurse -> Merrick, to help with the pain, hold a pillow against her belly when she coughs or stands. Keep up the short walks. And follow the surgeon's plan of alternating the oxycodone with the acetaminophen.
Caller -> Pillow. Walks. Alternate. Okay. She's doing that.
Nurse -> Does she have the incentive spirometer, the breathing device from the hospital?
Caller -> The little plastic thing with the ball. She does it ten times every hour.
Nurse -> Excellent. That helps prevent pneumonia.
Nurse -> Call us if she has a fever of one hundred point four or higher, redness or pus at the incisions, vomiting, yellow skin or eyes, or if the pain gets worse.
Caller -> A hundred point four. Red or pus. Vomiting. Yellow. Worse pain. Okay. I'll watch.
Caller -> What about the little bruises around the cuts? There's a purple one near her belly button.
Nurse -> Bruising near the incisions is very common. It fades over a week or two.
Nurse -> Is she resting well?
Caller -> Hang on, let me move to the other room. It's loud in here.
Nurse -> No problem, take your time.
Caller -> Pretty well. She's in the recliner. It's easier than the bed.
Caller -> I'm sleeping on the couch next to her. If she calls out, I'll hear it.
Nurse -> Good. Just don't forget your own sleep.
Nurse -> That's common. Anything else?
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> No. That's all. Thanks, Gwendolyn.
Nurse -> Take care, Merrick.
Caller -> I'll check the sheet. Thanks again.
Caller -> One last thing, can she shower?
Nurse -> Ask the surgeon's sheet. Most allow a quick shower after forty eight hours with the dressings covered.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Magnolia Home Health, this is Teodora.
Caller -> Hi. I'm sorry it's so late. This is Delphine Aldridge. I'm a patient. I think the pharmacy gave me the wrong strength of my thyroid pill. I've been feeling awful.
Nurse -> Hi, Delphine. It's fine. Tell me what you've found.
Caller -> I couldn't sleep, again. So I got up and started going through my papers. I'm that kind of person at one in the morning.
Nurse -> Ha. Sometimes insomnia helps. Go ahead.
Caller -> I got a new bottle last week. Levothyroxine. And tonight I was reading the doctor's note, the one that came with my discharge from the clinic, and it says fifty micrograms. But the bottle says one hundred. One hundred micrograms.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me make sure I understand. The doctor ordered fifty, and the bottle you've been using says one hundred.
Caller -> Yes. Exactly. And I've been taking one every morning. For six days. A hundred.
Nurse -> Do you remember the pharmacist saying anything about the change?
Caller -> No. They handed me a bag and said have a nice day. I never looked.
Nurse -> That's most of us.
Nurse -> Okay. When did you start the new bottle?
Caller -> Last Friday. I had a little left from the old one, and then I switched. The old bottle was fifty. I didn't look at the strength on the new one. They look similar. They're both white.
Nurse -> How many tablets are in the new bottle?
Caller -> It's a ninety day supply. I'd taken six, so there are still eighty four. Oh no, I counted wrong, eighty something.
Nurse -> It doesn't matter. Keep the bottle as it is.
Nurse -> And when did you start feeling off?
Caller -> About a week ago. I thought it was stress. I've been jittery. My heart's been racing. I can't sleep. I lie in bed and my heart is pounding. I've been so wired.
Nurse -> Any weight loss, sweating, shakiness in your hands?
Caller -> My hands shake a little. I've been sweating at night. I assumed it was menopause.
Nurse -> Those can overlap. We'll tell the clinician all of it.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a way to check your pulse?
Caller -> I have a blood pressure cuff. It gives the pulse. Hold on. It says one oh eight. One hundred eight. That's high for me. I'm usually in the sixties.
Nurse -> Take it again in a minute, after sitting still.
Caller -> Sitting still. Okay. Hold on. It says one oh six this time. A little better.
Nurse -> Thank you. That's useful.
Nurse -> Okay. Any chest pain? Shortness of breath? Fainting?
Caller -> No chest pain. No fainting. I'm a little short of breath when I climb the stairs. But not now.
Nurse -> Okay. Delphine, what's your date of birth?
Caller -> October fifth, nineteen seventy five.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Eight one six, five five five, zero one five two.
Nurse -> Is that your cell?
Caller -> Yes. It's by the bed, on loud.
Nurse -> Got it. First, don't take tomorrow's dose from that bottle. Hold it until the clinician calls you. Keep the bottle and the doctor's note together so we can show the pharmacy.
Caller -> Don't take it. Keep them together. Okay. I won't. I'll put them in a bag.
Caller -> I should tell you, the new bottle has a different name on it. The old one said Synthroid. The new one says the generic.
Nurse -> That's normal. The strength is what matters.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now about your racing heart and the strength mix up.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I was so worried it was something worse.
Nurse -> And I'll call the pharmacy first thing to find out what happened.
Caller -> Please. They open at eight. It's the one on Calvin Street.
Caller -> I'm so embarrassed. A grown woman who can't read a label.
Nurse -> It's not a reading problem. It's an easy mistake, and the pharmacy shares responsibility.
Nurse -> I'll take care of it. I'm also sending a nurse to see you tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Good.
Caller -> Is there anything I should bring to the pharmacy? Like my insurance card?
Nurse -> I'll handle the call. Just keep the bottle and the doctor's note ready for the nurse.
Nurse -> Will someone be home with you?
Caller -> My husband's asleep upstairs. I'll wake him after we hang up. He'll want to help.
Nurse -> If you get chest pain, if you faint, if you get very short of breath, or your heart keeps racing and won't settle, call nine one one.
Caller -> Chest pain. Faint. Short of breath. Racing that won't stop. Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> Try to rest, sit quietly, and drink water. Avoid coffee.
Caller -> I had coffee all week. I thought it was making me tired. I've been having three cups.
Nurse -> Skip it tomorrow. Let your heart rest.
Caller -> No coffee. Okay. That's going to be hard.
Nurse -> Herbal tea is fine. Chamomile, peppermint.
Caller -> I have chamomile somewhere. In the back of the cupboard.
Nurse -> Ha. I know. The clinician will call within about fifteen minutes.
Caller -> I'll keep the phone next to me. Thank you, Teodora.
Caller -> Should I wake him now? So he's there when they call?
Nurse -> It's up to you. It might be a comfort to have him beside you.
Caller -> I'll wake him. He'll insist on making tea.
Nurse -> Anytime. Take care.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Evergreen Home Health, this is Magdalena.
Caller -> Hi. Magdalena. It's Pearlie Dunwoody. My husband is Orrin Dunwoody. He's on warfarin. He had black stools this morning. Two of them. Black and sticky. And he's weak and dizzy. I'm scared.
Nurse -> Okay, Pearlie. I'm glad you called. Is Orrin awake?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm shaking. I keep dropping things. Hold on, I picked the phone up off the floor.
Nurse -> Take a breath, Pearlie. I'm right here.
Caller -> He's awake. He's on the couch. He's pale. He looks gray. He's talking but slow.
Nurse -> Is he sweating? Cold or clammy?
Caller -> Cold hands. A little sweaty on his forehead.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the stools. What time?
Caller -> The first at six. The second around nine. Black. Not dark brown, black. Like tar. And a terrible smell. I looked. I know what I saw.
Nurse -> Has he taken iron pills or Pepto-Bismol? Those can darken stools.
Caller -> No. Nothing. I checked the pill box. I know what that looks like.
Nurse -> Any red blood in the stool? Vomiting? Blood in the vomit?
Caller -> No red. No vomiting. He says his stomach feels a little burned. But no vomiting. No blood.
Nurse -> Any belly pain, cramping, swelling?
Caller -> Not really. It's more a burning. Higher up.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics that.
Nurse -> How about his dizziness? When does it happen?
Caller -> When he stands. He stood to go to the bathroom and he had to grab the wall. The room spun. And he's weak. He can barely lift his arms. He can't open a jar.
Nurse -> Has he passed out or nearly passed out?
Caller -> No. He grabbed the wall. I caught his arm.
Nurse -> Good. Keep him down from now.
Nurse -> Do you have a way to check his pulse?
Caller -> The cuff has it. Let me. Hold on. It says one hundred. A hundred. That's fast for him. He's usually seventy.
Nurse -> Pearlie, I want you to call nine one one now. Black stools with weakness and a fast pulse, on a blood thinner, could mean bleeding inside his stomach or bowel. He needs to be seen in the emergency room.
Caller -> Oh my God. Okay. Okay. Should I hang up? Should I call? My phone's in the kitchen.
Nurse -> Put me on speaker if you can and call from your cell. Or have someone else call. I'll stay on the line.
Caller -> My son's here. He's in the garage. Daniel! Daniel! Come quick! Call nine one one! Dad's bleeding inside!
Nurse -> Good. Is Daniel calling?
Caller -> He's on it. He's dialing. Okay. Yes.
Nurse -> Perfect. Help Orrin lie down on the couch. Raise his legs on a pillow. Don't let him stand or walk. Give him nothing by mouth. No food, no water.
Caller -> Lie down. Legs up. Nothing by mouth. Okay. Orrin, honey, lie back. I've got you. There. His legs are on the pillow.
Nurse -> Good. Now, has he taken his warfarin today?
Caller -> He takes it in the evening. Four milligrams. He took it last night at seven.
Nurse -> Okay. Do not give the evening warfarin tonight. And tell the paramedics he takes warfarin. They'll want to know.
Caller -> No warfarin. Tell the paramedics. Okay. I will. Daniel! Tell them he's on warfarin!
Nurse -> Does Daniel know your address?
Caller -> He lives here. Thank goodness.
Nurse -> Pearlie, I need his date of birth, for the paramedics.
Caller -> September fourteenth, nineteen forty two.
Nurse -> And your cell number?
Caller -> Nine one nine, five five five, zero one five five.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm going to page the on-call clinician now so they can notify the emergency room.
Caller -> Thank you. They said six minutes. Daniel says six minutes.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is his color changing? Is he getting sleepier?
Caller -> I'm holding his hand. It's cold. Orrin, squeeze my hand. He squeezed.
Nurse -> That's good. Keep checking that he responds.
Caller -> He's pale. He's still talking. He's saying, I'm okay, I'm okay. He doesn't want to go.
Nurse -> It's important that he goes. Tell him the nurse said so.
Caller -> Orrin, the nurse says you have to go. He's nodding. He knows.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have his medicine list handy? Anything else the paramedics should see?
Caller -> On the fridge. Daniel has it. And I'll grab his hospital bag. I keep it packed. It's by the door.
Nurse -> That's very smart.
Caller -> After the last time. We've done this before. Two years ago. A bleeding ulcer.
Nurse -> Which hospital was it, do you remember?
Caller -> Mercy. On the east side. They know him there.
Nurse -> Tell the paramedics. They may choose it.
Nurse -> Then they'll want to know that too. Tell them about the ulcer.
Caller -> I will. Ulcer, warfarin, black stools, six and nine.
Nurse -> Perfect. You're doing everything right.
Caller -> I hear the siren. It's close. Daniel is at the door.
Nurse -> Good. Let them in. Go with him to the hospital if you can.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Magdalena.
Nurse -> We'll call the hospital. Take care of each other.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Magnolia Home Health, this is Teodora.
Caller -> Hi, Teodora. This is Bernadette Whitcombe-Park. I'm the evening aide at Sunset Terrace Assisted Living. I'm calling about one of our residents. Albert Kessling. Or Albert Kessler. I'm checking.
Nurse -> Hi, Bernadette. Which is it?
Caller -> I wish I knew. I've been here three years and this is the first time I've had to ask.
Nurse -> It's a good thing you're asking. Go on.
Caller -> Okay. So we have two. Albert Kessler is in room twelve. Albert Kessling is in room fourteen. They're both Albert. Both ninety something. They look alike. They've been mixed up before. And I'm not sure which one is yours.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds tricky. Let me ask what you're seeing first. Then we'll sort out the name.
Caller -> Um. Let me think. I'm trying to remember.
Nurse -> Take your time, there's no rush.
Caller -> Okay. Good. He's got a wet cough. Since this afternoon. A rattly cough. Wet. And he sounds congested.
Nurse -> Did it start suddenly, or did it build over time?
Caller -> Afternoon. After lunch. He coughed through dinner. Our day aide said he'd been clearing his throat all morning.
Nurse -> So it built during the day.
Nurse -> Is he short of breath?
Caller -> A little. Not terrible. I put the oxygen clip on him. It says ninety one. Ninety one percent.
Caller -> The clip is the kind you put on the finger. It shows a number and a pulse. The pulse is steady.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> What does he usually run?
Caller -> Wait, say that again? I missed the first part.
Nurse -> Of course. Let me say it slower.
Caller -> I think ninety five or six. It's in the book. I don't have the book. It's at the desk. I'm in the room.
Nurse -> Okay. Any fever?
Caller -> I took it. It's normal. Ninety eight something. No fever. And no chest pain. He says no. He's pretty clear.
Nurse -> Is he sitting up?
Caller -> In his chair. I propped him up with pillows. He's coughing and he brings up a little white stuff. He looks tired.
Nurse -> Is he able to speak in full sentences?
Caller -> Yes. He told me his granddaughter's name and what he ate for lunch. He's clear.
Nurse -> Okay. Now, which resident is he? Albert Kessler or Albert Kessling?
Caller -> I'm in his room. The door says Kessling on the card. But the wristband says, hold on, K E S S, I can't read it. The print is tiny. I need my glasses. I left them at the desk. Hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Let me grab my glasses, one second.
Nurse -> Sure, I'll wait.
Caller -> Okay. I have them. It says K E S S L E R. Kessler. No wait. The band says Kessler. The door card says Kessling. I'm in room fourteen. That's Kessling's room. But the band says Kessler. Maybe they switched bands? Or maybe I'm in the wrong room?
Nurse -> Does the room have a bed name tag, or a personal item with his name? A photo?
Caller -> A photo on the nightstand. A man in a Navy uniform. And the name Albert on the frame.
Nurse -> Albert. That fits both.
Caller -> Ha. Yes. That doesn't help.
Nurse -> Okay, Bernadette. That's important. Let's slow down. Is there a chart nearby? A medicine sheet?
Caller -> I have the med sheet clipboard. It says Kessling on top. K E S S L I N G. Albert. And a date of birth. It's smudged. It says nineteen, I think, thirty one? Thirty seven? I can't tell. It's blurry.
Nurse -> That's fine. Don't worry about the date. We'll get it from our system.
Caller -> I'm sorry. It's the copy machine. It makes everything gray.
Nurse -> So the sheet says Kessling. The door says Kessling. The band says Kessler.
Caller -> Yes. Two of three. I think it's Kessling. I think the band got swapped. It's happened.
Nurse -> That's a safety concern in itself. Please don't give any medicine or oxygen changes based on the band. Verify by the face and the other residents' staff. Is there another aide who knows him?
Caller -> Phyllis. She's been here twenty years. She's on break. I'll get her.
Nurse -> Please do. While you do, I'm going to page the on-call clinician about the oxygen and the cough. I'll ask them to confirm which resident we have.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. That's good. Thank you. Phyllis! Phyllis, can you come to fourteen? I need you to ID someone.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this down as we go.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pause.
Caller -> Phyllis says, it's Kessling. She says Albert Kessling has the ring on his left hand with the blue stone. And he's got the hearing aids. Kessler doesn't. This one has the ring and hearing aids. So it's Kessling. She's sure.
Nurse -> Does Phyllis know which Albert is on our service, the one who sees our nurse on Thursdays?
Caller -> She says Kessling gets the visiting nurse. Kessler goes to the clinic.
Nurse -> That matches. Thank you, Phyllis.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring. Please fix the wristband tonight, and chart the swap.
Caller -> I will. I'll get a new band from the nurse. I'll write it all down.
Caller -> I'll also tell the day shift to put a name sticker on each door in big print.
Nurse -> That would help a lot.
Nurse -> Do you have his date of birth from a reliable source?
Caller -> The face sheet. Hold on, Phyllis has it. It says, no, it's the other resident's face sheet. I'm getting confused. I'll have to call you back with the date. The sheets are in the office and the office is locked.
Nurse -> That's okay. We'll get it from our own records. What's a good callback number?
Caller -> Five oh five, five five five, zero one two nine. That's the unit phone.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm going to send a nurse out tonight to look at him.
Caller -> Tonight. Oh thank goodness. Thank you.
Nurse -> Meanwhile, keep him sitting upright. Check his oxygen every thirty minutes and write it down. And before anyone gives him anything, check his face against his photo on the chart, not just the wristband.
Caller -> Upright. Oxygen every thirty minutes. Check the photo. Okay. I'll tell the other aides.
Nurse -> Call nine one one if his oxygen drops below eighty eight, if he's struggling to breathe, if his lips turn blue, or he becomes confused.
Caller -> Under eighty eight. Struggling. Blue lips. Confused. Nine one one. I'm writing it on the whiteboard.
Nurse -> Good. Is there oxygen available in the building?
Caller -> Yes. A concentrator in the med room. We use it for emergencies. I'll wheel it in.
Nurse -> Don't start it until the clinician says so. I'll have them call within fifteen minutes.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. What was the question?
Nurse -> I'll repeat it, no trouble.
Caller -> Okay. I won't. I'll wait for the call.
Caller -> I'm going to make him some warm tea with honey, if that's okay? His throat sounds scratchy.
Nurse -> Small sips are fine if he's sitting up and swallowing well.
Nurse -> Thank you, Bernadette. You did well to double check.
Caller -> It's scary. We had a med error last year because of exactly this. Two Alberts.
Nurse -> I'm sorry that happened. Is the facility doing anything about the name alerts?
Caller -> They put red stickers on both charts. But the stickers peel. I peeled one off just now, by accident.
Nurse -> Ha. Stickers are a common weak point, and that is a good reason to check twice.
Nurse -> It happens. That's why we double check.
Caller -> I'm going to write a note to the director. This needs to change. They should be on different floors.
Nurse -> That sounds like a good idea.
Caller -> I'll go check on him. He's coughing. Thank you.
Nurse -> Good luck. Call back if anything changes.
Caller -> Will do. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Tidewater Pediatric Home Health, this is Hortensia.
Caller -> Hi, Hortensia. It's Tobias Lindgren. I'm calling about my daughter, Saoirse Lindgren. S A O I R S E. It's Irish. It's Seer-sha. I'm doing the weekly update.
Nurse -> Hi, Tobias. Seer-sha. Beautiful name. How's she doing?
Caller -> Thank you. Everyone mispronounces it. We had a nurse who called her Sah-oh-ers for a month. Saoirse corrected her.
Nurse -> Ha. A strong-willed girl.
Caller -> She's four and a half going on forty.
Caller -> Great. She's great. She's been great all week. She's actually, I think, bored of being a medical kid. She wants to ride her scooter.
Caller -> I should say, I took the day off to do this call. I never get to just sit and talk. So if I ramble, stop me.
Nurse -> Ramble away. This is your time.
Nurse -> Ha. A good sign. Can I have her date of birth?
Caller -> July ninth, twenty twenty two. She's four and a half. She'll tell you she's four and three quarters.
Nurse -> Ha. Of course. And your best number?
Nurse -> Is it the cell number on file?
Caller -> The cell, yes. I changed carriers, but kept the number. You might have the old one.
Nurse -> Let me confirm the new one with you.
Caller -> Nine one eight, five five five, zero one one three.
Nurse -> Got it. Let's start with the breathing. Any changes?
Caller -> No changes. Her secretions are thin and white. They've been thin and white all week. We're suctioning about four times a day. The morning, noon, after nap, and bedtime. Sometimes once more if she coughs. It's easy. She hardly notices.
Nurse -> How about the sound of her breathing? Any wheeze, rattle, or noise through the tube?
Caller -> Quiet. Occasionally a little whistle when she's laughing hard. But it passes when she calms down.
Nurse -> That's normal for some kids with a tube.
Nurse -> That's great. Any fever? Any fast breathing, or color changes?
Caller -> No fever. We check her every morning. No fast breathing. Her color's good. Pink. The monitor has been quiet. A couple of false alarms from the cord, but nothing real.
Nurse -> Do you use the forehead thermometer or an under-the-arm one?
Caller -> The forehead one, because she fights the under-the-arm. She calls it the beep gun.
Nurse -> Ha. A very medical vocabulary.
Nurse -> Excellent. How about supplies? Where are you with the catheters and the spare tubes?
Caller -> I have three suction catheters left. The size ten. And one spare tube. Her size. I know we're supposed to have two. I've been meaning to call.
Nurse -> Which size is she using these days?
Caller -> A ten French. The pulmonologist said we might go down to an eight soon, as the tube gets smaller.
Nurse -> That sounds right. We'll follow his lead.
Nurse -> Right. I'll order more catheters and a spare tube. Let me put that in right now.
Caller -> Thank you. I knew you'd say that. I meant to reorder last week and then the week got away from me.
Caller -> I keep a sticky note on the cupboard that says reorder, but then I take the note off to use the cupboard and forget.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll put a reminder on our side too, to call you each month.
Caller -> That would be amazing.
Nurse -> It happens. Tobias, tell me about school. You said she started preschool?
Caller -> Yes! Two days a week. Tuesday and Thursday. Mornings. She has a nurse aide with her, a private duty aide. She sits right next to her. She loves it. She came home with a drawing. A purple horse.
Caller -> It has five legs. I asked her why. She said, he's special.
Nurse -> Ha. Of course he is.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. How did the first week go?
Caller -> The first morning she wouldn't let go of my leg. By Thursday she ran in. I cried in the car.
Nurse -> Every parent does.
Caller -> The aide texted me a photo of her at the sand table. I looked at it fifty times.
Caller -> Better than I expected. Honestly I cried more than she did. The teacher knows how to call us. She has the emergency steps on the wall. The aide knows suction and the trach changes.
Nurse -> That's what we like to hear. Does the school have a spare tube and the emergency bag?
Caller -> They do. The bag has the suction machine, the catheters, a spare tube, and the smaller size, the ambu bag. The aide checks it every morning.
Nurse -> Do they have a way to charge the machine?
Caller -> A wall outlet in the classroom. And a battery. The aide plugs it in at lunch.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Perfect. Do you have a copy of the emergency plan on the wall at home too?
Caller -> We did a fire drill at home last month, for the monitor and the oxygen and the suction. I carried her out in my arms like a football.
Nurse -> Practice is exactly right.
Caller -> The dog was very confused.
Caller -> On the fridge. And in the bag. And on the back of the front door.
Nurse -> You're very organized.
Caller -> I wish. I lose my keys daily. But Saoirse's things I never lose. It's strange. My brain just keeps hold of that.
Nurse -> That's what parents do.
Caller -> My wife is the organized one. I just do what's on the list.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good system.
Caller -> And she keeps the calendar. The appointments, the supply dates, the tube changes. I'd be lost without her.
Nurse -> Every team needs a calendar keeper.
Caller -> It is. Okay. So I had two questions. One is about swimming.
Nurse -> Before that, how's your own health? Are you sleeping?
Caller -> Better. I told you. A bit better. Five or six hours. My wife and I switch off the monitor on weekends.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Rest is part of the job.
Nurse -> Go ahead.
Caller -> Saoirse's cousins have a pool. We're invited to a party in the summer. Can she swim? Even just sit on the steps and splash? I know it's far away, but I want to know now.
Caller -> It's in Florida, a long way away. But the invitation came and I thought, I'd better ask now so I can plan.
Nurse -> That's smart planning.
Nurse -> That's a question for her pulmonologist. A tracheostomy and water need special care, and I don't want to guess. I'll message the doctor and ask.
Caller -> Please. Thank you. I assumed no. But I wanted to ask. She's been watching the neighbor kids with floaties.
Nurse -> I'll let you know what they say. What was the other question?
Caller -> The other one is about the tube. At her last visit, the doctor mentioned a different kind of tube, one without a cuff. A cuffless. Is that coming up?
Nurse -> It's something the doctors may consider as she grows. Not today's decision. The team will talk with you at the next clinic visit.
Caller -> Okay. That's what I figured. I just don't want to be surprised.
Nurse -> Surprises are the hardest part. We'll prepare you well ahead of anything that changes.
Caller -> Thank you. That really helps.
Nurse -> Fair. Tobias, a reminder about the spare tubes. Keep two spares of her size with her at all times, and one smaller size, in case the tube won't go in. Change her tube on the schedule. And keep the humidifier going.
Caller -> Two spares her size. One smaller. Change on schedule. Humidifier. Okay. We're due for a change on the twenty fourth. A week from Thursday.
Caller -> Our humidifier makes a gurgling noise. Is that normal?
Nurse -> A little gurgle is normal when the water is low. Check the water level and refill with distilled water.
Caller -> Distilled. I've been using filtered tap. I'll switch.
Nurse -> Perfect. The nurse will do it with you.
Caller -> I'll be right there. I like to watch.
Nurse -> Tobias, I also have to go over the emergency steps, because it's good practice. If the tube is blocked and suction doesn't clear it, if the tube comes out and you can't put a new one in, if she turns blue or struggles to breathe, call nine one one.
Caller -> Blocked and can't clear it. Tube out and can't replace. Blue. Struggling. Nine one one. Yes. I could say it in my sleep. I think I do.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. You know it. I'm going to schedule a nurse visit on Friday to check the tube, her skin around the stoma, and the supplies.
Caller -> Friday. Okay. After lunch is best. She naps till one.
Nurse -> Friday afternoon. I'll note it.
Caller -> Do you want me to have her ready? Awake? Or is a nap okay?
Nurse -> A nap is fine. The nurse can start with the supplies check while she sleeps.
Caller -> Perfect. That works.
Caller -> Is it all right if my wife joins? She works from home on Fridays and she would love to meet the nurse.
Nurse -> Of course. The more family at the visit the better.
Caller -> Great. Hortensia, can I tell you something?
Caller -> It might be silly. But after all this I've started a little blog for other parents of kids with trachs. Nothing fancy. I post what works.
Nurse -> That's generous. Parents learn so much from each other.
Caller -> I've had messages from three families already. One from Canada.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> I don't tell this to many people. I used to be so scared. In the beginning. Every night I'd stand in her doorway and just listen to the monitor. I didn't sleep for months. And now, now I sleep. I'm still a little scared. But I sleep.
Nurse -> A little scared is healthy. It keeps you careful.
Caller -> That's what my wife says. She says the day I stop being scared is the day I need to call you.
Nurse -> Ha. She's wise.
Nurse -> That's a huge change. You've learned so much.
Caller -> I never thought I'd be able to do a trach change. My hands shook the first time. Now I could do it in the dark.
Nurse -> Which, I hope, you never have to.
Caller -> Ha. Knock on wood. But yes, I could.
Caller -> I really have. And she's so brave. She tells the other kids, this is my special straw. She calls the trach her special straw.
Nurse -> Oh, I love that.
Caller -> Yeah. The teacher put it on the wall. Saoirse's special straw.
Nurse -> She sounds like a wonderful kid.
Caller -> She told her teacher that her trach is for breathing and for talking to dolphins. I don't know where she got the dolphins.
Nurse -> Ha. Imagination.
Caller -> I love it.
Caller -> She's the best. Okay. I'll let you go.
Caller -> Oh, one thing, sorry. Her little brother is coming in a few months. Is there anything we should plan, like with the tube and a newborn in the house?
Nurse -> That's wonderful news. Congratulations. Bring it up with the team at the next clinic visit, and think about hand hygiene, space, and who can help.
Caller -> Thank you. I'm excited and terrified.
Nurse -> Both are normal.
Nurse -> Call us any time with questions about the tube, school, or the supplies.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Hortensia. Have a good weekend.
Nurse -> You too, Tobias. Bye.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Harborlight Pediatric Home Care, this is Ottilie.
Caller -> Ottilie, hi, it's Camille Winterbourne. My baby is Odessa Winterbourne. I think I gave her too much Tylenol. I mixed up the bottles. I'm freaking out.
Nurse -> Okay, Camille. Take a breath. I'm going to help you. Is Odessa awake and breathing okay?
Caller -> I'm sorry. I don't want to waste your time. I'm not making sense.
Nurse -> You're making perfect sense. Keep going.
Caller -> She's awake. She's fussy. She's in my arms. She's breathing normally. She looks fine. I'm the one who isn't fine.
Nurse -> That's okay. Tell me exactly what happened. Slowly. What did you give her?
Caller -> She had a fever. A hundred and one point two. And she's teething. She's been up since midnight crying. I went to give her the Tylenol. We have two bottles. The infant drops and the children's syrup. They're both in the cabinet. In the dark I grabbed the infant drops, and I used the syringe from the children's syrup. And I gave her five milliliters. A full five.
Nurse -> Okay. Five milliliters of the infant drops, the concentrated ones. Is that correct?
Caller -> Yes. The infant drops. The little bottle. It says eighty milligrams per point eight milliliter. And I gave her five milliliters. I only realized when I read the bottle after. The dose for her is point eight. I just, I used the wrong syringe.
Nurse -> Okay. I understand. When did you give it?
Caller -> Twenty minutes ago. Two forty. It's three now. Almost.
Nurse -> Did she spit any of it out?
Caller -> A little dribbled down her chin. Maybe a milliliter. Not much.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll assume she got most of it.
Nurse -> Okay. How much does Odessa weigh?
Caller -> Seventeen pounds. We weighed her at the pediatrician last Tuesday. Seventeen pounds even.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. I'm going to explain what this means. The concentrated drops are much stronger than the children's syrup. Five milliliters of the drops is about four hundred milligrams. For a baby her size, a safe dose is much less than that. So she needs to be seen right away.
Caller -> Oh my God. Oh my God. She's going to die. I killed my baby.
Nurse -> Camille, stay with me. I'm right here.
Caller -> I'm sorry. I'm here. I'm here.
Nurse -> Camille, listen to me. She is not going to die. We caught this early. Acetaminophen overdose can be treated, and the sooner she's seen, the better. That's why I'm telling you what to do now. Okay?
Caller -> Okay. Okay. What do I do?
Nurse -> First, don't give her any more acetaminophen, or any cold or fever medicine, tonight. Second, call poison control now. The number is one eight hundred, two two two, one two two two. They'll tell you what to do and confirm. Third, take her to the emergency room. Bring both bottles and the syringe.
Caller -> No more medicine. Poison control. The emergency room. Both bottles and the syringe. Okay. I'm writing it. My hands are shaking.
Nurse -> I'm going to stay on the line while you write. Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. One eight hundred two two two one two two two. Is that right?
Nurse -> That's right. Now, is there another adult at home who can drive you?
Caller -> My husband. He's upstairs. He's asleep. I'll wake him. Dom! Dom! Wake up! We have to go to the hospital!
Caller -> He's coming. He's in his boxers. He's getting the car.
Nurse -> Good. Tell him the car seat and the bottles.
Nurse -> Good. Is Odessa vomiting? Is she unusually sleepy? Is her color okay?
Caller -> No. No vomiting. She's alert. She's looking at me. She's grabbing my hair. Her color's normal. A little flushed from crying.
Nurse -> Good. That's a good sign. Her fussiness?
Caller -> She's been fussy since midnight. It's the teeth. Her gums are red and swollen. She's been chewing on everything.
Nurse -> Okay. Camille, I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, and ask them to call the emergency room so they're expecting you.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you. Please.
Nurse -> Can I have her date of birth?
Caller -> May fourteenth, twenty twenty six. She's seven months.
Nurse -> And the best number for you?
Caller -> Three one two, five five five, zero one six one. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Does your phone have good battery? Is it charging?
Caller -> Sixty percent. I'll plug it in the car.
Nurse -> Got it. I'd like you to leave for the hospital now. Don't wait for poison control to call you back. You can call them from the car.
Caller -> Okay. Dom is up. He's getting the car seat. I'm putting on my shoes. Odessa, baby, we're going for a ride.
Nurse -> Good. Keep her in the car seat. Don't give her anything by mouth. If she vomits, turn her on her side. If she vomits repeatedly, gets very sleepy or hard to wake, has trouble breathing, or turns yellow, pull over and call nine one one.
Caller -> Should I sit in the back with her?
Nurse -> Yes. One adult in the back watching her face the whole way.
Caller -> I'll sit with her. Dom will drive carefully.
Caller -> Vomiting. Sleepy. Breathing. Yellow. Nine one one. Okay. I have my phone.
Nurse -> I'll call you back within fifteen minutes to see where you are and what the emergency room says.
Caller -> Fifteen minutes. Okay. Please do.
Nurse -> Camille, you caught this quickly. Your quick call is what matters.
Caller -> I'm so stupid. I do this for a living. I'm a dental hygienist. I read labels all day.
Nurse -> This isn't about being stupid. It's three in the morning and you were exhausted. It happens in the best families.
Caller -> I feel awful. She trusts me.
Nurse -> She does, and that won't change. She'll just remember snuggles and a fun car ride.
Caller -> I hope so.
Nurse -> She does. And you're doing exactly what she needs. After this, we'll talk about how to prevent it.
Caller -> What should we do? To prevent it?
Nurse -> Keep only one concentration in the house. Write the dose on the bottle with a marker. And always use the syringe that came with the bottle.
Caller -> One bottle. Dose on it. Its own syringe. Okay. I'll throw out the syrup.
Nurse -> Bring it to the hospital with you, so they can see it. Don't throw it away yet.
Caller -> Right. I'll take it. We're in the car. Dom's driving. The seat is buckled.
Nurse -> Good. Call poison control now.
Caller -> I'm dialing. It's ringing. Hello? I have to go. Thank you, Ottilie.
Nurse -> Go. I'll call you back.
Caller -> Bye.
